requests.title: Founding of the California–Hawaii Confederation in 1856
requirements: Pacifica is declared in Honolulu on 31 July 1856, Lā Hoʻihoʻi Ea, as a confederation of the independent Republic of California and Hawaiian Kingdom.
Kamehameha IV, Kaiulani as Kuhina Nui, Robert Wyllie, California President Vallejo and First Minister Elias are principal signatories; ratifications by both countries take effect by November 1856.

Shared defense, navy, customs union, gold currency and foreign relations coexist with member-state domestic sovereignty; an elected Confederal Assembly and state-delegation Council coexist. The Council elects Elias Chancellor after ratification. English is the common working language; California retains English–Spanish guarantees and Hawaii its language and domestic institutions. CR-021 fixes Monterey as the common seat through 1885, no common head of state, initial property-holding male Assembly franchise, member residual powers and three-language confederal publication.

Article XIV allows a one-year Protectorship during war or grave danger by two-thirds Council vote and institutional assent from both member governments; renewal requires both member legislatures. The elected Assembly receives notice and can revoke emergency measures. No exclusive personal Kuhina Nui countersignature is required.
Elias and Kaiulani marry in February 1857 after the treaty is in force, so marriage is not the price of union.

requests.title: American Civil War, Northwestern expansion and continental settlement; Vance, Sherman, Ericsson and Turner
requirements: Follow consolidated CR-013 revision 3: retain all thirty stable questions, distinguish approved directions from open implementation, and apply CR-014 precedence to origins and constitutional machinery.
Use the Hawaiian packet crisis, Kaiulani's independent demand for protection and limited authorization, and Thorne's subsequent expansion of the war; no automatic emergency annexation.
Marcus commands the Northwestern expedition, owns both Columbia successes and the Townsend reverse, contains federal reinforcements and later transfers field command before a small eastern mission.

Sherman remains in California, chooses Pacifican allegiance before 1861, performs institutional military service, criticizes expanding commitments and refuses a Confederate military assignment. Historical Union field roles are superseded.

Introduce CT-LOGAN-TURNER as a Kentucky-born boy who migrates as an adolescent and becomes a Californian naval engineer, with New Orleans success, reciprocal professional development with Marcus, costly loss at Vicksburg and potential later business influence.

Farragut's initial New Orleans attempt fails with limited Pacifican technical and financial assistance; Grant captures Vicksburg after an authorized costly withdrawal preserves much of the Confederate mobile army. New Orleans and Port Hudson remain Confederate through 1863.
Confederate commanders retain command; Pacifica does not send a large field army into Tennessee. Retain competent Union opposition and independent Indigenous and worker agency.

Distinguish occupation, peace recognition, provisional association and later accession; the Northern and Confederate republics survive. CR-015 now governs the 1865 peace framework, 1867 ratification and approved interior line; exact instruments, surveys and Northwestern membership stages remain qualified.
Update the character bible and registry together, preserve legacy profiles/crosswalk and Marcus generational distinctions, and synchronize relevant storyline and approval-index references.

Author-approved inclusion in principle of John Ericsson, Theodore Judah, Andrew Smith Hallidie, Peter Donahue, Collis P. Huntington, Charles Crocker, William Chapman Ralston, William Kelly, Alexander Lyman Holley and Yung Wing in Pacifica's developing technical-commercial network. Ericsson supplies a central naval-engineering connection. Cumulative and compounding effects of building, prototyping, innovation, investment and training are a major cause of Pacifica's rise; establish the network before the Civil War and carry its effects into later decades.

Ericsson comes west around 1855 on an initially commercial, paid experimental assignment through Marcus's procurement network; Thorne supports workshops, commercial rights and measured trials. Sustained commitment develops around 1856–1858; existing American and Delamater ties persist. Exact dates and contracts are provisional.

Develop prewar propulsion, pumps, testing and skilled teams, followed by a working 1859–1860 armored-harbor-defense programme. Ericsson mentors adolescent immigrant Logan Turner, with productive friction over ideal design versus operating conditions. Donahue apprenticeship is a working route. Logan leaves for the eastern mission in 1861 before the Columbia ship fights.

An Ericsson turret ship helps defeat a Union attempt to recover the lower Columbia in 1862 after the conventional 1861 conquest. Manufacture/procure difficult components in California and assemble at a protected lower-river yard as the working deployment solution, subject to capacity audit. Preserve mechanical limits, combined arms, Union survival and the earlier Townsend defeat.

No timely historical Monitor intervention at Hampton Roads: greater Confederate success, with Minnesota's loss the working additional outcome. Virginia retains draft, machinery and base constraints. Union alternative designs and the Pook–Eads western ironclads survive; revise availability and schedules, not all Union naval competence.

New Orleans failure remains principally a locally earned defense against Farragut's wooden fleet: Turner applies Ericsson training to practical repairs, gun handling and coordination; Louisiana placement/mountings plus obstruction and concentrated fire form the working mechanism. No perfected propulsion or Pacifican battle fleet. Atlantic alarm and Northwest diversion affect resources without retrospectively removing ships already in the Gulf.

Delay sufficient Union armored support at Mobile beyond the 1864 election on the working chronology, denying a timely reassuring victory. Rebuild Gulf logistics around surviving Confederate New Orleans. Drewry's Bluff, Charleston and Wassaw Sound require reassessment, not automatic additional Confederate wins.

Organize industrial contributions through three author-approved connected undertakings: (1) Donahue manufacturing and Huntington procurement help get Ericsson's Columbia vessel into service; (2) Ralston finance and Crocker transport sustain and consolidate wartime gains; (3) Kelly experiments, Holley plant engineering and Hallidie material handling contribute to postwar industrial growth. Their exact projects, dates, contracts and prominence remain open.

Develop complementary capacity and independent private interests: prewar imports become wartime assets; finance bridges timing gaps without equating private banks with public gold; short transport works precede larger postwar projects. Hallidie may also aid wartime supply handling, and Holley may assess armor/manufacturing. Specific rescue advances, crossings and shipments remain possible incidents, not fixed events.

Keep metallurgy gradual and collaborative, requiring outside inventions/licensing, appropriate raw materials, fuel, machinery and workers. No automatic modern steel armor in 1862, completed mountain railway, moved 1873 cable railway, early-war Bank of California, guaranteed bank rescue or automatic territorial accession. Preserve Chinese and other workers' agency and partners' sovereignty.

Integrate the gold-finance thread: independent California increasingly invests its own public revenues/reserves and private capital in Pacifican capacity before the war; war disrupts dependable Northern access to bullion and Pacifican credit. International gold trade and Northern taxation, bonds and paper money remain possible. Coin obligations, overseas settlement, borrowing and confidence make reduced access a compounding war burden, not a sole automatic cause of defeat. Exact policies, flows and causal weight remain open to audit.

requests.title: Mountain Elias, Kentucky Logan, bilingual republic and productive constitutional concentration
requirements: Elias has a Rocky Mountain upbringing, developed in the southern Rockies/Taos trading world. Retain c.1824 birth, French veteran education, geological curiosity, pastor incident, 1837 family dispossession, 1840 Texas witness, 1841–1842 captivity with Caleb and 1844 California arrival as far as compatible. Exact birthplace and migration remain open.

Logan is the boy from a Kentucky holler, born approximately 1838–1840, who reaches California as an adolescent and develops through Carquinez apprenticeship and technical instruction. Retain his New Orleans–Vicksburg arc, Marcus relationship and open commercial future; do not transfer Elias's whole childhood to him.

California is founded through an explicit Californio–Anglophone constitutional bargain in 1845–1846, with English and Spanish public standing, religious liberty, civil citizenship and recognizable procedural protections. Later common-law courts and commercial practice retain vested rights and selected Mexican rules; Indigenous claims require their own negotiation.
English is the confederal working language; California retains English–Spanish guarantees and Hawaii retains Hawaiian-language government and domestic institutions.

Legal protections and opportunities produce a real capabilities influx. Public procurement, education, infrastructure guarantees and professional careers make expanding capabilities increasingly dependent on the administration, creating a constituency for Elias's continued authority.

An elected Confederal Assembly coexists with the member-state Council. Article XIV authorizes a one-year emergency Protectorate with institutional state assent, notice and Assembly revocation; renewal requires both member legislatures. Initial powers do not amend constitutions or annex territory.

A separate dissolution power allows the Protector with cabinet responsibility to dissolve the elected Assembly, with elections within sixty days and only once for the same cause. State institutions and Council continue. Dissolution does not reverse an enacted revocation.

Constitutional amendment requires two-thirds approval in both confederal chambers and ratification by both founding states. During the working 1864–1865 consolidation, dissolution/election and negotiated enabling legislation authorize cabinet laws departing from specified constitutional provisions, with formal institutions and Hawaiian protected provisions preserved; CR-021 fixes the life Providentorship and the delegation’s lapse in 1887.

Elias controls ministerial appointment/dismissal, legislative agenda and senior appointments, turning delegated cabinet authority into personal predominance. Ordinary private-law protections continue beside expanding security/reconstruction exceptions. Some people identify the danger accurately; others underestimate, accept or benefit from it.

Kaiulani remains Kuhina Nui from 1855, an explicit divergence from Victoria Kamāmalu. She has Hawaiian co-executive/regency standing, no personal Article XIV veto. Washoe restraint is a coalition victory; packet-crisis support and enabling-law negotiation establish agency and complicity.

Lot does not abolish the Kuhina Nui in this timeline. He bargains for kingship, co-executive, local institutions and revenues in the enabling settlement. Formal preservation of Hawaiian institutions coexists with growing confederal encroachment and the disputed 1874 incorporation.

Use Weimar Articles 48 and 25 and enabling legislation as comparative structural models, not texts known to nineteenth-century characters. Explain law through its effects on recruitment, enterprise, political choices and the concentration of power.

requirements: Lincoln loses the 1864 election; the 1865 peace framework preserves both American republics and frees Pacifica's rear. The Western treaty is ratified in 1867. McClellan's exact electoral and executive-armistice route remains PROPOSED.

The interior line follows CR-015 H5: Northwest and Great Basin, whole Arizona/Utah/Nevada/Idaho/New Mexico, western Montana gold country, southwest Wyoming, Western Slope and San Luis Valley; Denver, Front Range, Leadville and Plains remain Union. Survey details remain proposed.
Deseret accedes in 1862–1863 under religious freedom for all; John D. Lee is tried and hanged in 1863. Washoe is retaken in 1863–1864 and confirmed in the 1865 settlement, ratified 1867.

Bear River occurs under a Pacifican local commander. Avoid the Navajo Long Walk by treaty. Abolish New Mexican peonage/captive trade gradually with compensation by 1866, with a short Hispano revolt. Apache and Mexican conventions remain proposed.

Pensacola, Ship Island and Key West sustain the Union Gulf fleet. No Red River campaign in 1864; no further New Orleans attack before 1870. Mobile fails in February 1865 and Farragut is killed; use broadside Union armor rather than Ericsson monitors.

Grant's 1870–1871 war fails. Pacifica sends naval/technical/financial aid, no field army and no overlapping Asian military commitment. Sherman negotiates the 1871 convention. Pacifica guarantees Confederate independence and binds it by credit, customs, rail, recruitment, Mobile and Birmingham.

The Union keeps Tennessee and Memphis–Vicksburg. Indian Territory goes Confederate except the Public Land Strip; the northern cession through the 1871 convention is a proposed mechanism. Black Union regulars and freedmen homesteads support escape networks.

Johnston follows Davis in 1868; Gordon governs 1874–1880. Greeley wins in 1872 and dies before the electors meet; Brown takes office through a disputed count and Freedom Act bargain. Union pressure produces free-womb reform 1874–1875 and final abolition 1888–1889.

Pacifica enforces the fugitive agreement until abolition. The border/travel-paper mechanism and enabling-law court override remain proposed. Compensation bonds are secured on co-administered Confederate customs; Pacifica pays guarantee calls in 1893–1895.

Rebuild Part III on friendship, limited surgical strikes and the Power Timeline cadence. Remove the Bering railway and Baikal campaign. Buy Alaska for the route in 1867; defer gold income to later discoveries. No populated mainland annexations outside North America, no Pacifican land war against Russia and no British war before 1900.

Japan's 1870–1871 alliance grants full tariff autonomy and no consular courts, with dockyard/coaling/coal/credit rights and no sovereign Pacifican base. Back the Meiji government in 1877 despite betrayal of Saigō.

The 1873 Jolo incident and one-day Manila Bay action lead to the 1876 sale including Marianas, Carolines and Palau. CR-021 fixes a Philippine Crown dependency with council, courts, organic act, language rights and 1890s reforms; Madrid loan and unprovided estate/Moro details retain qualifications.

Marcus Vance I dies at Vladivostok in February 1878. CR-016 later transfers the active Polytechnic role to an unrelated commander, Rafael Soberanes, whose name, 1847 Monterey birth and Carquinez seat are settled by CR-021; the former Marcus II parentage/age becomes retired provenance. Proposed later campaigns remain under review.

China receives technology in Chinese ownership, education, protection and no missionaries. The Customs Inspectorate passes to Pacifican leadership in 1885; Edmund Fong Kai-ming, born San Francisco 1859 to a Taishan merchant family, serves in customs from 1878 and faces the 1894 loyalty crisis. Appointment, agency and tax mechanics remain proposed.
Port Hamilton is a diplomatic near-war in 1885–1887. Korea remains independent and neutral under later guarantees; Pacifica does not annex it.

Kaiulani backs Japan short of combat in 1894, then brokers an October–November armistice. No Liaodong cession, Port Arthur massacre or Triple Intervention. Formosa stays Chinese with Pacifican revenue administration of camphor, coal and customs paying Japan; acknowledge the prize tension.

In the Primorye war Japan fights on land, Pacifica holds the sea and lends, China remains benevolently neutral and France stays neutral. Japan takes Ussuri/Vladivostok/Razdolnaya and all Sakhalin; China recovers the Amur's north bank. Do not infer a northern Russian coastal cession from the broad source slogan.

Whitney wins in 1896 with a supportive House; Senate follows 1898 state elections. Fairly tried Bread March prisoners return through the 1897 treaty. Pacifica rescues Union gold in 1895; terms and amounts require modeling.

In 1899–1900 Texas, Louisiana, Arkansas and Sequoyah form the Federal Republic of the Gulf; Virginia and North Carolina return to the Union; Alabama stays in the rump with South Carolina, Georgia, Mississippi and Florida. No Confederate state is Pacifican core by 1895. CR-020 supersedes the earlier three-year test: five general measures, two parity thresholds and binding compact conditions must hold for twenty-five years; admission is outside the novel.

Independent Cuba has no foreign base and is guaranteed jointly by Pacifica, the Gulf Republic and Union; Puerto Rico goes to the Union. Tomás Estrada Palma is first president. Debt, Finlay, Maine evidence suppression and Nicaragua rights retain proposed mechanics.

Extend women/family migration into the interior with Chinese, Japanese and Philippine partners. Forbid racial/origin marriage bans, include a 1870s test case and prosecute Rock Springs/Hells Canyon. Selective skilled/family immigration starts 1888; proclaim the Hapa ideal after the fugitive agreement lapses in 1889. Carry its tensions through later generations.

Integrate approved oil, turbine, canal-purchase and statistics/media programmes; keep electrical programme and other network moves proposed. Canal railroad/treaty 1880, French works bought 1889, opening target 1900–1902. Apply the financial ceilings only as unvalidated targets and merge the family-programme scenario into demographic audit scope.
open: All source PROPOSED components remain provisional; absence of numbered OPEN-015 items is not full implementation approval.

CR-021 resolves Philippine dependency and Formosan Revenue Convention mechanics. Remaining Gulf procedures, loan terms, territorial surveys, Northwest instruments and unprovided Fong details stay qualified.
All demographic, fiscal, industrial and force figures require the pending feasibility audit; existing workbooks are prior scenarios, not CR-015 validation.

source_items.source_text: **A1. The Union sues for peace after an electoral upset in 1864, and Pacifica must not have a hostile Union in its rear while it expands across the Pacific.** APPROVED
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**A2. Why a simple "McClellan wins" is insufficient.** PROPOSED  
McClellan's acceptance letter of 8 September 1864 made Union the condition of any peace (Hist.). Lincoln remains president until 4 March 1865 and committed in his "blind memorandum" of 23 August to win the war first (Hist.). A peace treaty needs two-thirds of the Senate, which state legislatures keep Republican (Hist.). The upset therefore needs three layers: a summer of collapse, an armistice that needs no Senate vote, and lasting structural reasons for Union restraint.
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**A3. Sequence, 1864–65.** PROPOSED

| When | What happens | Label |
|---|---|---|
| May–Jul 1864 | Grant's Overland Campaign costs about 55,000 men; Early's raid reaches Fort Stevens; gold peaks at 285 on 11 July. | Hist. |
| Summer 1864 | Without Sherman (Pacifican, canon), the western armies fall to Thomas or McPherson and advance more slowly. Davis does not replace Johnston with Hood (historically 17 July); Johnston's defense holds Atlanta into November. | Hist. → PROPOSED |
| Aug 1864 | Blind memorandum (23 Aug). Chicago convention nominates McClellan on a peace plank. Mobile delayed past the election (canon). | Hist.; canon |
| 8 Sep 1864 | McClellan's acceptance letter puts Union first. He is a Union man, not a peace man. | Hist. |
| 11 Oct 1864 | Democrats carry the Pennsylvania, Ohio and Indiana state elections. | Hist. (date) → PROPOSED |
| 8 Nov 1864 | McClellan wins. Lincoln historically carried New York by about 7,000 votes and Pennsylvania by about 20,000; a swing of a few points across the Lower North suffices. The soldiers' vote stays with Lincoln; the upset is civilian. | PROPOSED |
| Winter 1864–65 | Lincoln's last pushes at Petersburg and Mobile Bay fail (F2). The Thirteenth Amendment fails in the lame-duck House. The Hampton Roads conference (3 Feb 1865) breaks down over Confederate independence, showing Northern voters that peace means separation. | Hist. anchors → PROPOSED |
| Mar–Jun 1865 | McClellan takes office and signs armistice conventions with Richmond and with Pacifica as executive acts. The war never resumes. | PROPOSED |

source_items.source_text: **A4. Narrative mirror.** Elias's dissolution election (§12) and Lincoln's defeat fall in the same winter: one democracy rewards continuity, the other punishes exhaustion. PROPOSED
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text: **A5. Negotiating channel.** Sherman, Pacifica's Inspector-General and the advocate of modest terms, has a brother, John Sherman, sitting as Republican senator for Ohio (Hist.), in the body that must ratify the treaty. PROPOSED
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**A6. Settlement terms with the Union.** PROPOSED
- **Puget Sound.** The surviving federal enclave from §10 is evacuated by treaty, and the Union leaves the Pacific coast entirely. This is the indispensable term: without it the Union keeps a Pacific naval base, Russia sells Alaska to Washington, and a Union squadron sits on the flank of Part III.
- **The conqueror pays.** Pacifica pays in gold for its Western gains ($40 million as a vendor credit paid in instalments to 1872, which keeps the early budget tight), following the 1848 precedent in which the victorious United States paid Mexico $15 million. It adds a gold loan to the Union Treasury toward resumption of specie payments. The McClellan government can call the outcome a sale; the Eastern financiers of §13 become partners; Elias, dispossessed by creditors in 1837, becomes the creditor of the United States. Seeds the "creditor empire" of Part VI.
- **Take less than you hold.** Pacifica keeps everything draining to the Pacific or into the Great Basin, plus New Mexico, the Missouri headwaters gold country and South Pass; the line is set out in H5. APPROVED (line) It leaves Colorado's Front Range, Denver and the Great Plains to the Union. The Plains remain a moat: a thousand miles with no Union railway to anything Pacifican worth reaching (the Kansas Pacific reached Denver only in 1870, Hist.). Denver becomes the Union's only mountain city, on the border.
- **Ratification of the line.** The Senate cedes Mormon country, Hispano country and mining camps settled from California and Oregon. Losing Utah is close to welcome: the 1856 Republican platform condemned polygamy as one of the "twin relics of barbarism" (Hist.). Colorado, whose volunteers won at Glorieta, stays in the Union, which removes the hardest cession. The price is the Power Timeline's $40 million vendor credit; the feasibility audit tests it against the Montana and Idaho goldfields.
- **Ratification in 1867.** The Senate ratifies the treaty in 1867, alongside Pacifica's purchase of Alaska, so the West is settled before Grant's 1868 campaign and his target stays Richmond. APPROVED
- **Split recognition.** The Senate ratifies the Pacifica treaty (distant, paid for, Oregon's politics favorable). Confederate independence is recognized only by the executive, by McClellan receiving a Confederate envoy. The Senate never ratifies surrender of the claim to the South. The Union accepts losing the far West but never the South, so its grievance points at Richmond, with a moral cause attached: four million people remain enslaved there.
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**A7. Why the Union stays out of Pacifica's rear.** PROPOSED  
Because §12 keeps the Union's constitution, army and industry intact, restraint rests on money, geography, politics and distraction rather than collapse.
- *Capacity:* war debt (historically about $2.7 billion) without Southern trade or Western bullion; demobilization (historically the army fell to about 54,000 authorized men by 1866 and the navy was largely laid up even after victory); no Pacific port; no transcontinental line to build.
- *Will:* Democratic government 1865–69; a New York lobby profiting from Pacific transit and Pacifican loans; family ties to Pacifica's large American-born population.
- *Attention:* the unresolved claim on the South (border states, Mississippi navigation, fugitive slaves, freedmen in Union-held Louisiana and Tennessee); the Plains wars, which stay with the Union because the Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho live east of the 1865 line (Sand Creek 1864, Red Cloud's War 1866–68, the Bozeman Trail, Hist.; Montana is supplied from the west, so Pacifica has no use for the Bozeman Trail; a darker option is Pacifican rifles reaching the Lakota through Montana traders); Anglo-American quarrels (Fenian raids 1866–71, Hist.; Alabama claims left open because Britain recognized the Confederacy).
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**A8. Plot clocks.** PROPOSED
- 1867, Alaska: with no Pacific port and a hostile Senate the Union cannot bid.
- 1868: a revanchist Republican, plausibly Grant, wins on restoring the Union. His target is Richmond. Russia, historically the Union's friend, courts Washington.
- War with Britain comes only after 1900, under the regency (G9); Britain's acceptance of Pacifica's position is fixed first, in the 1899–1900 settlement during the Boer War (J2). Union Anglophobia still points the Union at Canada rather than Pacifica; Elias can encourage this.
- The real long-term threat is a North–South reconciliation. It comes only in part: Virginia and North Carolina return to the Union in 1898–99, while the Gulf Republic moves into Pacifica's orbit (E11).
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text: **A9. Postwar continental course.** The Confederacy slides into dependence on Pacifican credit and protection first. This is the route to the "contested local compacts" of §12 and to the "American military aristocrats" behind Silas in 1887. Developed in section E. APPROVED
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**B0. Part III extends from 1865–70 to roughly 1865–85 and interleaves with the Hawaiian story of Part IV.** The previous pace was too fast and its objectives were not logical. APPROVED (pace and logic); PROPOSED (dates) The full cadence to 1900, with its cheap network moves between commitments, is the Power Timeline's; this table lists the commitments CR-015 decides.

| Years | Move | Method | What it gives the next move | Label |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1865–68 | Consolidation and the ocean road: Alaska, Midway, Baja; talent from two armies; Juárez backed | Purchase, diplomacy, recruitment | Coaling stations, the northern route to Japan, a safe southern flank | PROPOSED |
| 1868–72 | Japan's civil war; alliance; Pacifican military missions | Friendship | Partner, coal, dockyard; Japan built on Pacifican standards | APPROVED (treaty terms); PROPOSED |
| 1868–72 | China: equal footing, technology, education | Friendship | Trust; a trained Chinese elite | PROPOSED |
| 1870–71 | Grant's war | Squadron, mines, credit | The guaranteed Confederacy; no Asian commitment overlaps it | APPROVED |
| 1872–76 | Philippines, Marianas, Carolines and Palau | One surgical strike, a loan, then purchase | Manila; Guam; the island line to Palau | APPROVED (Carolines and Palau; status); PROPOSED |
| 1874 | Hawaii incorporated; the massacre | Force against a friend | The central base | PROPOSED |
| 1874–79 | Formosa expedition support; Ryukyu mediation | Brokerage | Standing in Tokyo and Beijing | PROPOSED |
| 1876–80 | Korea's first Western treaty; famine relief for North China | Diplomacy through Li Hongzhang; wheat | Korea's door; goodwill at court | PROPOSED |
| 1878 | Vladivostok; southern Sakhalin to Japan | Surgical strike with Japan | Russia's Pacific ambitions deferred | PROPOSED |
| 1884–87 | Keelung; the Customs Inspectorate; the Carolines; Port Hamilton | Friendship, one surgical strike, arbitration | Formosa's coal; China's trade revenue; guarantor of Korea | PROPOSED |
| 1880–89 | Panama: transit treaty and railroad; the French works bought in 1889 | Patience, then purchase | The canal, opening about 1900–02 | APPROVED |
| 1894 | Sino-Japanese War | Support for Japan short of war; a brokered armistice | Arbiter of both; no Liaodong, no Triple Intervention | APPROVED |
| 1897–99 | The Primorye war | Japan fights; Pacifica holds the sea and lends | Russia off the Pacific coast | APPROVED |

source_items.source_text:
**B1. Consolidation and the ocean road (1865–68).** No wars. Long-service naval core, debt refinanced, Northwest integrated. PROPOSED
- State-subsidized transpacific steam line San Francisco–Honolulu–Yokohama–Hong Kong (Pacific Mail opened this route in January 1867, Hist.).
- Midway claimed in 1867 (claimed by the US that year, Hist.).
- Alaska bought in 1867 for the route, not for gold: the great-circle route from San Francisco to Yokohama runs along the Aleutians, and purchase denies the territory to Britain. Russia sells because the Union has no Pacific port and no money (A8).
- Yukon gold in 1867 is removed as premature (Juneau 1880, Klondike 1896, Hist.).
- The Bering project is reduced to Perry Collins's Russian–American telegraph, under construction 1865–67 and abandoned after the Atlantic cable (Hist.).
- *Talent from two armies (1865–67).* Thousands of Confederates emigrated to Brazil and Mexico, and about fifty American officers served the Khedive from 1869 (Hist.). Pacifica offers land, rank and contracts to naval officers, ironclad builders and railway and West Point engineers from both sides, and keeps the Sierra railway's Chinese crews employed on interior lines. Risk: divided loyalties and Union anger. PROPOSED (Power Timeline)
- *Mexico (1865–67).* Arms and credit for Juárez through Sonora as France withdraws (Maximilian is shot in June 1867, Hist.). In return: the purchase of Baja California in 1867, a railway concession to Guaymas with a free port, and a joint Apache convention ending Mexico's scalp bounties (H6). Sonora is not annexed (G9). PROPOSED; price to the feasibility audit
- *The mail line* coals at Honolulu, Midway and Hakodate, so passengers, mail and silks keep moving through San Francisco after Suez opens in November 1869 (Hist.). PROPOSED
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**B2. Japan (1868–72).** The 1868 "fleet before Edo" guarantees the transition rather than coercing a collapsing shogunate. PROPOSED
- Edo surrenders without battle in May 1868 through Saigō Takamori and Katsu Kaishū (Hist.). Katsu captained the *Kanrin Maru* on its 1860 San Francisco visit, so Pacifica knows both men; its fleet underwrites the deal.
- Enomoto's Hakodate regime falls in 1869 (Hist.). The decisive ironclad *Kōtetsu*, historically the ex-CSS *Stonewall*, is supplied through Pacifica.
- Kuroda Kiyotaka heads the Hokkaido Development Commission and hires foreign advisers from 1871 (Hist.); here they are Pacifican. Founding figure of the later Kuroda line; brings Japan's northern frontier, and Russia, into the story.
- 1870–72: with France beaten by Prussia, Pacifica replaces the French army mission and pre-empts Britain's 1873 naval mission; Japanese officers train in Pacifica and Japanese yards build to Pacifican designs and calibres. The Iwakura Mission makes its first landfall at San Francisco in January 1872 (Hist.). Japan learns well, and the Kuroda faction's later resentment starts here. PROPOSED (Power Timeline)
- 1870–71 alliance treaty: Pacifica offers what Britain and France withheld until 1911, an equal treaty with Japanese tariff autonomy and no consular courts, in return for a naval alliance, dockyard rights at Yokosuka, a coaling lease at Hakodate, Takashima coal and Japan's first foreign loan (raised in London in 1870, Hist.). Japan grants full tariff autonomy to itself and no sovereign base to Pacifica: the equal treaty is Pacifica's capital in Tokyo, and the absence of a base keeps Japan a partner, not a client. APPROVED (terms)
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**B3. Spain (1872–76).** PROPOSED
- Spain deposes its queen (1868), becomes a republic (1873) and fights the Carlists (1872–76) and Cuban insurgents (1868–78) (Hist.). Filipino reformers are alienated after the 1872 Cavite mutiny and executions (Hist.).
- Pretext: Spain's 1870s Sulu blockade, which historically seized British and German traders, seizes a Pacifican schooner off Jolo in 1873. APPROVED
- Elias offers to buy; Madrid refuses on grounds of honor. A one-day naval action at Manila Bay during Spain's cantonal revolt (summer 1873, Hist.) makes the money acceptable. APPROVED There are no ground operations before the purchase; instead a Pacifican loan to Madrid in 1874–75 for the Carlist war is secured on the islands. PROPOSED (Power Timeline)
- The purchase of 1876 includes the Marianas, the Carolines and Palau, which Spain barely holds and Germany will contest in 1885 (B7). APPROVED The reformers Spain deported to Guam in 1872 are freed when the Marianas change hands. PROPOSED Price to the feasibility audit.
- *Status.* The Philippines become a separate crown or protectorate with its own assembly, not an incorporated territory. APPROVED Friar estates are bought out and a treaty is signed with the Moro sultanates. PROPOSED Autonomy is given in that form rather than delayed; the remaining insurgency, smaller than in §15, ebbs in the 1880s, and its record must be clean by 1890 (J3). The risk stands: if the assembly stays hollow, the reckoning comes in the 1890s, as it did for Spain.
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text: **B4. Hawaii (1874), linked to B3.** Lot dies in December 1872, Lunalilo in February 1874; the following election (Kalākaua against Emma) ended historically in a riot at the Honolulu courthouse (Hist.). The fleet is assembling for Manila and the admirals insist that Pearl Harbor cannot depend on Hawaiian consent. The massacre of §17 gains a strategic cause; it is the one place the friendship doctrine fails, and it fails with the oldest friend. PROPOSED
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**B5. Formosa and Ryukyu (1874–79).** PROPOSED
- After the Mudan incident (1871), Japan's 1874 expedition to southern Formosa obtains an indemnity from China (Hist.). Pacifica supplies the shipping that Britain and the US historically refused Japan.
- Japan's Ryukyu claim is confirmed (annexed 1879, Hist.). Elias mediates the Ryukyu dispute between Tokyo and Beijing, the role Ulysses Grant played in 1879 (Hist.), formally in 1879: Japan keeps Ryukyu, and China receives trade guarantees backed by Pacifica. Both capitals accept Pacifica as the fair broker of East Asia.
- 1877: in the Satsuma Rebellion (Hist.) Pacifica backs the Meiji state against Saigō and its oldest Japanese friends, who are betrayed. Kuroda is on the government side. APPROVED
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**B6. Russia, limited and maritime (1877–78).** PROPOSED
- Russia's Pacific position is weak until the Trans-Siberian railway (begun 1891, Hist.). Russia fights Turkey from April 1877 to March 1878; in February 1878 a British fleet passes the Dardanelles (Hist.). London tacitly welcomes a strike.
- Pacifica and Japan strike Vladivostok, the Russian Pacific base since 1871–72 (Hist.), in one concentrated action in February 1878; there is no Siberian land army. Southern Sakhalin, traded to Russia in 1875 (Hist.), is restored to Japan; all of Sakhalin follows in 1899 (D7). The settlement is folded into the Congress of Berlin (June–July 1878), and Britain owes Pacifica its recognition of the Philippine purchase. PROPOSED
- Russia is checked, not destroyed. Its Pacific ambitions slip by a decade; the Trans-Siberian is begun at Vladivostok in May 1891, as in history, and reaches the Pacific only about 1903–04 (Hist.). The years 1873–78 now hold four operations, so nothing else military is added before 1880.
- Marcus Vance I dies in a winter action at Vladivostok in February 1878, keeping the ice and burning-fuel imagery of the former §16. As Part III's only clash with Russia, his death gives the episode its cost and passes command to the next generation. APPROVED
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**B7. Korea, Formosa's coal, the Customs and the Carolines (1876–87).** PROPOSED
- Japan opens Korea at Ganghwa in 1876 (Hist.). Pacifica signs Korea's first Western treaty around 1878–80, through Li Hongzhang's mediation and with no gunboats; historically the US failed with gunboats in 1871 and signed only in 1882 (Hist. → PROPOSED).
- 1882–87: Korea becomes a neutral state under joint Chinese and Pacifican guidance, with Pacifican advisers. In the 1884 Gapsin coup (Hist.) the advisers know in advance and stand aside; its failure teaches Elias the limits of reformers and points toward the 1894 settlement (D4). APPROVED
- 1884–85: China fights France (Hist.). France holds Keelung and blockades Formosa. After the retreat from Lạng Sơn brings down Ferry's government (March 1885, Hist.), a Pacifican squadron places Keelung's coal trade under its protection and France makes peace. Surgical strike, with demonstration preferred over battle.
- Pacifica receives the Keelung coal concession as a gift, not a cession; a Chinese–Pacifican company works it and builds Liu Mingchuan's railway (Hist. → PROPOSED).
- China rebuilds the Fujian fleet, destroyed at Fuzhou in August 1884 (Hist.), in Pacifican yards on Pacifican credit; historically its battleships came from Stettin. PROPOSED
- 1885: the Customs Inspectorate passes to Pacifica (see C3).
- 1885: Germany takes the Marshalls and contests the Carolines (Hist.). The Carolines came with the 1876 sale, so Pacifica accepts papal arbitration and gives Germany trading and coaling rights, as Spain did historically. The Marshalls are left to Germany. PROPOSED
- 1885–87: Port Hamilton is a near-war that Britain loses diplomatically. APPROVED Britain leaves in 1887 against a guarantee of Korean territory by China, Russia and Pacifica, which makes Pacifica a formal guarantor of Korea without owning any of it. PROPOSED
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**C1. Friendship with China and Japan replaces the European humiliation approach, but the treaty with China is not to be made too sweet.** APPROVED

| China gets | Pacifica gets | Label |
|---|---|---|
| Technology: arsenals, shipyards, mines and railways in Chinese ownership | The standard treaty rights of the other powers (treaty ports, consular courts, fixed 5% tariff); no new humiliations, nothing given up | APPROVED (China's side); PROPOSED (Pacifica's side) |
| Education | Guaranteed emigration of Chinese labor and families, on the model of the 1868 Burlingame Treaty (Hist.); from 1888 narrowed to skilled migrants and sponsored families (I3), which Beijing feels as a broken promise | PROPOSED; APPROVED (1888 change) |
| Credit on favorable terms | Coal and mining concessions (Keelung; a share in Kaiping) | PROPOSED |
| No missionaries | Loans secured on customs revenue | APPROVED (no missionaries); PROPOSED |
| Protection and rights for Chinese Pacificans | The Customs Inspectorate from 1885 | APPROVED |
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**C2. Anchors for the friendship.** PROPOSED

| When | Anchor | Pacifican version | Label |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1865 | Yung Wing buys machinery in the US for Zeng Guofan's Jiangnan Arsenal | Bought at Carquinez, installed by Pacifican machinists | Hist. → PROPOSED |
| 1868 | The Burlingame mission and treaty | An equal-footing treaty with Pacifica, with migration clauses | Hist. → PROPOSED |
| Oct 1871 | Los Angeles Chinese massacre (about 18 killed) | Elias has the rioters tried and hanged; Beijing takes note | Hist. → PROPOSED |
| 1872–81 | Chinese Educational Mission, 120 boys sent to Connecticut and recalled in 1881, partly because the US refused them West Point and Annapolis (Hist.) | Hosted in San Francisco, with places at the naval academy; alumni become China's engineers, officers, railway builders, diplomats and customs officers. Qing conservatives may still recall it, so it must stay useful to Li Hongzhang | Hist. → PROPOSED |
| 1872–78 | China Merchants steamship company; Kaiping mines | Pacifican engineers and loans, Chinese ownership | Hist. → PROPOSED |
| 1876–79 | North China famine, roughly 9–13 million dead | California wheat through Tianjin, with Chinese Pacifican relief committees beside Li Hongzhang's officials; the goodwill opens the door to the Inspectorate | Hist. → PROPOSED |
| 1896 | Li Hongzhang's world tour; the Chinese Eastern Railway granted to Russia | Railway credit offered before he leaves, so China builds its own Manchurian line and Pacifica finances the Hankow–Canton trunk | Hist. → PROPOSED |
| 1898 | The Hundred Days' Reform crushed; Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao flee | Honolulu and San Francisco shelter reformers and revolutionaries alike, so whoever governs China after the Qing owes Pacifica | Hist. → PROPOSED |
| 1900 | The Boxer rising; the southern viceroys stay out | A contingent for the relief force, a guarantee for the southern viceroys, prompt withdrawal, and the whole indemnity turned into scholarships | Hist. → PROPOSED |
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**C3. The Customs Inspectorate.** The Inspectorate of the Chinese Maritime Customs is an important prize and must not remain in British hands, especially since Pacifica can be more evenhanded in the role. APPROVED
- *Mechanism.* In 1885 Robert Hart was appointed British minister in Peking and briefly accepted; the succession question, with Li Hongzhang backing the German Gustav Detring, was one reason he stayed (Hist.). Here Hart takes the ministership and Li's candidate is a Pacifican, as China's reward for Keelung and the famine relief, for a small agency fee. The appointment belongs to China; Britain protests but has no veto, and its later demand that the post remain British (historically 1898) comes too late. PROPOSED
- *Evenhandedness.* Multinational staff kept; Chinese promoted into senior grades (largely excluded under Hart), drawing on Educational Mission alumni; published accounts; equal duties for every flag. PROPOSED
- *Power.* The Inspector-General sees all of China's foreign trade, collects the revenue that services foreign loans and runs the lighthouses, later the post. PROPOSED
- *The man.* Edmund Fong Kai-ming (方啟明, "opening light"), born in San Francisco in 1859 to a Taishan merchant family, bilingual and a Pacifican customs officer from 1878. In 1894, when Kaiulani backs Japan, the Inspectorate becomes his personal loyalty crisis and a live test of the Hapa thread (I4); his two names carry the split inside one man. APPROVED

source_items.source_text:
**C4. Opium.** A self-imposed opium ban is not adopted without further justification. Proposed treatment: PROPOSED
- Pacifica cannot win the trade because Britain controls Indian supply, so staying out of it costs little. This is circumstance, not virtue.
- Pacifican merchants carry Turkish and Persian opium privately, as American houses did (Hist.). The state does not stop them.
- Under the 1885 additional article to the Chefoo Convention the customs collected inland opium tax together with duty (Hist.). A Pacifican Inspector-General collects it strictly, making China richer and British opium dearer.
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text: **D1. In the Sino-Japanese War of 1894, Regent Kaiulani backs Japan's case for Korean independence, then brokers the armistice.** APPROVED
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text: **D2. Rationale.** Japan is inside the empire's institutions (the Japanese naval sphere of the 1888 settlement) and is the coherent military power; the Qing court diverts naval funds from 1888 and will crush its reformers in 1898 (Hist.). Consistent with the master storyline's Japanese pillar, Fleet-General Kuroda and Lady Chiyo. PROPOSED
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text: **D3. Form.** Support short of open war, in Kaiulani's style rather than Elias's: coal, equipment, credit and diplomatic cover; no Pacifican combat. APPROVED
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**D4. The armistice and its terms (October–November 1894).** APPROVED unless marked
- *Anchor:* the Donghak rising brings Chinese and Japanese troops into Korea in mid-1894; Japan wins at Pyongyang and the Yalu in September; Cixi wants peace before her sixtieth birthday in November and China seeks mediators, while Japan fears a European intervention (Hist.).
- *Terms:* Korea independent and neutral under the guarantee of China, Japan and Pacifica, with Japanese economic predominance (the Seoul–Busan railway, mines and ports); China gives up suzerainty; a moderate indemnity; the commercial rights Japan won at Shimonoseki; no mainland territory. Pacifica guarantees the terms against any European challenge.
- *Consequences:* no Port Arthur massacre, no Liaodong cession and no Triple Intervention, so Russia loses its pretext. China is not bankrupted and Cixi stays a friend. Queen Min is not murdered and King Gojong does not flee to the Russian legation, since both followed historically from Japan's victory and Russia's rise (Hist.).
- *Money:* a smaller indemnity facility for China, still secured on the customs revenue Pacifica's Inspector-General collects. A Pacifican gold loan to Japan, held with the indemnity in San Francisco, funds Japan's move to gold in 1897, which historically rested on the indemnity kept in London. Japan's currency rests on Pacifican deposits. PROPOSED
- *Risk:* Japan's army and public feel robbed of victory, as after the 1905 peace in history. Their outlet is the Primorye war (D7).
- *Formosa.* Pacifica takes control, for its camphor, the raw material of celluloid and film, and for Keelung coal, at the least cost and friction. APPROVED (control) Form: sovereignty stays Chinese, so no port is taken from China (G9). China secures its indemnity on Formosa's revenues, and a Pacifican administration of the camphor monopoly, the Keelung coal and the island's customs, on the Inspectorate model, collects them. Japan, which has wanted Formosa since 1874, is paid from that revenue instead of receiving the island; the tension with "never take a prize from Japan" has to be played, not ignored. APPROVED (form, 18 Oct)
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text: **D5. Resonance.** In 1881 King Kalākaua proposed a Japanese prince as husband for the historical Princess Kaʻiulani, as part of a union of Asian nations (Hist.). The 1914 Thorne-Kamehameha settlement with a Japanese consort quietly fulfills it. PROPOSED (optional)
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text: **D6. No Triple Intervention.** Without a Liaodong cession, Russia, France and Germany have nothing to reverse in April 1895. The resolution of 17 October (Liaodong returned for a larger indemnity) is withdrawn (§6). Japanese resentment of a victory cut short still feeds the Kuroda faction's later demands for autonomy inside the empire. APPROVED
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**D7. The Primorye war (1897–99).** APPROVED
- *Anchor:* Germany seizes Kiaochow in November 1897 and Russia demands an ice-free port. Russia's Far East has no rail link to Europe until about 1903; the Ussuri line joins Vladivostok only to Khabarovsk, in 1897, and Vladivostok has about 29,000 people (Hist.).
- *Trigger:* Russia demands Port Arthur or a Korean harbour, against the 1887 and 1894 guarantees.
- *Conduct:* Japan fights on land in 1898–99. Pacifica holds the sea so that Russia cannot reinforce through Suez, and lends the money; China stays benevolently neutral. There is no Pacifican land army (G9).
- *Settlement:* Japan takes the Ussuri region with Vladivostok and the Razdolnaya valley, and all of Sakhalin; its economic predominance in Korea is confirmed; China recovers the Amur's north bank. Pacifica takes no port in China and declares against partition.
- *Consequences:* Russia loses its Pacific coast, the Chinese Eastern Railway loses its purpose and Kiaochow is isolated. Japan needs Pacifica's guarantee against Russian revenge indefinitely. The next test is that revenge, once the Trans-Siberian is finished about 1903–04, aimed at Manchuria and northern Korea. France stays neutral. Its 1894 alliance with Russia is aimed at Germany, and from September 1898 France is caught in the Fashoda crisis with Britain and in the Dreyfus affair (Hist.). Paris keeps lending to St Petersburg, so Japan is in effect fighting French money, and Pacifica's credit is the answer. APPROVED
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**E1. Target picture for 1895: a divided continent in which Pacifica is the only power with friends on both sides, and the arbiter between them.** APPROVED
- *The Confederacy* is independent in name and associated with Pacifica in fact. Slavery is abolished. It is bound by debt, customs co-administration, rail and careers. No Confederate state is yet a Pacifican member. Accession becomes possible only after the 1887 imperial constitution, when membership no longer carries democratic weight at the center, and the statistics bureau's thresholds decide it (J2). In 1895 the Gulf states sign an economic compact with Pacifica, the first step toward the Gulf Republic of 1899–1900 (E11).
- *The Union* remains intact and the largest power on the continent (plausibly 40–45 million people against about 15 million in the Confederacy). A generation after 1865 its grievance has aged into a legal claim no majority will fight for. In the February 1895 Treasury gold crisis (Hist.: rescued by the Morgan–Belmont syndicate) the gold is Pacifican; the gold loan awaits financial modeling. Its price is Union recognition of Pacifica's canal rights, neutrality in any Asian war and tariff concessions (PROPOSED). The Union is quarrelling with Britain (Venezuela boundary crisis, 1895, Hist.) and has no Pacific coast.
- *The balance:* Pacifica guarantees Confederate independence. The Union knows an attack on Richmond means war with Pacifica; the guarantee is also Pacifica's leverage in Richmond.
- *Why not the alternatives:* full reunion creates a continental power of 60 million (the partial return of Virginia and North Carolina in 1898–99 is accepted, E11); annexation by 1895 would let some 15 million Southern citizens swamp Pacifica's North American electorate and bring its race politics with them; further break-up of the Union is unrealistic and invites European intervention; an outright Confederate victory would leave the Confederacy stronger and less dependent.
- *Clocks still running in 1895:* the Union naval revival (the "new navy" authorized 1883, Mahan's book on sea power 1890, Hist.) and Cuba's war of independence from February 1895 (Hist.).
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**E2. The 1865 armistice line.** The Union keeps Tennessee and the Mississippi from Memphis to Vicksburg. The border is long and porous, with Union freedmen's communities along it; the abolition mechanism of E5 depends on it. APPROVED
- *Black Union soldiers* stay in service as regulars garrisoning the Tennessee border, and freedmen receive homesteads along it. Together they become the engine of the escape networks in E5. APPROVED
- *Indian Territory goes to the Confederacy.* APPROVED (18 Oct) The Five Tribes signed alliances with the Confederacy in 1861, with delegates in the Confederate Congress; the Union held the Cherokee and Creek north from 1863, and Stand Watie was the last Confederate general to surrender, in June 1865 (Hist.). The 1865 armistice freezes that division along the Arkansas River. In the spring 1871 border convention the Union cedes the north as well, the only territory it gives up after Grant's war, so all of Indian Territory except the Public Land Strip is Confederate; the strip stays with the Union and the Plains. The cession hands the Cherokee to Watie's southern party and leaves the old Union party of John Ross with a grievance. The tribes keep slavery until Confederate abolition in 1888–89, and the adoption of their freedmen becomes a fight of the 1890s. The Union's Boomers, who historically pushed into the Unassigned Lands from 1879 (Hist.), now press across a Confederate border from Kansas. The northern cession matters most for the oil: the first commercial well, at Bartlesville in the Cherokee Nation in 1897, and Glenn Pool in the Creek Nation in 1905 (Hist.) lie in the land the Union gives up. PROPOSED (mechanism)
- *The Power Timeline* assumes that Tennessee leaves the Confederacy in 1898–99 and tells the reader to adjust to the armistice map. Under this line Tennessee is already Union, so the Upper South that leaves is Virginia and North Carolina (E11).
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**E3. Material basis of the association, beyond the shared enemy.** PROPOSED

| What Pacifica gains | What the Confederacy gains |
|---|---|
| The Atlantic: the Sunset Route across Texas to New Orleans (historically completed 1883) as Pacifica's route to the Gulf before the canal, and the Atlantic-side base for the Panama works | Capital for railways, ports and industry that Richmond cannot finance and London lends dearly |
| Coal and iron: the Birmingham district (coal, iron ore and limestone together; city founded 1871, Hist.), developed with Pacifican capital, Kelly and Holley as a steel base Britain does not control | Markets: Japanese cotton mills (Osaka, from the 1880s) and the Chinese treaty ports, reached through Pacifican shipping, as Britain turns to Indian and Egyptian cotton |
| Cotton for Asia: Pacifican merchant houses as middlemen, earning freight and commission at both ends | Industrial skill: Logan's Louisiana works (§13) as a regional engineering base |
| Men: trained, unemployed Confederate veterans for the Atlantic Auxiliary, supplying soldiers Pacifica's demography cannot (Philippines from 1876; Colonel Armistead's thread) | Refinancing of the 1863 Erlanger cotton loan (Hist.) and other war debts held mostly in Britain, on better terms and secured on customs |
| A Gulf naval station in lower Mobile Bay, coaled from Birmingham, with Galveston as a commercial port tied to Pacifica (E6) | Protection, formalized in 1871; later access to the canal |

Frictions (PROPOSED):
- *Sugar:* Louisiana sugar competes with Hawaiian sugar inside Pacifica's customs union.
- *Labor:* planters want Chinese labor, as a real 1869 Memphis convention tried to arrange (Hist.); Pacifica refuses because its China policy forbids it.
- *Race:* Pacifica's civic incorporation threatens the Southern racial order.
- *Pride:* Southern elites resent dependence, and Britain remains a rival patron some in Richmond prefer.
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**E4. Timeline.** APPROVED (entries), except where marked.

| When | What happens | Label |
|---|---|---|
| Spring 1865 | Armistice. A Pacifica–Confederate Treaty of Amity and Commerce gives Pacifica's canonical recognition of Confederate independence. Britain and France recognize; the Union does not. | canon (recognition) → APPROVED (form) |
| 1865–67 | The Confederate currency is worthless; cotton falls from its wartime peak as Egypt and India expand; the Erlanger bondholders press for payment. Pacifican and British banks compete to refinance. | Hist. (cotton, Erlanger) → APPROVED |
| 1866–67 | Railway treaty: Huntington's line across Texas to New Orleans, with Pacifican capital and Confederate land grants. | Hist. (route) → APPROVED |
| 1866–68 | For revenue, Richmond levies tolls on Mississippi traffic past Port Hudson and New Orleans, breaking the free navigation it promised in February 1861 (Hist.). Midwestern grain farmers are furious. | APPROVED |
| Nov 1867 | Davis's single six-year term ends (Feb 1868). Joseph E. Johnston, who held Atlanta in 1864, is elected president. | Hist. (term) → APPROVED |
| Nov 1868 | Grant is elected in the Union on a platform of restoring the Union. | Hist. |
| 1869 | Border crises: fugitives cross into Union Tennessee, pursued by Confederate raiders; tolls rise. Grant demands free navigation and border revisions; Richmond refuses. | APPROVED |
| Jul 1870 | The Franco-Prussian War occupies Europe (Hist.). Grant strikes for the lower Mississippi, for the Midwest, and in Virginia, to force negotiations on reunion. | Hist. → APPROVED |
| Summer 1870 | Pacifica sends no field army: a Gulf squadron, turret ships, mines and obstructions under Logan, rifles and credit. It closes its Pacific ports to Union shipping, hitting the New York merchants in the Asia trade. | APPROVED |
| Autumn 1870 | The surgical strike: at the mouths of the Mississippi, Pacifican turret ships and Logan's mines repulse the Union attack on New Orleans. In Virginia, Grant's offensive stalls against entrenched lines at a cost on the scale of Cold Harbor and Petersburg. Union midterm losses follow. | APPROVED |
| Spring 1871 | Armistice and border convention, negotiated by Sherman with Grant, his closest friend from the old war. Pacifica formally guarantees Confederate independence; Richmond restores free navigation of the Mississippi; the Union cedes northern Indian Territory, the Cherokee and Creek lands it has held since 1863 (E2). The Union Senate never ratifies recognition. The war costs Pacifica money and ships during the Japanese alliance negotiations. | APPROVED |
| 1871–72 | Association treaties: Pacifica refinances the Erlanger debt on customs security, with Pacifican officers co-administering the Confederate customs. Richmond grants a naval station in lower Mobile Bay, commercial privileges at Galveston, Atlantic Auxiliary recruitment and Birmingham concessions. Pacifica covers the toll revenue Richmond gave up. The fugitive agreement (E7) is signed. | APPROVED |
| Nov 1872 | Horace Greeley, the peace-seeker of 1864, defeats Grant on the Liberal Republican–Democratic fusion ticket (his candidacy is Hist.) and dies on 29 November, before the electoral college meets (Hist.). | Hist. → APPROVED |
| Dec 1872 – Mar 1873 | A disputed succession between his running mate, B. Gratz Brown, and Congress. Greeley's electors cast their votes for Brown; the Republican Congress challenges the count, as it historically refused to count Georgia's votes for the dead Greeley (Hist.), and seats Brown in February 1873 only after he agrees to sign the Freedom Act. A weak president who owes his office to his opponents. The party of reconciliation has lost its leader just after Grant's war has failed, and the Union enters the depression without a settled government. Pacifica keeps strict silence and correct diplomacy. | APPROVED |
| 1873 | The Republican Congress redirects the energy of reunion into an anti-slavery cold war: a Freedom Act makes every refugee free on arrival and a citizen after one year's residence; a discriminating duty of about 25% falls on slave-grown cotton, enough to drive the cotton lobby to London but short of a blockade; the Union lobbies London to buy free-labor cotton. Brown signs the Act as agreed. | APPROVED |
| Sep 1873 | The Panic of 1873 opens the Long Depression (Hist.). Cotton prices fall, and with them the value of enslaved people as capital. The Union's railways have no West to build into, so the bubble bursts harder; Pacifica recruits the engineers and skilled workers the Union lays off, and its press prints the first wage comparisons. | Hist. → APPROVED |
| Nov 1873 | John B. Gordon, the Georgia general, is elected Johnston's successor (inaugurated Feb 1874). He meets the constitution's age and residence rules without dispute. Historically the leading promoter of the industrial "New South", he works naturally with Pacifican railways, Birmingham coal and credit; his reputed leadership of Georgia's Ku Klux Klan (Hist.) sits uneasily with the free-womb convention he must carry. Benjamin becomes Secretary of State (E8). | Hist. (person) → APPROVED |
| 1874 | The Confederate debt crisis deepens. Pacifica's new refinancing carries a quiet condition. Benjamin, who offered emancipation for recognition through Kenner in 1865 (Hist.), drafts the plan. | Hist. (Kenner) → APPROVED |
| 1874–75 | Free-womb amendment. The Confederate constitution protected property in slaves (Art. I, Sec. 9), so a convention is needed, which any three states can demand, with ratification by two-thirds of the states (Art. V). Children born after 1 January 1875 are free; masters keep their labor until 21 or surrender them to the state for compensation, on the model of Brazil's 1871 law. | Hist. (Brazil; CSA Art. V) → APPROVED |
| 1875–85 | The Union carries the load: constant flight across the border, aided by freedmen's settlements and Black veterans' networks; collapsing slave prices in the upper South; Frederick Douglass's campaign; smuggled abolitionist papers. The 1879 Exodus to Kansas (Hist.) becomes a flight across the border. | Hist. anchors → APPROVED |
| 1876–77 | The disputed Union election of 1876 has no South to trade. Rutherford Hayes is seated by the Electoral Commission's party-line 8–7 votes, as in history (Hist.), with no bargain to offer the losers; Democrats call him "His Fraudulency" (Hist.). The 1877 railway strike meets a president without legitimacy and comes close to insurrection; historically troops killed about a hundred strikers (Hist.). A Republican keeps the anti-slavery cold war (E5) going. | Hist. → APPROVED |
| 1883 | The Sunset Route is completed (Hist.). Texas is economically bound to Pacifica. | Hist. |
| 1884 | States' rights cut both ways: Texas abolishes slavery by state law to qualify for closer association with Pacifica, as Ceará did in Brazil in 1884 (Hist.). Upper-South states, already draining through flight, follow. | Hist. → APPROVED |
| 1885 | A sexagenarian law frees enslaved people over sixty, following Brazil's law of the same year (Hist.). | Hist. → APPROVED |
| 1888–89 | Final abolition by amendment, with compensation bonds (E9). The Deep South holdouts give way once slavery is unworkable, unmarketable and isolated. Brazil abolishes in May 1888 (Hist.). | APPROVED; figures to the audit (E9) |
| 1889–95 | Emancipation is followed by sharecropping and coerced labor; freed people's citizenship is contested; the Union border remains a magnet. | APPROVED |
| 1890 | Wounded Knee happens on Union soil (Hist.); the prestige weekly's first great campaign sets it beside the Navajo treaty and the Apache peace (H6, J2). | Hist. → APPROVED |
| 1891 | A Deep South nationalist narrowly wins the Confederate presidency, and the Gulf states feel shut out. | PROPOSED |
| 1893–95 | The Panic: cotton falls to about 5 cents a pound in 1894 (Hist.); Richmond misses coupons on the compensation bonds and Pacifica's guarantee pays them. In the Union, Coxey's Army and Pullman (1894, Hist.), and the Bread March is stopped at the divide (E10). | APPROVED |
| 1895 | The Gulf economic compact with Pacifica: lower tariffs, rail and port agreements, a currency pegged to the Pacifican gold dollar, no free movement of people. Pacifica rescues the Union's gold (E1). | PROPOSED (compact); APPROVED (rescue) |
| Nov 1896 | Whitney is elected Union president (E10). | APPROVED |
| 1897–1900 | The Confederacy splits; the Gulf Republic forms (E11). | APPROVED |
| 1898 | Cuba becomes independent after the Maine; Puerto Rico goes to the Union (E12). | APPROVED |
