source_items.source_text: **E5. How the Union does the heavy lifting.** After 1870 force has failed, and a second attack means war with Pacifica. An anti-slavery cold war lets the Union keep fighting the Confederacy without fighting Pacifica, and it reunites a party split by reconquest. Its weapons are a free-soil border that turns every mile into an exit, citizenship for refugees, market discrimination against slave-grown cotton at home and in London, moral campaigning in Europe, and the example of free labor next door. Each Union success makes the Confederacy poorer, more frightened and more dependent on Pacifican credit: the Union frees the South's enslaved people and delivers the freed South into Pacifica's association. APPROVED
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**E6. The roles are split: the naval station is in lower Mobile Bay, and Galveston is the commercial port.** APPROVED
- *Mobile Bay as naval station:* PROPOSED
  - *Shelter.* The anchorage lies in the protected lower bay near Fort Morgan, not on an exposed barrier island. The deep water is at the entrance; the city, at the head of a shallow bay, is reached by lighter and rail. Hurricane risk was visible to planners in 1871: the 1875 storm destroyed the Texas port of Indianola (Hist.).
  - *Coal.* Mobile is Alabama's port, so Birmingham's coal and iron reach the station by river and rail, fixing Pacifica's oldest weakness at the base itself (E3).
  - *Position.* Slightly closer than Galveston to Havana, the Florida Straits and the approaches to the canal.
  - *Cost.* Union-held Pensacola, with its navy yard, lies about fifty miles east. Elias reads the proximity as deterrence; his critics read it as exposure.
- *Galveston as commercial port:* Texas's outlet and the link to the West, and the Gulf Republic's main port after 1900 (E11). Pacifican engineers build the bar jetties earlier than their historical completion around 1896, and a seawall in the 1890s, which historically was built only in 1902–04, after the storm. APPROVED (seawall) The September 1900 hurricane, which destroyed Galveston and killed at least 6,000 people (Hist.), strikes a protected city in the year the canal opens. PROPOSED
- *Dependency:* Mobile must remain Confederate at the 1865 armistice. Resolved by section F: the Union attack on Mobile Bay fails in February 1865.
- *Excluded:* Pensacola, the Gulf's best natural harbor, was Union-held from 1862 and stays Union under E2.
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**E7. Fugitives and Pacifican soil.** By agreement with the Confederacy, Pacifica prevents enslaved people from fleeing to its territory, and enforces the agreement so as not to antagonize its partner. APPROVED
- *Mechanism:* Pacifica's founding law prohibits slavery and its 1846 bill of rights guarantees habeas corpus, so Pacifica cannot return people as property. It acts through border and immigration control instead: persons arriving from the Confederacy without Confederate travel papers are refused entry and handed back at the Texas border, on the Sunset Route, at Galveston and at the Mobile Bay station. Signed with the 1871–72 association treaties. PROPOSED
- *The court test:* a Pacifican court frees a returned fugitive on habeas corpus. The cabinet overrides the ruling under the 1865 enabling law, which allows cabinet legislation departing from specified constitutional provisions. It is an early, quiet use of that power. Kaiulani objects to the policy; Sherman objects to the use of the enabling law rather than to the policy. PROPOSED
- *Consequences:* every escape route points north to the Union, strengthening E5. Abolitionists in the Union and Britain call Pacifica an accomplice. Pacifica's Chinese and Hawaiian citizens draw their own conclusions about whose rights are secure. Mexico and Canada historically refused to return fugitives (Hist.); Pacifica chooses differently. The agreement lapses with abolition in 1888–89. PROPOSED
- *After the lapse:* the 1888 switch to selective immigration (I3) means the lapse does not open Pacifica's door to the freed. Critics, Frederick Douglass among them, call the policy anti-Black racism; a quiet understanding with Gulf planters who fear losing their labor after abolition may be the real motive, and the novel can leave it open. APPROVED (Power Timeline)
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**E8. Benjamin's office.** APPROVED (recommendation below)
- *Constraint:* Benjamin, as Confederate Secretary of War in 1861–62, clashed bitterly with Johnston (Hist.), so President Johnston (1868–74) will not appoint him.
- *Recommended:* Confederate senator for Louisiana from 1868, chosen by the Louisiana legislature, where he champions ratification of the 1871 association treaties; then Secretary of State from 1874 under Johnston's successor, Gordon, negotiating the refinancing with Pacifica and steering the free-womb convention, demanded by Louisiana, Texas and Virginia. PROPOSED
- *Alternatives:* Secretary of the Treasury from 1874 (fits the debt crisis, less the diplomacy); minister to Pacifica 1871–74 (puts him face to face with Elias); president (legally eligible under the Confederate constitution, but antisemitism and his Davis-era enmities make him unelectable, which can be said aloud in a scene).
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text: **E9. Compensation finance.** The compensation bonds of 1888–89 are long bonds secured on the Confederate customs that Pacifica co-administers, so that abolition deepens dependence. They are modeled together with the gold loan to the Union in the financial feasibility audit. APPROVED (structure); figures to the audit In 1893–95 Richmond misses coupons and Pacifica's guarantee pays them (E4).
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**E10. The Union, 1872–1900.** APPROVED unless marked
- *1872–77:* the Greeley affair, a deeper Long Depression, the disputed election of 1876 and the 1877 strike (E4). Pacifica stays out, recruits and publishes. The Union is discredited without a shot.
- *1890:* Wounded Knee, photographed and campaigned on by the prestige weekly (J2).
- *1893–94:* the Panic, Coxey's Army and Pullman. The statistics bureau's wage and unemployment tables, newsreels of Pacifican works and relief, and open recruitment of Union skilled workers let the Union's own voters make the comparison.
- *1894, the Bread March:* with Pacifica's door closed since 1888 and the Union in depression, industrial armies gather in Colorado while its populist governor, Davis Waite, looks away, and armed men try to force the passes; a border post is attacked and men die. Pacifica detains the marchers by the hundreds and tries the armed men fairly, on Pacifican film. Revanchism and silver populism are tied to a bloody fiasco.
- *1895:* the gold rescue and its price (E1).
- *1896:* William C. Whitney, Navy Secretary in 1885–89 and leader of the gold Democrats (Hist.), is nominated and beats McKinley's platform of tariffs and recovering the West, with a supportive House; the Senate follows after the 1898 state elections. His policy: compete with Pacifica, don't fight it; neutrality in the Primorye war; Union capital in Pacifican projects; a recovery from 1897 fed by Klondike and South African gold passing through Pacifican banks.
- *1897:* the Bread March prisoners are returned to the Union in a prisoner deal, against a commerce and arbitration treaty with Pacifica, Whitney's first diplomatic success.
- *Risk:* the charge of a bought president; the revanchists go underground.
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**E11. The Confederacy splits, 1889–1900.** APPROVED (split and Gulf Republic); PROPOSED (dates)
- *Pressures:* abolition removes the Confederacy's founding purpose; the Panic bankrupts cotton and Pacifica's guarantee pays the missed coupons; Whitney's Union offers the Upper South a way home; single six-year presidential terms make the 1897 election the breaking point.
- *Sequence:* 1891, a Deep South nationalist wins the presidency; 1895, the Gulf economic compact; 1897, the election deadlocks between the Gulf, Deep South and Upper South blocs, and Whitney offers the Upper South a customs union; 1898–99, Virginia and North Carolina leave and negotiate reunion with the Union while Pacifica stays neutral; 1899–1900, Texas, Louisiana and Arkansas secede and form the Gulf Republic, taking Indian Territory with them as the state of Sequoyah, the name the Five Tribes historically proposed for their own state in 1905 (Hist.), with a trade treaty and a mutual defence pact with Pacifica, and Pacifican ships at Mobile deter Richmond from marching on Louisiana; from 1900 a rump Confederacy of South Carolina, Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi and Florida survives, tied to Lancashire's cotton. APPROVED (members, 18 Oct)
- *Adjustment to E2:* Tennessee is Union under the 1865 line, so it is not among the states that leave. Arkansas, which the Power Timeline does not name, joins the Gulf Republic for its rail and river ties to Louisiana and Texas. Alabama, which the Power Timeline places in its Gulf Federation, stays with the rump: its ties run to Georgia and Mississippi, and the Gulf Republic is in effect the old Trans-Mississippi Department (Hist.) with New Orleans. APPROVED
- *The Federal Republic of the Gulf* (República Federal del Golfo, République fédérale du Golfe), "the Gulf Republic" for short: one name in the region's three languages, with no echo of either the Confederacy or the Union. APPROVED Austin is the capital and New Orleans the economic centre. Its constitution follows Pacifica's model: a strong executive, a merit civil service, independent courts and equal civil rights, with a narrow franchise earned by examination that votes only in certain referendums. It has its own citizenship, so there is no free movement into Pacifica before accession, and the Gulf Republic's ports, Galveston above all, are open to Pacifica's fleet under the defence pact.
- *Oil.* The Gulf Republic is born an oil republic: Sequoyah's fields, found earlier with Pacifican survey help, and in its first weeks Spindletop at Beaumont, Texas, in January 1901 (Hist.). Pacifica's fuel-oil programme (J2) supplies the technology and the buyer, so the oil ends with Pacifica's partner rather than in Pacifica itself, and the partnership gains a material core beyond the shared enemy. PROPOSED
- *Accession measures:* five statistics bureau measures, each held for three consecutive years at or better than the weakest Pacifican member state: infant mortality, literacy, real wages, homicide and typhoid deaths. A sixth is the gap between Black and white citizens on each, the Five Tribes' freedmen included, which must stay within a set margin, so accession requires emancipation to be real and answers the 1888 critique (E7). APPROVED
- *Mobile and Birmingham in the rump.* With Alabama in the rump Confederacy, the Mobile Bay naval station and the Birmingham concessions lie outside the Gulf Republic. Both rest on the 1871–72 treaties, which the rump inherits as Richmond's successor, so Pacifica keeps them as treaty rights: a leased enclave and foreign-owned works inside a resentful state that still depends on Pacifica's bond guarantee. Galveston, protected by its seawall since the 1890s, is the fallback base if the lease is ever challenged. PROPOSED
- *Risks:* New Orleans depends on a Mississippi that runs through the Union; Texan land hunger presses on Sequoyah's tribal self-government; Texan republicanism may resist accession; critics call it a planters' republic under Pacifican protection.
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**E12. Cuba, 1895–1902.** APPROVED (end state, guarantee, first president from the New Orleans junta); PROPOSED (sequence)
- *End state:* an independent Cuba under Pacifican influence, Puerto Rico to the Union, no foreign bases in Cuba. The first president is Tomás Estrada Palma, who historically led the junta from New York and became Cuba's first president in 1902 (Hist.). Here he runs it from New Orleans, and the readiness he later showed to invite US intervention (1906, Hist.) turns toward Pacifica. APPROVED Pacifica, the Gulf Republic and the Union jointly guarantee its independence, so any intervention needs all three.
- *Sequence:* the exile junta works from New Orleans and the weekly campaigns against Weyler's camps; in February 1898 the Maine explodes, and Pacifican engineers privately suspect a coal-bunker fire, a finding Kaiulani keeps in a drawer; Whitney's ultimatum to Spain renounces annexation from the start; the Union wins at sea while Pacifica, committed to the Primorye war, stays neutral; Pacifica buys Cuba's share of the Spanish colonial debt at a discount, serviced from Cuban customs on the Inspectorate model, so there is no Platt Amendment; Carlos Finlay, funded by Pacifica since 1881, frees Havana from yellow fever in 1899–1901.
- *Nicaragua:* Pacifica buys exclusive Nicaraguan canal rights around 1899–1900, so the victorious Union cannot build a rival canal. PROPOSED
- *Risks:* Cuban sugar's natural market is the Union; and if the Maine finding ever comes out, the Union learns Pacifica let it fight over a probable accident.
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**F1. Constraints.** APPROVED
- *Pensacola replaces New Orleans as the Union's Gulf base.* Confederate troops leave Pensacola in early 1862 to concentrate for Shiloh, and the Union occupies it in May. With Ship Island and Key West (Union-held from 1861–62, Hist.) it carries Farragut's operations. Union forces in the Gulf stay small; without a New Orleans base there is no 1864 Red River campaign.
- *The Union's river ironclads cannot reach the Gulf.* Eads's twin-turret river monitors (commissioned 1864; two fought at Mobile Bay historically) are built at St Louis and trapped above Confederate Port Hudson. With Ericsson in Pacifica, the ocean-going Tecumseh-class monitors that led Farragut into Mobile Bay do not exist (canon: no Ericsson-derived production). Armored support must come by sea from an Atlantic fleet that needs it at Charleston and Hampton Roads. This is the material cause of the canonical delay at Mobile.
- *Pacifica's supply route runs through Matamoros.* As a belligerent, Pacifica's ships are fair game on the blockade. Credit and materials go round Cape Horn to the neutral Mexican Rio Grande and overland into Texas, the real blockade-runners' route.
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**F2. Timeline.** APPROVED (entries), except where marked.

| When | What happens | Label |
|---|---|---|
| Apr–Sep 1861 | Lincoln proclaims the blockade (19 Apr). Fort Pickens at Pensacola stays Union throughout; the Union occupies Ship Island in September. | Hist. |
| 1861 | Logan travels east with the small technical mission. Pacifican credit and materials for the Confederacy are routed round Cape Horn to Matamoros and overland into Texas. | canon (mission) → PROPOSED (route) |
| Feb–Mar 1862 | Bragg's troops leave the Gulf coast to concentrate for Shiloh. | Hist. |
| 24 Apr 1862 | Farragut's attack on New Orleans fails. The Louisiana's guns are better placed, the obstruction holds and concentrated fire throws the column into disorder. His squadron survives and the blockade continues. | canon (outcome); Hist. (date) → PROPOSED |
| 9–10 May 1862 | The Confederates evacuate the Pensacola navy yard. The Union occupies it, and it becomes Farragut's main Gulf base in place of New Orleans. | Hist. → PROPOSED (role) |
| Oct 1862 – 1 Jan 1863 | The Union seizes Galveston; the Confederates retake it on New Year's Day. | Hist. |
| Late 1862 – early 1863 | Marcus leaves for the Confederacy and meets Logan in a New Orleans repair yard. | canon |
| Summer 1863 | Vicksburg falls and its army escapes. Porter's gunboats raid below the city, but Port Hudson holds, and the river from Port Hudson to New Orleans stays a contested Confederate corridor. | canon |
| Sep–Oct 1863 | Union pressure on Port Hudson from the north stops when the defeat at Chickamauga draws Grant's forces to Chattanooga. | Hist. (Chickamauga) → PROPOSED |
| 8 Sep 1863 | A Union landing on the Texas coast is repulsed at Sabine Pass. | Hist. |
| Nov 1863 – Jul 1864 | The Union's Rio Grande expedition takes Brownsville to cut the Matamoros trade, which here is also Pacifica's channel. The Confederates retake it in July 1864. | Hist. → PROPOSED (Pacifican stake) |
| Late 1863 – 1864 | Marcus returns to Pacifica. Logan leads the technical mission and moves part of it to Mobile. | canon; PROPOSED (Mobile) |
| Feb–May 1864 | The ironclad Tennessee is commissioned (16 Feb) and floated over the Dog River bar into the lower bay (May). Logan's men fix the two faults that doomed her historically: exposed steering chains and jamming gunport shutters. Her engines remain underpowered at about six knots. | Hist. → PROPOSED |
| Spring–summer 1864 | Eads's monitors are trapped upriver, and the Atlantic fleet can't spare ocean-going armor. Farragut waits at Pensacola. The historical attack of 5 August 1864 does not happen. | canon (delay) → PROPOSED (cause) |
| Summer 1864 | Mobile's rail and river links help supply Johnston at Atlanta. | PROPOSED (link to A3) |
| 8 Nov 1864 | Election day: Mobile and its bay are untaken. | canon |
| Dec 1864 – Jan 1865 | The Union assembles a seaborne armored force of broadside ironclads of the New Ironsides type (no Ericsson monitors exist), with troops at Pensacola. The Confederate defense adds the weak ironclads Nashville and Huntsville, but the battle stays a duel between the Tennessee and Logan's mine field. | APPROVED |
| Feb 1865 | **The lame-duck attack fails.** Farragut tries to force the main channel under Fort Morgan. His lead armored ship is sunk in a mine field that Logan has made denser, echoing the Tecumseh in August 1864. The column breaks up under the fort. Admiral Buchanan's Tennessee, her steering and gunports now working, engages. Farragut is killed; his squadron withdraws with heavy losses, and the troops landed on Dauphin Island are re-embarked. Paired with the failure at Petersburg, this is the Union's last push before McClellan takes office. | APPROVED |
| Mar–Jun 1865 | Armistice. The Gulf line: the Union holds Pensacola, Key West and Ship Island. The Confederacy holds Mobile and the whole bay including Forts Morgan and Gaines, New Orleans, Port Hudson, Galveston and the Texas coast including Brownsville. | PROPOSED |
| 1871–72 | Pacifica's naval station in lower Mobile Bay faces the Union navy yard at Pensacola, fifty miles away. | E6 |
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**F3. Consequences.** PROPOSED
- Mobile and the lower bay, where the naval station goes, are Confederate at the armistice.
- The New Orleans–Port Hudson corridor connects Texas and the trans-Mississippi to the east, which is why the Confederacy survives as a coherent state.
- Pacifica's part is skill rather than fleets, consistent with G3: Logan's practical fixes and mine work pay off, his training with Ericsson shows, and Buchanan, who commanded the Virginia at Hampton Roads, wins a second time.
- Pensacola and Ship Island give Grant's 1870 attack on New Orleans its geography.
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**F4. Farragut's fate in February 1865.** Killed at Mobile. APPROVED
- His famous order to ignore the mines becomes, in this world, the order that sank his fleet.
- A martyred Farragut gives Grant's 1868 revanchism its symbol, and marks Logan, whose mines killed him, for the rest of the book.
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**H0. Decisions.** APPROVED
- The Mormons, Utah Territory and Nevada (Washoe) join Pacifica as early as possible; the Civil War is the opportunity.
- Religious freedom for all is a founding principle of Pacifica. Toleration of the Mormons is an expression of it, not an exception.
- The 1865 line runs roughly along the continental divide. Colorado's Front Range and the Great Plains stay with the Union; New Mexico comes to Pacifica, with further adjustments where defense, demography or economy require them (H5).
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**H1. Religious freedom.** APPROVED (principle); PROPOSED (detail)
- *Anchor:* the 1846 bill of rights. A Californio republic choosing religious freedom breaks with Mexico, whose 1824 constitution made Catholicism the state religion (Hist.). Hawaii knows the issue first-hand: in 1839 France forced the kingdom to tolerate Catholics (Hist.).
- *Belief and practice.* Freedom of religion protects belief; marriage law is reserved to the member states (H3). Deseret's marriages are protected by confederal structure, not by a Pacifican right to polygamy. The US Supreme Court drew the belief–practice line against polygamy in 1879 (Hist.); Pacifica draws it the other way, through federalism.
- *Abroad.* Freedom at home is compatible with "no missionaries" in China (C1), but Pacifican churches will press the point. A council scene.
- *The Defense Law of 1855.* Pacifist sects perform alternative service in an irrigation and engineering corps, so the Mennonites build the interior's irrigation districts (I2). APPROVED In 1874 some 18,000 Mennonites left Russia for North America after losing their exemption from service (Hist.).
- *Magnet.* Religious freedom draws Irish and German Catholics, Mennonites, Russian Jews after 1881, Mormon converts and Basque Catholics (I3).
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**H2. Deseret: sequence.** PROPOSED unless marked

| When | What happens | Label |
|---|---|---|
| 1851–57 | Mormons found San Bernardino inside Pacifica (Hist.). In 1857 Brigham Young recalls the colony (Hist.); Elias lets its leaders, Amasa Lyman and Charles Rich, keep their titles, and the channel stays open. | Hist. → PROPOSED |
| 1857–58 | The Utah War (Hist.). Brigham Young asks discreetly about protection. Pacifica, not ready to face the United States, offers trade and discretion only. | PROPOSED |
| Sep 1857 | Mountain Meadows (Hist.). The murdered emigrants were bound for California; Pacifican opinion turns violently against the Mormons. | Hist. |
| Jul–Oct 1861 | The Union abandons Camp Floyd (Hist.). Pacifica's telegraph and road reach Carson Valley; Salt Lake's trade turns west. | Hist. → PROPOSED |
| Jan 1862 | The Deseret constitutional convention (Hist.) meets with a Pacifican envoy quietly present. | PROPOSED |
| Jul 1862 | The Morrill Anti-Bigamy Act (Hist.): Washington threatens the church's property and marriages. The breaking point. | Hist. |
| Late 1862–63 | Deseret accedes to Pacifica as a confederate state, ratified by its own legislature. Lot Smith's Mormon cavalry, which guarded the mail road for the Union in spring 1862 (Hist.), guards Pacifica's supply road. Follows from Pacifica's entry into the war in early 1862. | APPROVED (entry date); PROPOSED |
| 1863 | Brigham Young surrenders John D. Lee as the private price of accession; Pacifica tries and hangs him for Mountain Meadows. Elias gets a scene of cold bargaining, and Brigham Young owes him a debt he resents. | APPROVED |
| 1865 | The cession treaty confirms the old Utah Territory to Pacifica. | PROPOSED |
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**H3. Terms of accession.** PROPOSED
- *Deseret gets:* full confederate statehood on the Hawaiian precedent; its own marriage and church-property law, subject to the confederal marriage floor (I2); Brigham Young as governor; the Nauvoo Legion as Deseret's militia within the Defense Law; a wheat market by the Sierra railway; protection from the Union.
- *Pacifica gets:* the overland route; Salt Lake as the supply base for the interior campaigns; a buffer across the Great Basin; the church's European convert emigration (about 70,000 crossed the plains 1847–69, Hist.) routed through San Francisco or Galveston.
- *Pacifican opposition:* the Protestant American-born third and the Kentucky pastor antagonist make polygamy under Pacifica's flag a line of attack on Elias. Brigham Young must see accession as the lesser evil forced by the Morrill Act.
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**H4. The other territories.** PROPOSED

| Territory | Anchor | How it joins | When |
|---|---|---|---|
| New Mexico and Arizona | Confederate Arizona proclaimed 1861; Sibley turned back at Glorieta, March 1862; Carleton's California column takes Tucson and reaches the Rio Grande (Hist.) | The California column is Pacifican. The Confederacy renounces its Arizona claim for credit and the Sunset Route. The Hispano Catholic majority is better served by a bilingual, Californio-founded republic than by Washington, which kept New Mexico out of statehood until 1912 (Hist.). | 1862 |
| Idaho | Gold at Pierce (1860) and the Boise Basin (1862), worked by miners from California and Oregon, supplied from Walla Walla and Portland (Hist.) | With the Northwest Pacifican, Idaho's only supply line runs through Pacifica. | 1863 |
| Western Montana | Gold at Bannack (1862), Alder Gulch (1863), Last Chance Gulch (1864); supply by the Montana Trail from Salt Lake and the Mullan Road (completed 1862) from Walla Walla (Hist.) | Supplied by Pacifica; the Missouri route to Fort Benton is cut in wartime. | 1863–64 |
| Washoe and Nevada | Part I Washoe sequence (APPROVED); Nevada Territory 1861, statehood 31 Oct 1864 (Hist.) | Caught between Pacifica and Deseret, Washoe cannot be held by the Union and is retaken. The Union still admits Nevada on 31 October 1864 for Lincoln's votes, and signs it away months later. APPROVED | 1863–64 |
| Southwest Wyoming, the Western Slope, the San Luis Valley | Almost unsettled before 1867 except Fort Bridger and the Hispano San Luis Valley (San Luis founded 1851, Hist.) | Ceded by the 1865 treaty with the line of H5. | 1865 |
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**H5. The line.** APPROVED (segments); PROPOSED (survey detail)

| Segment | Line | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Montana | The mountain front, roughly 111°W, from the 49th parallel to the Yellowstone plateau | Montana's gold camps lie on the Missouri side of the divide; a strict divide line would give the Union the gold and a foothold in the mountains. Helena, Virginia City, Bannack and the Gallatin valley are Pacifican; the Union keeps Fort Benton as a border trade post at the head of steamboat navigation. |
| Wyoming | The divide through Yellowstone and along the Wind River crest; round the Great Divide Basin by the divide's eastern branch to the Sierra Madre | South Pass, the Green River basin, Fort Bridger and the Rock Springs coal. Pacifica's coal deficit (Part I) is closed here and in Utah. |
| Colorado | The divide crest (Berthoud, Tennessee and Marshall passes); then by Poncha Pass to the Sangre de Cristo crest | North and Middle Park and the Western Slope (Ute country; San Juan silver from the 1870s) are Pacifican; Denver, the Front Range, the Pikes Peak goldfields and Leadville stay with the Union. The high passes close in winter: the best defensive wall on the line. |
| San Luis Valley | The Sangre de Cristo crest south to 37°N | Hispano, and drained by the Rio Grande into New Mexico. |
| New Mexico | 37°N east to 103°W, then 103°W south to Texas | The whole territory: the largest Hispano population, the end of the Santa Fe Trail, the Rio Grande corridor to El Paso and the Sunset Route. Raton Pass and Fort Union (1851, Hist.) are the eastern bastion. The eastern plains border Confederate Texas, a partner. |
| Arizona, Utah, Nevada, Idaho | Entire | West of the divide or within the Great Basin. |
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**H6. Native nations.** PROPOSED
- Pacifica's interior nations are the Navajo, Apache, Ute, Shoshone (Washakie's Eastern Shoshone as the first ally), Bannock, Paiute, Nez Perce and Blackfeet (who straddle the Montana line).
- Two atrocities were committed historically by Californian troops, who are Pacifican here: Bear River (January 1863) and the Navajo Long Walk (1864, under Carleton). Bear River is committed under a local Pacifican commander. The Long Walk is avoided: instead of Kit Carson's scorched-earth campaign of 1863–64 (Hist.), Pacifica signs a treaty with Navajo leaders, among them Barboncito and Manuelito (Hist. persons), recognizing a homeland reservation like the one the 1868 treaty historically restored. One stain and one success make the friendship doctrine a choice rather than a given. APPROVED
- In 1865 Pacifica makes peace with the Apache bands on the terms Howard and Cochise later agreed: homeland reservations, honest agents, paid Apache scouts and prosecution of settler massacres, paired with the Mexican convention ending scalp bounties (B1). The interior garrison shrinks and the future Sunset route runs through quiet country; the risks are settler backlash and continued raiding into Sonora. PROPOSED (Power Timeline) Sand Creek stays a Union atrocity, which Pacifica can use as a grievance.
- New Mexico's debt peonage and Native captive trade, banned by Congress only in 1867 (Hist.), conflict with Pacifica's founding law. Pacifica abolishes them gradually, with compensation, by 1866, and meets a short Hispano revolt on the model of the Taos revolt of 1847 (Hist.). Pacifica's founding law gets a domestic test that contrasts with its compromise in E7. APPROVED
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**H7. Consequences.** PROPOSED
- *Denver* is the Union's only mountain railhead (the Kansas Pacific reached it in 1870, Hist.). Part I's friends of Pacifica around Denver become a Pacifican party inside a Union city.
- *Economy:* Pacifica holds Montana and Idaho gold, Comstock silver, Utah and Rock Springs coal, Butte (on the divide; later the great copper camp) and Arizona copper. Leadville's silver, and much of the 1893 silver crash, fall to the Union. Pacifica stays bimetallic until 1873, then goes to gold, and mints a silver trade dollar for Asia, as the US historically did from 1873. The silver territories get an outlet in Asia, and silver politics stays a slow-burning clock. APPROVED The trade dollar is minted to compete with the Mexican peso in Chinese ports; with Asia on silver, Pacifica's gold buys more there every year, and Pacifica buys distressed Union railway and mining securities after 1873. PROPOSED (Power Timeline)
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**I0. Decisions.** APPROVED
- The assisted immigration of women, and the other measures that raise population, extend to the new territories, which need them most. China, Japan and the Philippines assist as partners.
- Over a few generations of family migration and integration from Asia, Hapa marriages become as commonplace in Pacifica, and as much a symbol of it, as mulatto and mestizo unions are in Brazil.
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**I1. The problem.** PROPOSED
- Mining societies were overwhelmingly male: California in 1850 was over 90% male (Hist.), and the interior territories were several men to one woman in 1870. Without women there are no families, no natural increase and no settled loyalty.
- The interior's Chinese were already numerous and almost all men: in 1870 Chinese made up nearly 30% of Idaho's population (Hist.). The program's first task is to turn sojourners into settlers.
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**I2. Instruments.** APPROVED (extension to the new territories); PROPOSED (instruments)
- *Assisted passage for women.* Precedents: the filles du roi of New France (1663–73), Australian assisted female emigration from the 1830s, and Asa Mercer's parties of women brought to Seattle in 1864 and 1866 (Hist.). Here the Mercer parties are a Pacifican program, and the model is extended inland.
- *Family land law.* On the model of Oregon's Donation Land Claim Act of 1850 (Hist.): a larger grant for a married couple than for a single man, with the wife holding her half in her own name. Unlike the historical act, there is no racial bar, so the law rewards marriage, including intermarriage.
- *The confederal marriage floor.* Member states, Deseret included, keep their marriage law but may not forbid marriage on grounds of race or origin. Children born in Pacifica are citizens. Historically California banned marriages between whites and Chinese from 1880 (Hist.); Pacifica never does. The floor forbids only bans by race or origin. The first test case, in the 1870s, is a Mormon–Shoshone or Mormon–Chinese marriage that goes from a Deseret court to the confederal court, putting federalism against the Hapa ideal on stage. APPROVED
- *Carrying capacity:* state irrigation districts in the 1870s, ahead of California's Wright Act of 1887 (Hist.), drawing on Mormon irrigation practice; railways into the interior from the west; homesteads.
- *Religious freedom as recruitment* (H1).
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**I3. Asian partners.** APPROVED (partners); PROPOSED (mechanisms)
- *China.* The 1868 treaty (C2) includes a family article: Qing consent to the emigration of wives and families, with brokers licensed jointly by Pacifican consuls and the district associations, which gives a recurring cast of brokers as antagonists. APPROVED Custom kept most wives in the home villages (Hist.), so the first families come from groups that already migrated as families, above all the Hakka, whose families went to Hawaii and Borneo with Basel Mission sponsorship (Hist.). There is no Page Act (1875) and no Exclusion Act (1882). When the Union, the Australian colonies and Canada close their doors in 1880–85 (Hist.), Pacifica stays open to Chinese families, merchants and capital and offers naturalization; a Chinese merchants' bank in San Francisco handles the diaspora's remittances. PROPOSED (Power Timeline) The brokers' trade in women, which flourished in historical San Francisco, is the program's dark side and ties to the Part I broker problem.
- *Japan.* Government-sponsored emigration, historically begun only in 1885 (about 29,000 to Hawaii by 1894, Hist.), starts in the late 1860s. The Wakamatsu Tea and Silk Colony, founded near Coloma in 1869 by refugees from Aizu after the Boshin War and failed by 1871 (Hist.), succeeds with Pacifican support and becomes the model. Arranged "picture" marriages, historically 1908–20 (Hist.), come a generation earlier. Japanese farmers settle the new irrigation districts.
- *The Philippines.* After the Spanish settlement of 1873–76 (B3), Catholic, partly Spanish-speaking Filipino families settle in New Mexico and Arizona, where church, language and Spanish-derived law already fit. A trickle of reformers and families follows after 1876, with larger flows only once the insurgency ebbs in the 1880s; the insurgency remains the pacing constraint. APPROVED
- *Interior hotspots:* the Rock Springs massacre (1885, 28 Chinese miners killed) and the Hells Canyon massacre (1887) (Hist.) fall on Pacifican soil. Neither is prevented; both are punished promptly. The trials are what make the program credible, and they give Pacifica the clean record it needs before the 1890 Wounded Knee campaign (J3). APPROVED
- *1888: from open borders to selective immigration.* Kaiulani replaces the early republic's open door with a programme of skilled migrants and sponsored families. The family programme with China, Japan and the Philippines continues; unskilled drifters, above all from the Union, are refused. Selection lifts every figure the statistics bureau reports. APPROVED (Power Timeline) It narrows the 1868 labor clause (C1), and it is the policy critics set against the lapse of the fugitive agreement (E7).
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**I4. Hapa as Pacifica's identity.** APPROVED (direction); PROPOSED (detail)
- *The word is already Pacifican:* Hawaiian *hapa*, from English "half." In 19th-century Hawaii, Chinese men married Hawaiian women in large numbers (Hist.); the Californio society of 1846 was itself largely mestizo. Pacifica begins with two mixing traditions and adds a third.
- *The dynasty embodies it.* Elias and Kaiulani's children are hapa haole; the Japanese consort of the 1914 Thorne-Kamehameha settlement (D5) carries it into Asia.
- *Pace.* By 1895 the first generation of mixed children is coming of age; the norm and the symbol belong to the 1900s–1920s.
- *The Brazilian parallel cuts both ways.* Brazil's celebrated mixture coexisted with a policy of "whitening" through European immigration and a firm color hierarchy; Gilberto Freyre's 1933 image of a "racial democracy" was later widely criticized (Hist.). To be believable, Pacifica's Hapa ideal needs its own tension: nativist politics (the historical Workingmen's Party of 1877), the interior massacres (I3), and the 1871–89 fugitive agreement (E7). The agreement stays an open wound that Kaiulani and Chinese Pacificans name aloud; its lapse in 1889 becomes the moment the Hapa ideal is proclaimed. APPROVED The proclamation comes the year after the switch to selective immigration (I3), and critics will hold the two side by side.
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**I5. Population effect.** PROPOSED (figures to verify)

| Interior territory | Historical, c. 1895 |
|---|---|
| Utah | ~245,000 |
| New Mexico | ~180,000 |
| Western Montana | ~150,000 |
| Idaho | ~125,000 |
| Arizona | ~105,000 |
| Western Slope and San Luis Valley | ~75,000 |
| Nevada | ~45,000 |
| Southwest Wyoming | ~25,000 |
| **Total** | **~1 million** |

In this timeline, without the eastern railroads but with section I, the interior holds about 0.7–1.5 million in 1895. With the coast (about 3–5 million; ceiling about 5 million), North American Pacifica holds roughly **4–6½ million**, against about 3.2 million on the same land historically. The 1.2 million base of 1861 (Part I, still open) remains the largest single lever. After 1888, generic arrivals fall under selective immigration while the family programme's flows continue.
source_items.status_policy: Preserve component labels in source_text; mixed APPROVED/PROPOSED items are not blanket approvals.

source_items.source_text:
**I6. Timeline additions.** PROPOSED unless marked

| When | What happens | Label |
|---|---|---|
| 1864 onward | Mercer-model women's parties, extended inland after 1865 | Hist. → PROPOSED |
| Late 1860s | Japanese government-sponsored emigration begins | Hist. → PROPOSED |
| 1869 | The Wakamatsu colony is founded and survives | Hist. → PROPOSED |
| 1870s | State irrigation districts; Hakka family emigration | PROPOSED |
| 1870s | First marriage-floor test case reaches the confederal court | APPROVED |
| After 1876 | Filipino reformers and families begin to settle in New Mexico and Arizona; larger flows in the 1880s | APPROVED |
| 1880–85 | Pacifica stays open to Chinese families and capital as others close | PROPOSED |

requests.source_text:
# CR-016 — The managed succession, 1883–1889

**Status:** Submitted for approval · **Raised:** 18 October 2026 · **Basis:** author decisions from the working session of 18 October 2026
**Affects:** Part IV §§18–21 (the sons' timing; Kaiulani's government during Elias's decline; Julian's birth; the 1887 constitution); Part V §§22–25 (the succession, the adoption, the Truce of Thalassia, the regency's institutions); Part VI §28 (the retiring commander); character trajectories of Kaiulani, Caleb Vance, Marcus Vance II and III, Silas, Kiyoshi (section H), Julian and his mother; explicitly unresolved decisions 10, 11 and 12
**Related:** CR-015 (B7 Keelung and Port Hamilton; B6 Vladivostok; E11 and J for the regency's later programmes); the Pacifica Power Timeline, 1865–1900 (1887: no foreign commitment within a year of the succession)

**Labels.** **APPROVED** marks a decision the author stated. **PROPOSED** marks working detail developed to carry it out; it awaits approval item by item. **OPEN** marks a question this CR raises or leaves unresolved. **Hist.** marks a real event used as an anchor; **Hist. → PROPOSED** marks an anchor whose outcome changes.

---

## 1. Summary

Elias's death in August 1887 does not start a civil war. There is no legitimate heir; Kaiulani has taken Julian as her hānai son and rears him as the successor. The three adult power centres, Silas's American military aristocrats, the Japanese naval party and the Polytechnic officers, can each block the others but cannot win without a war none can afford, and an infant heir under a regent is every faction's second choice. Kaiulani negotiates the Truce of Thalassia while Elias still lives; his death triggers the pact instead of a war. One armed standoff at Donner Pass, where Caleb Vance dies, is the price.

The Polytechnic role formerly held by Marcus Vance II passes to a decorated commander of the Pacific wars who is unrelated to the Vances by blood: Rafael Soberanes, the officer who brought the squadron home from Vladivostok after Marcus Vance I fell.

---

## 2. Decisions

### A. Principles

**A1. The regency is established without a civil war; Pacifica consolidates in 1887–89 instead of recovering.** APPROVED (general shape)

**A2. There is no legitimate heir. Kaiulani adopts Julian and rears him as the successor.** APPROVED

**A3. The Polytechnic leader of Part V is a decorated commander from one of the Pacific conflicts, unrelated to the Vances by blood.** His role, character arc and later retirement stay as in the master storyline; only his name and lineage change. APPROVED

### B. Historical precedents

| Precedent | What happened (Hist.) | What it gives the story | Label |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cixi and the Guangxu Emperor, 1875** | The Tongzhi Emperor died in January 1875 without a son. Against the succession rule, Cixi had her three-year-old nephew adopted as the son of the late Xianfeng Emperor and enthroned, which restored her regency. The princes and the Grand Council accepted; there was no war. Guangxu grew up, backed the 1898 reformers against her, and was confined on an island in the palace lake until his death. | The core model: no heir, a dowager adopts a child, the factions prefer a minor. Kaiulani watched it from Pacifica's position in China. The Union press calls her "the Pacific Cixi" from 1887. The 1932 ending inverts it: the adopted son confines the regent. | PROPOSED |
| **Hānai adoption** | Hawaiian chiefly families routinely raised kin's children as their own; Liliʻuokalani and Bernice Pauahi were both hānai children. Adoption of heirs was equally normal among the Japanese elite. | Julian's adoption is an ordinary aliʻi act, legible to the Hawaiian and Japanese constituencies. | PROPOSED |
| **Kaʻahumanu, 1819** | On Kamehameha I's death his favoured widow declared that he had wished her to share rule as kuhina nui and made it stick, at the cost of one short battle, at Kuamoʻo. | Hawaiian legitimacy for a widow who holds the Kuhina Nui office; one fight, not a war. | PROPOSED |
| **Spain, 1885** | Alfonso XII died in November 1885, leaving a foreign-born widow and a posthumous heir. The party leaders Cánovas and Sagasta agreed at El Pardo to sustain the regency and alternate in office. Villacampa's republican rising of September 1886 failed in a day; the regency lasted to 1902. | The pact among elites made while the ruler is dying. | PROPOSED |
| **Boulanger, 1889** | In January 1889 the popular general's supporters urged him to march on the Élysée; he did not, and fled within months. | Silas's moment at Donner Pass: the coup that is ready and never ordered. | PROPOSED |

### C. Before August 1887

| When | What happens | Label |
|---|---|---|
| c. 1858–65 | Silas and Kiyoshi are born, so that they are adults leading constituencies in 1887. Kiyoshi, the eldest, is born in 1859 (section H). Elias's infidelities therefore begin before the legitimate son's death, not after it, which darkens the marriage early. | PROPOSED; Silas's mother and date OPEN (OPEN-016-01) |
| Late 1870s | The legitimate son dies; Kaiulani, born 1838, can bear no more children (canon §18). | canon |
| 1883–87 | Elias declines. Kaiulani governs in practice. Keelung and the Customs Inspectorate (1884–85) and above all the Port Hamilton crisis (1885–87, CR-015 B7) become her successes, so she reaches 1887 with a record as well as a title. The Coral Sea war of old §21 stays removed (CR-015). | PROPOSED |
| June 1884 | Sherman, Pacifica's Inspector-General, gives the answer the real Sherman gave in June 1884 when a faction offers him power: if nominated he will not accept, if elected he will not serve (Hist.). The General Staff follows him; officers swear to the constitution, not to a person. He dies in February 1891 (Hist.), covering the critical years. | Hist. → PROPOSED |
| 1886 | Julian is born (canon c. 1886–87, here fixed to 1886). While his mother lives, Kaiulani takes him as her hānai son; Elias, already incapacitated, consents in writing. | APPROVED (adoption); PROPOSED (timing, form) |
| 1886–87 | The Truce of Thalassia is negotiated in Hawaii and signed in spring 1887, while Elias lives (section D). | PROPOSED |
| Summer 1887 | The imperial constitution of the 124 states (canon §21) includes a regency article naming Kaiulani regent with a regency council, and Julian heir. Elias's office of Providentor ends with him. Japan, China, Britain and the Confederacy agree in advance to recognize the regency within days, so the Union has no window to recognize a rival government; Pacifica is creditor to most of them. | PROPOSED |
| August 1887 | Elias dies (canon). The pact takes effect. | canon → PROPOSED |

### D. The Truce of Thalassia, moved before the death

**D1. Why it holds.** PROPOSED
- *Mutual veto:* Silas is unacceptable to the Japanese party, the Hawaiians and the Polytechnic; Kiyoshi is unacceptable to the American officers; neither can win without civil war. A one-year-old is everyone's second choice, as Guangxu was in 1875.
- *The only acceptable regent:* Kaiulani is the founder's widow, a Hawaiian aliʻi holding the Kuhina Nui, the diplomat of Port Hamilton, patron of the examination institutions and a friend of Japan; she controls Hawaii's harbours and coal (canon §22). At 49 she is credible and has years ahead of her.
- *The Polytechnic's choice:* Soberanes (section F), who controls the telegraph, prefers institutions to a strongman and sides with her. He plays the part of Cánovas.

**D2. Terms.** The terms of canon §24, signed a year earlier: PROPOSED
- an inland command for Silas, as warden of the interior West and the divide;
- a defined Japanese naval sphere under central oversight (the "1888 settlement" of CR-015 D2, now signed in 1887), with Kiyoshi as the naval party's leader (section H);
- the professional administration, the Polytechnic and the telegraph for Soberanes;
- the regency for Kaiulani, with a regency council in which each signatory sits;
- Julian as heir under the regency.

**D3. Donner Pass, the one crisis (autumn 1887).** Replaces the war of the inheritance. PROPOSED
- In the weeks after the funeral, Silas's frontier veterans and the Polytechnic corps face each other at Donner Pass over control of the Sierra line. It is a standoff, not a campaign.
- Someone fires (OPEN-016-03). Old Caleb Vance steps between the lines and is killed saving Soberanes, a man he is not related to: the frontier veteran dies for the institution man. The canon's theme survives intact: the younger man's instruments matter less than the veteran's judgment.
- Caleb's death shames both sides into honouring the Truce. Silas has his Boulanger moment: his officers wait for the order and he does not give it.

### E. Julian and his mother

**E1. Julian is the designated heir from infancy.** APPROVED (rears him as successor); PROPOSED (designation in the 1887 constitution)

**E2. His mother becomes a rival claim.** As Julian's natural guardian she is a competing claim to the regency of her own child. Her death after Elias's (canon §23) removes that claim, which strengthens the motive pointing at Kaiulani while the record stays inconclusive, as the Chronicler requires. Her name, family and agency stay OPEN (unresolved decision 11; OPEN-016-04). PROPOSED

**E3. The 1914 tension.** Passing over a designated, raised heir in favour of Kalanimoku in 1914 is now a broken promise, not merely a choice. It gives Julian's 1931 Restoration a real grievance and sharpens unresolved decision 12 (OPEN-016-05). PROPOSED

### F. Rafael Soberanes, replacing Marcus Vance II

**F1. Who he is.** PROPOSED
- *Born* 1847 at Monterey, the year after the Republic: a child of the founding. His Californio family, a fictional branch of the Monterey Soberanes, loses its rancho in the 1850s to squatters, debt and litigation even though Elias defended the land grants. Like Elias in 1837, he is a dispossessed boy; he concludes the opposite. Elias builds a personal state; Soberanes builds impersonal records, examinations and audits, so that no family's fate depends on a patron again.
- *Rise:* enters the naval academy by competitive examination in 1861, at fourteen, the first of his family to rise by merit rather than land. Gunnery officer at Manila Bay in 1873 (CR-015 B3).
- *Vladivostok, February 1878:* chief of staff to Marcus Vance I. When Marcus falls in the winter action, Soberanes completes the operation and brings the squadron home through the ice (CR-015 B6). The mantle passes by merit, not descent, which is the argument of his whole later regime.
- *1879–84:* builds the fleet signal service, the state telegraph and the officers' examinations.
- *Keelung, 1884–85:* commodore of the squadron that places Keelung under protection and makes France stop without a battle (CR-015 B7). He becomes the commander who wins without fighting, the friendship doctrine in uniform.
- *1885:* Superintendent of the Polytechnic and Director of Telegraphs. In 1887 he is forty.
- *No dynasty:* no son follows him into the service; his heirs are his graduates.

**F2. Unchanged from canon** (now attached to Soberanes): he organizes the Polytechnic officers and controls the communications in 1887 (§22); founds the examination regime and with Kaiulani gradually reduces the autonomy of bankers, hereditary commanders and families (§§19, 25); retains broad military and financial authority in the 1914 settlement (§27); retires in 1914–15, aged about 67, and recognizes that his system now runs without him (§28); later recognizes its excesses. APPROVED (role); PROPOSED (attribution)

**F3. Name.** Soberanes is a real Monterey family name; Rafael is fictional, so no real person is portrayed. PROPOSED

**F4. The Vance line.** Removing Vance II leaves Marcus Vance I (d. 1878) and Marcus Vance III (fall c. 1930–31). Recommended: Vance III is Marcus I's grandson through a son outside public life, and the Polytechnic's top graduate under Soberanes, heir to the system rather than to a father. OPEN (OPEN-016-06)

### G. What Kaiulani pays

| Trade-off | Consequence | Label |
|---|---|---|
| She rules through a pact | For years she governs by bargaining, within a council; consolidation is slow. This fits the Power Timeline's rule of no foreign commitment within a year of 1887, and canon §25. | PROPOSED |
| Silas guards the divide | His inland command makes him warden of the border with the Union: a natural target for Union intrigue, and tested in the Bread March of 1894 (CR-015 E10). | PROPOSED |
| Japanese autonomy is constitutional | The naval sphere buys peace in 1887 and is the root of the Kuroda faction's later demands. | PROPOSED |
| Julian is the designated heir | Every faction courts him from childhood; the 1914 bypass becomes a broken promise (E3). | PROPOSED |
| Elias's enabling law lapses | The 1865 power of cabinet legislation ends with the regency. It reassures the signatories and costs her a tool. | PROPOSED |
| Optional: the 1888 immigration switch | The move to selective immigration (CR-015 I3) may be part of the price paid to Silas's American faction, alongside the planter motive the Power Timeline suggests. | OPEN (OPEN-016-07) |

### H. Kiyoshi: Elias's eldest son and the Japanese naval party

**H0. Kiyoshi is Elias's eldest son, born to a Satsuma mother, and leads the Japanese naval party in 1887.** APPROVED

**H1. Origins, Kagoshima, 1858–59.** PROPOSED
- In 1858, the year of the Treaty of Edo, Elias visits Kagoshima through the Satsuma channel and tours the Shūseikan, Shimazu Nariakira's industrial works, with its furnaces, shipyard and the glassworks that made Satsuma cut glass (Hist.).
- His mother is the daughter of a Shūseikan glass master, trained in Dutch learning, who interprets for the visitors. Proposed name: Uehara Hisa. She has a life of her own and keeps the boy from Elias for thirteen years.
- Kiyoshi is born in 1859, two years into Elias's marriage and before the legitimate son. His name, 清, means "pure" or "clear": defiance or cruel irony for a child Satsuma calls *ainoko*, "half-blood".
- In August 1863, aged four, he watches the British fleet bombard Kagoshima and wreck the glassworks where his mother worked (Hist.). His first memory is sea power deciding what a city may be.

**H2. The rise, 1872–1887.** PROPOSED

| When | What happens | What it gives him |
|---|---|---|
| Jan 1872 | He arrives in San Francisco among the students of the Iwakura Mission, which made its first landfall there (Hist.), and meets his father for the first time, aged twelve. Kaiulani meets the living proof of an affair from the first year of her marriage. | Entry to Pacifica's naval academy, opened to Japanese cadets when Pacifica replaces the French military mission (CR-015 B2). Soberanes, then 25, is among his instructors. |
| 1872–77 | He trains in Pacifica, as the real Tōgō Heihachirō, also of Satsuma, trained in Britain from 1871 to 1878 (Hist.). Elias gives him patronage but not his name: he remains Uehara Kiyoshi, and the American officers call him "Thorne's Japanese boy". | Skill, and the grievance over his name that drives him. |
| 1877 | In the Satsuma Rebellion Pacifica backs Tokyo against Saigō, its oldest friends (CR-015 B5). Kiyoshi, eighteen, serves with the squadron supporting the government; a maternal uncle dies with Saigō at Shiroyama (24 September 1877, Hist.). | His defining wound, and his credential with Tokyo's government. |
| Feb 1878 | At Vladivostok he serves under Marcus Vance I and Soberanes and is decorated, then acts as liaison for the return of southern Sakhalin to Japan (CR-015 B6). | The first officer of Japanese blood honoured in a joint operation; a hero in Tokyo. |
| 1879 | Interpreter and aide to Elias in the Ryukyu mediation (CR-015 B5). | Father and son on the diplomatic stage, the closest they come. |
| 1884 | In the Gapsin coup the Japanese legation backs the plotters, as it historically did, while Pacifica's advisers stand aside (CR-015 B7). Kiyoshi sides with the Japanese. | His first act on his own account; Pacifica's leaders mark him as Japan's man. |
| 1884–85 | At Keelung he captains the Japanese-crewed ships in Soberanes's squadron (CR-015 B7). | A record beside the rival who once taught him. |
| 1885–87 | Commander of the western squadron based at Yokosuka and Hakodate. | A command, a base and men. |

**H3. Why the Japanese naval party follows him.** PROPOSED
- *Blood:* the founder's eldest son gives the Japanese officers a claim inside the dynasty.
- *Satsuma:* "the Satsuma navy, the Chōshū army" was a real saying; Japan's navy was a Satsuma preserve, so his birthplace makes him theirs despite his blood.
- *Record:* Vladivostok and Keelung.
- *Limits:* at 28 in 1887 he is the party's face more than its brain; older Satsuma officers use him, and part of his story is growing into the role. He is an outsider in both worlds, *ainoko* in Japan and an "Asiatic bastard" to Silas's officers, and needs the party as much as it needs him.
- *Why he signs the Truce:* the Americans will never accept him on the throne, so a defined naval sphere is worth more to him than a war he cannot win. He wants autonomy for his people, not the crown.

**H4. Precedent.** Kusumoto Ine (1827–1903), daughter of the German physician Philipp Franz von Siebold and a Nagasaki woman, became Japan's first woman doctor trained in Western medicine (Hist.). She shows that a child of a famous foreigner could rise in Japanese institutions through skill and patronage while remaining marked by her origins. PROPOSED

**H5. Where it leads.** PROPOSED
- *1889:* when Kaiulani proclaims the Hapa ideal, Kiyoshi is its living proof and its reproach, a child of an affair rather than a marriage.
- *1899:* in the Primorye war he commands at sea and enters Vladivostok, where Marcus Vance I died and where he won his first decoration (CR-015 D7).
- *Kuroda:* his relationship with the Kuroda house, the Japanese faction's later conflict with the regency, and any link to Lady Chiyo stay OPEN while the later parts are reworked (OPEN-016-08).

---

## 3. Superseded canon

| Section | Current text | Change |
|---|---|---|
| §18, unresolved decision 10 | The order of the other sons' births to be reconciled with the legitimate son's death | Silas and Kiyoshi born c. 1858–65, before the son's death; Kiyoshi in 1859 at Kagoshima (C, H) |
| §19, §21 | "The younger Marcus Vance" leads the examination state; Marcus Vance II commands in Indonesia, Australia and the Coral Sea | Soberanes leads the examination state; the 1887 campaigns stay removed (CR-015) |
| §21 | The 1887 constitution; the founder incapacitated | Adds the regency article, Julian's designation and the end of the Providentorship |
| §22 | The war of the inheritance: mutinies, provincial risings, fierce fighting around San Francisco, battle at Donner Pass; Caleb saves his grand-nephew Vance II | One armed standoff at Donner Pass; Caleb dies saving Soberanes; the Truce holds |
| §23 | Adoption after the mother's death, c. 1887–89 | Hānai adoption in 1886 while the mother lives; her death removes a rival claim to the regency |
| §24 | The Truce of Thalassia in 1888 among exhausted factions | The same terms, signed in spring 1887 while Elias lives |
| §§25, 27, 28 | Marcus Vance II | Rafael Soberanes |
| Character trajectories | Marcus Vance I, II and III | Marcus Vance I and III (lineage OPEN-016-06); Rafael Soberanes |
| Character trajectories | Silas and Kiyoshi: mothers, dates and constituencies OPEN | Kiyoshi set out in section H; Silas still OPEN |

---

## 4. Open items

| ID | Question | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| OPEN-016-01 | Silas's mother and birth date (unresolved decision 10; Kiyoshi's are set in H). | Within c. 1858–65. |
| OPEN-016-03 | Who fires at Donner Pass. | A young officer of Silas's, so the shame falls on the faction that wanted war. |
| OPEN-016-04 | Julian's mother: name, family, agency and death (unresolved decision 11). | — |
| OPEN-016-05 | Why the designated heir is passed over in 1914 (unresolved decision 12). | — |
| OPEN-016-06 | Marcus Vance III's lineage. | Marcus I's grandson, the Polytechnic's top graduate under Soberanes. |
| OPEN-016-07 | Whether the 1888 immigration switch is part of Silas's price. | Leave it as one of several motives the novel does not settle. |
| OPEN-016-08 | Kiyoshi and the Kuroda house: marriage or patronage, the Japanese faction's later conflict with the regency, and any link to Lady Chiyo. | Held open until the later parts are reworked. |

---

## 5. Alternatives considered and not adopted

- **The war of the inheritance (canon §22).** Not adopted: it exhausts Pacifica in the years it must consolidate in the Pacific.
- **An adult son as heir.** Not adopted: Silas or Kiyoshi on the throne is the outcome each other faction would fight.
- **Marcus Vance II as the Polytechnic leader.** Not adopted by author decision: it creates a glut of father-son successions.
- **Logan as the Polytechnic leader.** Considered: an engineer of Ericsson's school fits the technocrat, but his war is the Gulf, not the Pacific, and merging the roles costs a character.

---

## 6. Follow-up

- Bring master storyline §§18–28 and the character trajectories into line with this CR.
- Record Soberanes's service in CR-015 B3, B6 and B7 (Manila Bay, Vladivostok, Keelung) when CR-015 is next revised.
- Decide the remaining unresolved decisions 10–12 with OPEN-016-01, 04 and 05.
- Record Kiyoshi's service in CR-015 B5, B6, B7 and D7 when CR-015 is next revised.

requirements: A1: Pacifica keeps the empire by making Japanese elites stakeholders. Endpoint: commanding institutions Pacifican in origin and location, many of their most influential people Japanese; Japan retains its domestic state and crown; Japan's national government cannot order the common empire into war.

A2: The imperial class wins the commanding heights. Japanese and Pacifican supporters of the empire, who leave national identity behind for the new imperialism, rise to its top offices. The new Japan persuades the old Japan to join politically and dynastically.

A3: Japan learning too well and becoming too powerful drives the tension. By 1914 Japan has about 52 million people against perhaps 10 million in North American Pacifica (Hist. for Japan; Pacifican figure to the audit).
A4: The Austro-Hungarian model is the constitutional template, reached through the Pacific Concord in 1927, with the 1928 lawful cure and five-year renewal fixed by CR-021.
A5: War with Russia, yes; no Afghanistan.

A6: The succession. Kalanimoku is the legitimate son killed in the late 1870s. Julian takes over from Kaiulani directly in 1915 and marries Chiyo. There is no separate emperor and no Chinese Pacifican head of government.
A7: The collapse ending is replaced: the Pacific becomes the dominant superpower on earth by 1932.
A8: The Union stays out of Europe's Great War. A peace brokered by Pacifica is one half of the story; the Pacific with Japan and China is the other.
A9: The Qing falls in 1911; there are enough reasons without Pacifica.
A10: Julian backs Sun and leaves Yuan to his fate. He saves his clout for persuading Tokyo not to move against Sun and not to create a Manchurian client state.
A11: The Second Founding of 1931 is dropped.

A12: Julian pursues the course that most increases Pacifica's freedom of action in the Pacific and makes future wins likelier for his successors. Taking territory from China or a prize from Japan is acceptable where it serves those aims. Pacifica's full military might must be tested, or Julian looks like a paper tiger.
A13: Pacifica wins in Siberia, and Japan expands there rather than into Manchuria. The Soviet state is kept in check and its collapse brought forward.
A14: The Soviets are the greater danger. No attack on Britain in the same decade, which could forge an alliance between London and Moscow.
A15: The line is held on the Ob, with Chinese cooperation.
A16: Canon correction: Russia never finishes the Trans-Siberian to the Pacific; Japan completes it and holds at least the terminal. The Amur's north bank went to China in 1899.
A17: No self-coup by Julian in 1931.
A18: Chiang Kai-shek succeeds Sun. Zhang Zuolin is still assassinated in 1928, and his son Zhang Xueliang holds Manchuria.
A19: OPEN-018-01 to 10 are decided as recommended (section 5).

A20: OPEN-018-11 to 17 and 19 are decided as recommended (section 5). Marcus Vance III's story is to be revised: he must not be a flat caricature of the aggressive American war criminal, the focus on his atrocity must fit a war whose massacres were far worse, and his arc needs emotional tension to earn its place (OPEN-018-18, section N).
A21: No mediated peace in 1905. Kaiulani wants Japan to win, and Theodore Roosevelt cannot mediate against her (CR-019 G).
open: OPEN-018-18: Marcus Vance III's story, revised by author decision (A20). Recommendation remains proposed: Section N: the Soberanes-raised foster brother of Julian, a cautious logistics officer thrust into command, whose gas attack in the Altai kills the partner's own prisoners; he tells Kaiulani the truth Julian buried, executes Julian's threat in 1931 and is killed in May 1932 by guards avenging the Altai, having left the true report with the Chronicler.
OPEN-018-20: resolved by CR-039 (28 October 2026): the peace of 1905 is signed at Urajio, the former Vladivostok.
All remaining PROPOSED mechanics and quantitative feasibility retain their source status.

# CR-018 — Pacifica, Japan, China and Siberia, 1887–1932: the stakeholder empire and the war in the north

**Status:** Submitted for approval · **Raised:** 18 October 2026, merged with CR-017 the same day · **Basis:** author decisions from the working session of 18 October 2026
**Supersedes:** CR-017 (Pacifica and Japan, 1887–1932: the stakeholder empire), never merged, folded in here. Where CR-017 and the later decisions of this CR contradict each other, the later decisions prevail (section 2).
**Affects:** master storyline of 18 October 2026, Part IV §18, Part V §§24–27, Part VI §§26, 28–32, Part VII §§33–37; CR-015 B6 and D7 (correction, section B); character trajectories of Kaiulani, Julian, Chiyo, Kiyoshi, Kuroda, Marcus Vance III, the Japanese partners and heirs, and the Chinese and Siberian partners; explicitly unresolved decisions 9 and 12
**Related:** CR-015 (Japan and China to 1900; the Primorye war); CR-016 (the managed succession; Soberanes; Kiyoshi, section H; Julian's succession, E3); the Pacifica Power Timeline, 1865–1900; a companion CR on Europe and the Union, to follow (section 7)

**Labels.** **APPROVED** marks a decision the author stated. **PROPOSED** marks working detail developed to carry it out; it awaits approval item by item. **OPEN** marks a question this CR raises or leaves unresolved. **Hist.** marks a real event used as an anchor. **Hist. (baseline)** marks a real office-holder used as the default incumbent; divergence may change who holds the office, but the baseline keeps domestic politics concrete.

---

## 1. Summary

Pacifica keeps its empire by making Japanese elites stakeholders in it. The empire's commanding institutions stay Pacifican in origin and location, but many of their most powerful people are Japanese by origin. Japan keeps its own state, army and crown, and its government cannot simply order the empire into war.

The supporters of the empire in both nations, who trade national identity for the imperial project, reach its commanding heights. It is this "new Japan", not ethnic Europeans, that persuades the old Japan to join politically and dynastically in 1927, at a moment of Japanese weakness. Each people is told it has absorbed the other. The union holds: when Japan's army defies its own government in 1931–32, the common institutions decide the crisis.

Kalanimoku, Elias and Kaiulani's legitimate son, dies in the late 1870s. Julian, Elias's son by a Hawaiian-American mother and Kaiulani's hānai son, takes over from Kaiulani directly in 1915, aged about 29, and marries Lady Chiyo. Kaiulani, born in 1838, is 77 when she hands over, 83 when she renounces her remaining role in 1921 and 89 at the union of 1927.

The novel ends in triumph: by 1932 the Pacific is the dominant power on earth. This CR sets out the Pacific half of that ending; the European half, the peace Pacifica brokers in 1918 and the Union's entry into its order, follows in a companion CR. Julian's aim is the course that most increases Pacifica's freedom of action and makes future wins likely for his successors. The old guardrails against taking land from China or prizes from Japan no longer bind him, and after decades of brokered peaces Pacifica must show that it can fight. Its test is Siberia. Where the historical intervention of 1918–22 failed, the Pacifican-led coalition of Japan, China, the Siberians and Pacifica wins, holds a line on the Ob and forces Moscow to sign in 1921. Japan expands into Siberia instead of Manchuria; the Soviet state is boxed in between the coalition and Germany's eastern order.

In China, the Qing falls in 1911 as in history. Pacifica backs Sun Yat-sen, educated in Honolulu, and leaves Yuan Shikai to his fate. Julian saves his influence over Tokyo for the moments that matter: stopping Japan's army from moving against Sun's movement and from creating a Manchurian client state. By 1932 China is reunified under Sun's successor, Chiang Kai-shek, allied and committed to the Siberian front; Japan's army has its frontier in the north; and the coalition's command, money and railways run from Thalassia.

---

## 2. Merging CR-017: what the later decisions change

| CR-017 passage | CR-017 text | Now |
|---|---|---|
| Summary | The common government escapes everyone; the dissenters of both nations rise together: Julian's Restoration and the Shōwa Restoration officers | The union holds; Japan's army plot and the May 1932 coup fail (I5, I6). No self-coup (A17). |
| A5 | War with Britain not yet decided | No war with Britain before 1932 (E4) |
| C, 1921–1927 | The machinery increasingly governs around Julian | Julian reigns and sets strategy; the machinery runs under him (D1) |
| C, 1927–1931 | The common ministries escape Julian too | Removed; the union works (D1) |
| C, 1931–1932 | Julian's Restoration; Vance III killed by his guards; Julian as Lord-Restorer | Removed (A17); Vance III's end is OPEN-018-18 |
| C1 | In 1931 Chiyo's husband turns against the institutions she helped build | Removed; in 1931 Chiyo carries Julian's threat to Tokyo (D3) |
| D, 1904–05 | "With the Trans-Siberian finished"; a mediated peace cuts the victory short; the Hibiya riots | Railway corrected (B); no mediated peace: Japan wins outright (A21; F, 1900–1905) |
| D, 1918–22 | The failed Siberian campaign and the dismantled railway | The Siberian war is won (G) |
| D, 1927 | The common ministries answer to neither people nor to Julian; Kaiulani opposes the union | Kaiulani opposes the decree, not the union (F, 1927) |
| D, 1927–31 | Julian, sidelined, turns to the frontier myth and the populists (canon §33) | Removed; the union's burdens and the Restoration circles stay (F) |
| D, 1931 to c. 1932 | The Restoration; the fleet's Japanese units sail home; Thalassia burns | The Manchurian plot is stopped (I5); the May coup fails and the units stay (I6) |
| G, 1931–32 | Kaiulani captive (canon §36) | Removed with the Restoration; she lives to see 1932 (M) |
| OPEN-017-01 | The British war | Resolved (E4) |
| OPEN-017-02, 03, 05, 06, 07, 09, 10 | Open | Carried forward as OPEN-018-11 to 17 and decided (section 5) |

---

### A. Author decisions
