source_excerpts: **CR-022 integration:** [Silas, Abigail Merritt and Donner Pass](CR-022.md), revision 3. Silas is Elias's eldest son, born in 1851 to Abigail Merritt, the pastor's daughter; Kiyoshi becomes the second son, reversing CR-016's seniority. At Donner Silas fires at Soberanes and Caleb dies in his place; the lie holds. Silas confesses to Victoria in 1912 and dies that winter. Where CR-016's summary above calls Kiyoshi the eldest son, CR-022 governs.

**[APPROVED — CR-022]** The pastor whose nose Elias broke takes in the widow and her son. His daughter Abigail, two years older than the boy, keeps the house while Mrs Thorne sinks under the loss; she feeds him, mends for him, reads with him and scolds him. He finds in her the mother that grief has taken from him.

**[APPROVED — CR-022]** Years later Abigail Merritt says her dying father told her to marry the boy he had taken in. Only she heard it. The story is persuasive, flattering and impossible for the Chronicler to verify; its source is her own papers, kept with the Thorne family Bible and the letters Elias's mother wrote to a son they never reached. Whether the pastor admired Elias, forgave him, or was remembered according to his daughter's needs remains uncertain.

**[APPROVED — CR-022]** In 1849 the Rev. Silas Merritt brings a Methodist mission to Sacramento, with his daughter Abigail, unmarried at twenty-seven. She seeks out the famous young man she once mothered; she alone calls him Eli. Her father dies in the cholera of 1850, telling her to marry him. They become lovers, but in 1851 Elias sails for Honolulu as the princes' guest, drawn by a larger world than Sacramento's settlers. Abigail finds that she is pregnant and does not tell him. Only Caleb knows. She marries Henry Pruett, a San Antonio man who shared the Mexican captivity, and goes home to Texas, where Silas is born late in 1851, legitimate in law as Pruett's son.

**[PROPOSED]** A Pacifican California column establishes control of Arizona and New Mexico in 1862; Richmond renounces its Arizona claim in return for credit and the future railway connection. **[PROPOSED — CR-022]** Before the renunciation the column drives Baylor's Texans from Mesilla in a brief clash both governments prefer to forget. Among the Texan dead is Captain Henry Pruett of San Antonio. Idaho's mining districts turn toward the Northwest in 1863, western Montana's camps toward Salt Lake and Walla Walla in 1863–1864. Washoe is retaken in 1863–1864. Washington still admits Nevada in October 1864 to claim its electoral votes, then loses it in the peace. Exact forces, routes, accession instruments and the new members' representation remain **[OPEN]**; civilian and Native authority require their own agreements.

**[APPROVED — CR-022]** Early in 1863 Elias goes to Texas in person to settle the Arizona renunciation and the Matamoros supply terms. Caleb insists that they carry Pruett's watch to his widow together. Abigail opens the door; behind her stands an eleven-year-old with Elias's build. Elias learns he has a son in the week the boy learns who his father is, from the men whose soldiers killed the father who raised him. She will not come to California and takes money only for the boy. She asks for the name, and Elias refuses it.

**[APPROVED — CR-022]** The examinations reach the officer corps in mid-career. Many of the old army's fighting officers fail them. Silas fails the mathematics and is capped below general rank; Elias refuses to intervene. The American officers' grievance against the examination state has his face.

**[APPROVED — CR-022]** One armed standoff at Donner Pass in October 1887 tests the pact. The Polytechnic corps comes up to take over the Sierra telegraph under its charter; Silas's veterans hold the summit as the inland command's line. Caleb brokers a parley in the telegraph hut inside the snowshed. Before it, Abigail has told her son that Soberanes must not come down from that pass. When Soberanes says that Elias's last instruction to him was that the wire must not be divided, Silas draws and fires at him. Caleb steps across and takes the bullet. Dying in Silas's arms, he says: "Don't give it." Silas's officers wait for the order to advance, and he does not give it. Soberanes dictates the first dispatch: shot from outside the shed. The inquest finds a person unknown. Every man in the room is bound by the lie, and Silas is praised for the restraint of a man who fired. There is no campaign, general mutiny or civil war. Caleb's sacrifice remains the working implementation of the managed-succession direction.

Victoria governs through bargaining. Elias’s enabling-law delegation lapses at the beginning of the regency, reassuring the factions while limiting her instruments. **[APPROVED — CR-022]** The 1888 restriction is presented as Silas's price, but it is what Victoria wanted, and she holds the Donner report. He takes the blame. In the Bread March of 1894 his border command detains the marchers, and he insists that they be fed and tried, not shot. Pacifica consolidates through 1887–1889, with foreign military adventures paused around the succession. The compact begins a relationship whose later Concord will depend on Japanese consent and on different understandings of who has gained command.

**[APPROVED — CR-022]** Silas's nativists raise a school-segregation crisis in 1906. His former adjutant Harlan Tate now runs Sacramento; his board segregates Japanese pupils and revokes the licence of the mission school Silas's mother endowed. Silas, declining into drink, lends the crisis his name and is privately ashamed of it. Roosevelt courts Tokyo and sends the Great White Fleet around Cape Horn to Yokohama, while his immigration restrictions make the courtship unreliable. A more confident Japan bargains hard in the 1907 compact renewal, securing Kiyoshi as Japanese Fleet-General, a joint war council, family immigration and civic equality for Japanese Pacificans.

In 1905–1906 Julian spends a year in Tokyo attached to the legation and navy, meeting Saionji as he becomes prime minister. Victoria's language education gives the nineteen-year-old access beyond interpreters and formal audiences. Coming of age in 1907 gives him no crown: the constitution leaves its establishment to an Act of Settlement, and Victoria delays while the eldest son lives. **[APPROVED — CR-022]** In 1909 Silas's younger daughter marries Lieutenant Commander Tanabe Makoto of Kiyoshi's staff in the chapel of her grandmother's mission school; the Fleet-General comes to Sacramento, and the two sons denied their father's name meet for the only time. In the autumn of 1912 Silas comes to Thalassia and confesses Donner to Victoria, who has known for twenty-five years; he dies at Sacramento that winter. In 1913 an examined officer receives the inland command. The Act of Settlement waits another year, because the founder's second son now claims to be his eldest.

**[PROPOSED — CR-022]** At his accession the regency's sealed papers pass to Julian. Looking for the truth of his mother's death, he finds instead the truth of Donner, kept by the woman who raised him. He tells no one that he knows.

**[PROPOSED — OPEN-018-18]** Julian approves a falsified report to protect the approaching treaty. Vance signs it, then tells Victoria the truth. She confronts her adopted son over the attack and the lie, renouncing her remaining political role in 1921 at about eighty-three. **[PROPOSED — CR-022]** He knows that she kept the Donner lie for twenty-five years. Whether he says so is **[OPEN-022-12]**. She withholds a public denunciation to preserve the settlement, becoming complicit in the silence she condemns. Vance retains command, but neither relationship recovers its former trust.

The Senate votes the rescue loan but refuses the treaty: Pacifica would pay sixty-five percent of common costs, Japan's mass threatens dilution, and county boards want leverage against the Commissioners. **[APPROVED — CR-022]** Harlan Tate, Sacramento's senator and Silas's old adjutant, leads the refusal, adding that foreign coupon-clippers already draw nearly $300 million a year from Pacifican industry. Julian claims provisional application under the treaty prerogative pending consent, though the Senate has already refused. This is illegal in substance. Japan's Emperor ratifies on the Privy Council's conditional advice and the Diet votes its quota; its side follows Japanese law and can lapse if Pacifica never obtains consent.

Victoria supports the Concord and opposes its illegal imposition. In 1928 she wins two-thirds Senate consent and an Act of Indemnity. **[PROPOSED — CR-022]** She calls on Tate once at Sacramento; neither mentions Donner. His bloc splits and he abstains. Julian accepts a five-year first term instead of ten, quota review at renewal, Pacifica's delegates chosen half by each chamber and a Polytechnic audit reported to the Senate. The constitutional case at Monterey is mooted before judgment. The legal cure gives the friendship institutions that can outlast it.

1. **The mountain upbringing and French veteran:** Elias's birthplace, family migration and holding, the jurisdiction and creditor claims behind the 1837 dispossession; the French mentor's name, actual Napoleonic service, credibility of his claimed rank, and his eventual relationship to Elias.
2. **Resolved by CR-022:** the pastor's daughter is Abigail Merritt; the source of the marriage story is her own papers; the pastor's denomination is proposed as Methodist and his place remains open.
3. **Texas:** Elias's position during the Council House Fight and his and Caleb's exact experiences on the 1841–42 Santa Fe expedition and subsequent captivity.
4. **The 1846 founding:** the final Santa Barbara convention date, leadership of the Californio coalition, reconciliation of Pico and Castro, and substantive obligations to Indigenous polities.
5. **The naval confrontation:** the battle with Frémont's irregulars, Sloat's exact response, British diplomacy, terms of recognition by Mexico, and how the debt settlement is financed before the gold rush.
6. **Gold and public finance:** precise discovery location, named Sonoran and Miwok/Yokuts collaborators, mining claims, private land titles, Indigenous rights, public royalty receipts and the state's credit system.
7. **California's legal consolidation:** transitional courts, common-law reception and retained Mexican rules, Indigenous claims, incorporation and patent statutes, citizenship/franchise, and the scope of Elias's revenue office under President Vallejo.
8. **Resolved by CR-027:** Victoria Kamāmalu holds the Kuhina Nui from 1855, succeeds Lot in 1872 and leases Puʻuloa in 1874; the February rising replaces the massacre. requirements: Japan uses its own fiscal cash to rebuild banks; Pacifica supplies the foreign exchange in the severe bank panic. The 1927 provisional Concord, 1928 indemnity and 1932 renewal retain CR-021’s chronology.

source_excerpts: **CR-024 integration:** [Japan's 1927 rescue](CR-024.md) makes the bank crisis the Concord's decisive negotiation: Japan rebuilds its banks with its own money, and Pacifica supplies the foreign exchange nobody else will. Its amounts are MODEL estimates. The 1927 provisional application, 1928 indemnity and 1932 renewal remain governed by CR-021 revision 9.

**[MODEL — CR-024]** About $400m of losses wipe out the affected banks' owners, and Japan puts in $400m of new capital; the Bank of Japan lends $295m. Three-quarters of $2bn in short foreign funding is not renewed. Outside Pacifican hands, London acceptance houses and British overseas banks hold about $400m of it, Union banks $250m, continental banks $100m and Chinese and Indian banks in Shanghai and Hong Kong $50m. Keeping six weeks of imports in reserve requires about $497m from abroad.

requests.title: Wartime credit, Japan’s boom and who pays
requests.authorization: Current user requests publication of the updated storyline and CR-027 Section E reconciliation.
requirements: Wartime Entente credit funds Japanese industry on short foreign money; peace and the earthquake leave unresolved debts. Champion foreign investment uses retained profits, savings and foreign/partner funding as described in the supplied storyline.
All numerical stocks, flows and facility terms in the supplied storyline remain MODEL; no financial workbook is recalculated here.

source_excerpts: **CR-025 integration:** [Wartime credit, Japan's boom and who pays](CR-025.md) explains how the Entente loans of 1914–18 build Japanese factories and shipyards on short foreign money, how peace and the 1923 earthquake leave those debts unresolved, and who finances the champions' growth abroad. Its amounts are MODEL estimates.

The champions grow first on their own profits, and the savings bank lends them the nation's deposits. The Crown's shares, taken in exchange for charters and patents, make the state an owner without building anything. Abroad the champions build with partners: Japanese and Chinese merchant houses and Gulf and Mexican investors take about a quarter of each venture. Before 1914 the champions sell bonds in London, Paris and Amsterdam, and in the 1920s on Wall Street and in Tokyo. Like the Union before 1914, Pacifica becomes a creditor through its Treasury and partly a debtor through its companies, and foreigners draw a growing income from its success. **[MODEL — CR-025]** By 1929 foreign holders own about $3.8bn of claims on the champions and draw about $280m a year from them.

**[MODEL — CR-025]** The advances total $8.5bn: $1.7bn from the Treasury, $2.85bn from Pacifican savers and $3.95bn from abroad, about half of it from Union investors and the rest from collateral loans, Japan, the neutrals, and the Gulf and Latin America. About $1.66bn becomes Japanese orders. Japanese firms keep about $124m of their profits for a $1.33bn expansion and borrow the other $1.2bn from their banks.

source_excerpts: **CR-026 integration:** [Kiyoshi's bid for the crown](CR-026.md), revision 6. With Silas dead, Kiyoshi claims the crown in 1913 and renounces it in 1914 in exchange for the Kuroda queen; the Act of Settlement names him as Elias's son. He founds his own Kuroda branch and is made a count in 1907; Kiyotaka's son Kiyonaka keeps the main house.

Kiyoshi has entered Kuroda Kiyotaka’s house in 1886 as an adopted son-in-law, marrying into it and taking the name Kuroda Kiyoshi. Japan gives him the name Elias withheld. His family position binds the naval party to a recognized Japanese house. Lady Chiyo belongs to another branch of that house; **[APPROVED — CR-026]** Kiyotaka's own son Kiyonaka remains heir of the main house. Kiyoshi's bride is Kiyotaka's adopted daughter Hyaku. After the victory of 1905 Kiyoshi founds his own branch house and is made Count Kuroda in 1907; his son will inherit it.

**[APPROVED — CR-026]** With Silas dead, Kuroda Kiyoshi claims the crown the Act is to create. Early in 1913 he petitions the Regent as the founder's eldest surviving son and asks that the crown follow the founder's blood. He offers to reign only for his lifetime, with Julian after him; Victoria sees that an eldest-son rule would carry the crown to his Kuroda son. He needs only to deny Julian two-thirds and outlast a Regent of seventy-five. In Tokyo his mother's cousin Uehara Yūsaku has just brought down a cabinet by resigning the army ministry; Kiyoshi lets it be known that if the Act passes over him, no officer of the naval party will accept the western squadron's command. In October the squadron anchors off Kāneʻohe Bay on a courtesy visit, in sight of Thalassia, and he gives no order.

Succession passes to the eldest son, then eldest daughter, otherwise to an heir adopted with Senate consent. Noe's Maui chiefly descent strengthens Julian's claim alongside his adoption by a Kamehameha queen. Loyalists dispute whether a hānai son may continue the Kamehameha line. The Act heals much politically, but does not reverse the Supreme Court's ignored judgment of 1876. **[APPROVED — CR-026]** The Act recites Kiyoshi's renunciation and names him "Kuroda Kiyoshi, son of Elias Thorne", the only public document that ever does. He never uses the name.

Julian marries Lady Chiyo, a Japanese woman of the kazoku and another branch of the Kuroda house. Kiyoshi arranges the match, binding the naval party to his half-brother’s throne. **[APPROVED — CR-026]** The match is the price of his renunciation: his house supplies the queen, and the heir after Julian is of Kuroda blood. Chiyo’s Japanese standing protects the imperial class from appearing to have abandoned Japan. Their son is named Kahekili for Noe’s Maui line, with the Japanese name 雷, Ikazuchi, given by meaning through Chiyo’s family; **[PROPOSED]** he is born about 1916. Exact wedding and birth dates remain qualified. The heir will reign in Hawaii as Kamehameha VII; he is distinct from Elias and Victoria’s lost Kalanimoku. Japan’s succession law excludes him, so the shared dynasty does not merge the crowns.

**[PROPOSED]** In her final months as regent, Victoria blocks the worst of Japan’s Twenty-One Demands on China. Tokyo retreats and concludes that access to Thalassia’s institutions offers more than direct defiance. **[PROPOSED — CR-026]** Kiyoshi backs her, the first service he renders the settled crown. The episode tests the limits of a partnership in which Japan has learned Pacifica’s methods and grown strong enough to demand a share in their direction.

Restoration officers strike against Inukai's government in May 1932 to stop the Concord's first renewal. Their manifesto names Chiyo and Kahekili's betrothal and attacks the Thalassia bakufu and the merchant houses that share in its champions. Emperor Shōwa and the navy stand against them, and the coup fails. Japanese-crewed carriers in the western squadron make the danger to Oʻahu concrete; Kiyoshi's son holds its Japanese units loyal. **[APPROVED — CR-026]** He learned in 1913 that a fleet cannot make a sovereign.

requests.title: Victoria Kamāmalu, the Puʻuloa lease and the Five
requests.authorization: User asks to apply Section E of supplied CR-027 and publish a new PR; supplied source marks author approval on 21 October 2026.
requirements: CR-027 A1: The fictional Kaiulani is replaced by the historical Victoria Kamāmalu (b. 1 November 1838), Kaʻahumanu IV, daughter of Kīnaʻu and Kekūanāoʻa. There is no fictional cousin. [APPROVED]
CR-027 A2: Elias first meets her in 1851, aged thirteen, as the princes' sister. Courtship from 1854 as in canon. [APPROVED]
CR-027 A3: At the Confederation ceremony of 31 July 1856 he hears her chant a mele of her own; her voice haunts him for the rest of his life. [APPROVED]

CR-027 A4: Her brothers block her childhood betrothal to Lunalilo for reasons of rank and press Kalākaua on her in 1857. She refuses both out of love for Elias; her songs *Pua Hau ʻo Maleka* and *Aita ʻOe e Parau* claim the right to choose. No Monsarrat affair, no alcoholism. [APPROVED]
CR-027 A5: The brothers accept Elias because his children would rank through her alone, he claims none of her lands, and he removes her from the missionary party's reach. [APPROVED]
CR-027 A6: The wedding is in **November 1858** at Kawaiahaʻo, after the Treaty of Edo. [APPROVED]
CR-027 A7: Kiyoshi is conceived in the spring of 1858 during the Edo negotiations, before the wedding, and born in Kagoshima in 1859. [APPROVED]

CR-027 A8: She is Kuhina Nui from January 1855, holds the crown's powers for a day on 30 November 1863 and proclaims Lot. Lot keeps the office (historically abolished in 1864) and names her heir. [APPROVED]

CR-027 A9: She founds the Kaʻahumanu Society in 1863, leads the Kawaiahaʻo choir and keeps a kahuna. Her kahuna dies in May 1865; Monterey's physicians save her in 1866. The turn toward measuring what works begins there. [APPROVED]
CR-027 A10: She becomes Queen in December 1872 under Article 22, without an election, and appoints Ruth Keʻelikōlani Kuhina Nui. Lunalilo leads the opposition and dies on 3 February 1874. [APPROVED]

CR-027 A11: The barracks mutiny of September 1873: Jajczay (hired by Lot) and Judd (her schoolmate) are dismissed; she goes to the barracks on the first day, refuses the admirals' marines, keeps the Queen's Guard under Moehonua and makes Kalākaua answerable for it. [APPROVED]

CR-027 A12: The surviving Guard is the admirals' decisive argument for Pearl Harbor. In February 1874 she keeps it in barracks during the rising in her name; the rising has deaths blamed by each side on the other. No massacre. [APPROVED]

CR-027 A13: In March 1874 she signs the Puʻuloa Convention, a fifty-year lease and a defence treaty: **LEGAL**. The ordinances of 1874–1876 and the appointed Territorial Council: **ILLEGAL**. Ruth resigns rather than recognize the Council; the Supreme Court declares the ordinances void; she lets the ruling stand on paper. [APPROVED (shape); dates and instruments PROPOSED]
CR-027 A14: Elias's motive is cold and strategic: Manila, the fleet and a legislature outside powers could sway. He never acts from hostility to Hawaiians. [APPROVED]

CR-027 A15: The English Schools Ordinance of 1876 is the Territorial Council's; Elias does not overrule it; the 1887 constitution entrenches Hawaiian too late; Victoria funds Hawaiian-language schools through the Society. [APPROVED]
CR-027 A16: Emma is the loyalists' counter-queen until 1885 and plants her coconuts at the fleet's gate at Puʻuloa; afterwards the loyalists look to Albert Kūnuiākea. [APPROVED]
CR-027 A17: Victoria keeps her own estate, so Ruth's, and later Pauahi's, are smaller than historically. [APPROVED]

CR-027 A18: Kalākaua is her minister of the image and envoy, not an administrator: legends, the Iron Knife, the 1881 world tour with Judd, the Oceania proposal and the Kaʻiulani–Komatsu match, *Hoʻoulu Lāhui*. He never touches the purse and dies in San Francisco in 1891. [APPROVED]
CR-027 A19: The historical Kaʻiulani (b. 1875) exists as a minor figure in the Cleghorn household. [APPROVED]
CR-027 A20: Noe nurses in 1881 at Emma's Queen's Hospital; her first patrons are loyalists. [APPROVED]

CR-027 A21: The Five: the heads of the chartered estates run the technocratic state. Soberanes, Logan Turner and Tesla hold seats in 1887; there are always five; the unwritten arrangement with the Crown (B6). [APPROVED]

CR-027 A23: The Office of Public Measures measures, as do the Polytechnic's audit and examinations; the Five's press seat publishes. The Regent's own life's work is the Office, not the press. [APPROVED]

CR-027 A24: From 1887 she is Regent of Pacifica and remains Queen of Hawaii. The 1914 Act joins her crown to Pacifica's and dissolves the Territorial Council; in 1915 she lays down both regency and crown, and Julian accedes. [APPROVED]
CR-027 A25: Names by register: "Victoria" for the narrator and Westerners, "Kamāmalu" for Hawaiians, "Kaʻahumanu" on state documents. [APPROVED]
CR-027 A26: The mythic structure in B9: four backbone myths and a table of echoes. [APPROVED (section); individual echoes PROPOSED]

# CR-027 — Victoria Kamāmalu, the Puʻuloa lease and the Five

**Status:** Approved by the author (21 October 2026) and merged into the master storyline of 21 October. Details marked PROPOSED carry that label into the storyline · **Raised:** 21 October 2026
**Depends on:** CR-021 (constitutional chronology), CR-022 (Silas, Abigail), CR-026 (Kiyoshi's bid). Apply after CR-026.
**Affects:** master storyline header, "The novel's larger movement", §6, §8, §11, §12, §17, §18, §19, §20, §21, §22, §23, §24, §25, §27, the character trajectories and unresolved items 8 and 19; every other passage through the rename rule (C0).
**Labels:** **APPROVED** = decided by the author · **PROPOSED** = recommended, awaiting decision · **OPEN** = undecided

---

## Summary

1. **The historical Victoria Kamāmalu replaces the fictional Kaiulani.** Born in 1838, sister of Kamehameha IV and V, Kuhina Nui as Kaʻahumanu IV from 1855. Every canon role of Kaiulani passes to her; references to Kaiulani in CR-016 to CR-026 refer to her.
2. **She chooses Elias.** He hears her chant at the Confederation ceremony of 1856 and her voice haunts him for life. In 1857 she refuses Lunalilo and Kalākaua out of love for him, and her brothers accept the match for reasons of rank, property and party. They marry in November 1858. Kiyoshi is conceived that spring, before the wedding.
3. **She survives 1866 and becomes Queen in 1872.** Monterey's physicians save her after her kahuna's failure; she succeeds Lot under his 1864 constitution and appoints Ruth Kuhina Nui.
4. **1874 is a lease, then a creep.** She ends the barracks mutiny of 1873 herself and keeps the Queen's Guard, which convinces the admirals they need Pearl Harbor. After Lunalilo's death she refuses a rising in her name, then signs a lawful fifty-year lease of Puʻuloa. The confederal ordinances of 1874–1876 and the Territorial Council that stretch it into rule are illegal; her Supreme Court says so, and she lets the ruling go. No massacre, no abeyance.
5. **Kalākaua is her mythmaker and envoy; the Five run the machine.** The heads of the chartered estates govern the technocratic state under an unwritten arrangement: the Crown does not touch the estates, and the estates never move against the Crown.
6. **From 1887 she is Regent of Pacifica and still Queen of Hawaii.** The Act of Settlement of 1914 joins her crown to the Crown of Pacifica; in 1915 she lays down both and Julian accedes.

---

---

## B. The design

### B1. Who she is

The portrait rests on the sources, read against their biases. Sophia Cracroft (1861), an Anglican guest of Wyllie and Emma, found her stately, imposing and of unpleasant countenance, and recorded the "very inconvenient influence" of the missionaries over her acts as Kuhina Nui. Hawaiian tradition held her Lunalilo's equal "in looks, intelligence, manners, and volatility"; Commissioner Gregg found her at fifteen well educated and more engaging than most girls her age. She was the pro-American Kamehameha, refused to leave the Congregational church when her family turned Anglican, led the Kawaiahaʻo choir, chanted and composed in the old style, and in her last historical years turned back toward Hawaiian tradition. Twice the American party tried to make her its candidate (1854 by Wyllie's account; 1863, when missionaries argued that the regency was hers), and twice she gave way to her family: in 1863 she proclaimed Lot herself, letting the constitution's form go for an orderly succession.

Her pattern: others mean to use her; she yields on form and keeps the substance. Her constant is her people's survival. What changes over the novel is the price she will pay for it.

### B2. The courtship and the marriage

Elias, driven by freedom, finds a woman with everything except freedom: rank, land, office, two brothers and a church deciding for her. She chooses him in a song; the man who cannot be given anything is chosen by the woman who cannot be given away. She carries the deepest genealogy in the Pacific, the one conquest money cannot buy, and the origin of the House of Thorne-Kamehameha. At seventeen she presides over the Privy Council; he has never met a partner who can sign a state into being. Their marriage is two households and two seats by design, which is why a restless man can commit to it and why it can die without ending.

### B3. 1863–1872

The Society, the choir, the kahuna, the illness of 1866 and the doctors from Monterey. She leaves 1866 trusting no power, Hawaiian or haole, that cannot show results, while keeping the chants, the language, Kalama's friendship and her faith.

### B4. Queen, the mutiny and the Guard

Kuykendall's account of September 1873 is the model: about sixty Household Troops against their drillmaster Jajczay and Adjutant General Judd; Lunalilo, sick at Waikīkī, vacillated for days, wrote to "my loving people" and disbanded the army, a humiliation that left the kingdom without force. Victoria does the reverse on every point. The cost is personal: Judd is her own schoolmate and her own party's man. The result is political: the kingdom keeps a guard loyal to its Queen alone, and that is what the admirals cannot accept.

Historical anchors: Jajczay was born in Buda, conscripted in 1850, imprisoned at Olmütz, rode with the hussars who escorted Maximilian to Mexico, reached Honolulu by 1872 and killed himself in Costa Rica in 1874. Judd (1835–1890), son of Gerrit P. Judd, Royal School classmate of Kalākaua, became Kalākaua's chamberlain and went with him on the 1881 tour. Moehonua succeeded Jajczay.

### B5. The settlement of 1874–1876

| Year | Instrument | What changes | Classification |
|---|---|---|---|
| March 1874 | **Puʻuloa Convention** | Fifty-year lease of Pearl Harbor and its shores; common defence treaty. Signed by the Queen, countersigned by Ruth, ratified narrowly | **LEGAL**: a lease, not a cession; the 1855 refusal reversed by the Queen herself |
| 1874–1876 | **Defence ordinances** | Harbour police, Honolulu port administration, defence districts under confederal officials | **ILLEGAL**: breach of the Enabling Law's protected provisions and Article XIV's bar on annexation |
| 1876 | **Territorial Council** | Appointed planters and confederal officials take over the legislature's business; the English Schools Ordinance follows | **ILLEGAL** |
| 1876 | **Supreme Court judgment** | The ordinances declared void; Ruth resigns as Kuhina Nui; the office stays vacant | Ignored; never reversed |
| 1914 | **Act of Settlement** | Dissolves the Territorial Council, restores the legislature, joins the Hawaiian crown to the Crown of Pacifica | **LEGAL**; cures much but not the 1876 judgment |

CR-021's rows for 1874 ("Incorporation settlement"), 1876 and 1914 are superseded by this table.

### B6. The Five and the unwritten arrangement

The constitutional basis is canon: the Polytechnic's chartered estate (examinations, audit, General Staff, telegraph), the Office of Public Measures, the Crown's shares in the champions and the Development Fund's claim on every surplus. The people at their head hold force, money, communications and the numbers; the Crown holds legitimacy and the land under its capital.

| Seat | 1887 | Later |
|---|---|---|
| Polytechnic and General Staff | Rafael Soberanes | Marcus Vance III after 1915 |
| Naval construction, heavy industry, champions | Logan Turner | **[PROPOSED]** Doheny (oil) |
| Power | Nikola Tesla | **[PROPOSED]** Steinmetz |
| Measures and tabulation | **[PROPOSED]** Herman Hollerith | **[PROPOSED]** Baekeland, Giannini, Montgomery as the realm's needs change |
| Press and image | **[PROPOSED]** William Randolph Hearst; W. K. L. Dickson's film from 1895 | — |

The terms, never written: the Crown does not touch the estates' charters, appointments or the Development Fund; the estates never take sides against the Crown and never let a faction capture them. Tests: Donner (1887) holds; Kiyoshi's bid (1913) is decided by the Five's neutrality; Julian's Senate quarrel (1915–1917) strains it; the Altai report (1921) breaks it, the priests lying at the Crown's request; their successors decide 1932.

### B7. The arc

The hardening comes between 1874 and 1887, not in 1874. She spends thirteen years defending a bargain everyone calls betrayal and finds that defending it requires more and more of what she disliked in Elias. By 1887 the Regent must make the bargain look justified, which is why she measures everything. The reader cannot tell whether her measures come from love of the people, guilt or rivalry with Noe.

### B8. Where the canon changes

- §6: no fictional cousin; the historical appointment of January 1855; the 1857 refusals and songs; the November 1858 wedding.
- §12: 30 November 1863; Lot keeps the office; the 1866 survival.
- §17: the accession, the mutiny, the February rising, the lease and the ordinances replace Lunalilo's reign, the election, the abeyance and the massacre.
- §19: Kalākaua; §24: the Five; §27: the Act joins the crowns rather than restoring an abeyant throne.

### B9. Mythic structure

**Backbone myths.**
1. **The Kumulipo:** night to day, and a genealogy that justifies a line. The Chronicler's history is the Kumulipo of the House of Thorne-Kamehameha.
2. **Lono and Kaikilani:** a queen regnant and her hot-headed, "instinctively generous" husband; when he wrongs her the chiefs rise in her name and she refuses their revolt. Victoria in February 1874. The echo stays political, not literal.
3. **The triple marriage of Laʻamaikahiki:** a voyaging hānai son, three wives, three founding lines. Elias's three women and the three sons of the Truce.
4. **Māui fishing up the islands:** the line that breaks when a brother looks back. The joined Pacific, and 1932.

**Echoes (PROPOSED).**

| Myth | Echo |
|---|---|
| Iwikauikaua, the landless knight who marries a queen and founds kings | Elias |
| ʻUmi-a-Līloa, the unacknowledged son recognized by tokens | The sons denied the name, inverted: the adopted heir reigns |
| Kaiana, the captain who turns on the conqueror at Nuʻuanu | Kiyoshi in 1913, who does not turn |
| The Destruction of the Temples: Kaʻahumanu and Kekuaokalani | Victoria and Kalākaua |
| The Iron Knife | The Japanese partnership |
| Kamapuaʻa and Pele: Olopana's heiau at Kāneʻohe; the island divided between rain and fire | Thalassia's ground; the Truce of 1887; Keawe |
| Pele and Hiʻiaka | The loyalists' reading of Noe's death |
| Hua of Hāna, whose bones rattled in the sun | The Altai falsification: the priests lie, the realm goes dry |
| Hāloa, the elder brother who feeds the younger | Silas |
| Kaʻahupāhau, guardian of Puʻuloa | The Pearl Harbor dry dock that collapsed in 1913, the year of Kiyoshi's bid |
| Makahiki, the season when war was kapu | The Senate's Season, October to March, broken by the anchoring of October 1913 |

Kalākaua's versions are Victorianized (Daggett's prose); retellings should be checked against Fornander, Kamakau, Beckwith and Pukui, and sacred material used through characters' own voices.

---

## C. Storyline passages

**C0. Rename rule (applied first).** Every occurrence of "Kaiulani" in the master storyline becomes "Victoria" (99 occurrences, including possessives and the §32 heading). The passages below are quoted after the rename. Earlier CRs are not edited; their "Kaiulani" reads as Victoria. "Kaʻiulani", with the ʻokina, is the historical Princess Kaʻiulani (A19).

**Header** (replace "CR-025 CR-026 -->"):
> CR-025 CR-026 CR-027 -->

**Header (new integration note after the CR-026 note)** (add as a new paragraph after "Kiyotaka's son Kiyonaka keeps the main house."):
> **CR-027 integration:** [Victoria Kamāmalu, the Puʻuloa lease and the Five](CR-027.md). The historical Victoria Kamāmalu, Kaʻahumanu IV (born 1838), replaces the fictional Kaiulani in every role; earlier change requests that name Kaiulani refer to her. She marries Elias in November 1858, becomes Queen of Hawaii in December 1872, leases Puʻuloa to the Confederation in 1874 and from 1887 governs Pacifica as Regent while remaining Queen, until Julian succeeds her in 1915. A February rising with disputed deaths replaces the 1874 massacre, and the Hawaiian throne is never in abeyance. Kalākaua serves her as mythmaker and envoy; the Five at the head of the chartered estates run the technocratic state under an unwritten arrangement with the Crown.

**The novel's larger movement** (replace the passage from "The most intimate version of that political history is the story of Elias and Victoria." through "neither she nor the kingdom's political leaders can stop."):
> The most intimate version of that political history is the story of Elias and Victoria Kamāmalu, sister of two Hawaiian kings. They begin in love and share an ambitious conception of Pacific cooperation. They marry and have a son. After Lot Kapuāiwa's death she becomes Queen of Hawaii. In 1874 she leases Puʻuloa to the Confederation, and Elias's government stretches the lease into effective rule over the kingdom; she refuses a royalist rising raised in her name and lets her own Supreme Court's judgment go unenforced.

**The novel's larger movement** (replace "Victoria becomes regent through a negotiated succession,"):
> Victoria becomes Regent of Pacifica through a negotiated succession while remaining Queen of Hawaii,

**§6** (replace "meets Victoria, their fictional cousin, born in 1838 and studying at the Chiefs' Children's School."):
> meets their sister, Victoria Kamāmalu, born in 1838 to Kīnaʻu and Kekūanāoʻa, a granddaughter of Kamehameha I and a pupil at the Chiefs' Children's School.

**§6** (replace "Historical Victoria Kamāmalu follows a different constitutional course in this alternate world. Victoria's office is not a courtesy offered to Elias's prospective bride;"):
> As in history, she takes the office in January 1855, at sixteen, and presides over the Privy Council; no Hawaiian public document is valid without her signature. The office is not a courtesy offered to Elias's prospective bride;

**§6** (replace the passage from "Kamehameha IV marries Emma in June 1856." through "how dangerous that expectation will become."):
> Kamehameha IV marries Emma in June 1856. **[APPROVED — CR-027]** Victoria has been betrothed since childhood to her cousin William Lunalilo, a match her mother Kīnaʻu arranged and the Hawaiian people love. Her brothers block it: Lunalilo's rank, estates and following on Hawaiʻi island would give the couple's children precedence over the king's own line. In 1857 they press David Kalākaua on her instead, and she refuses. Her answer survives in two songs of her own, *Pua Hau ʻo Maleka* and *Aita ʻOe e Parau*, which defy her brothers and claim the right to love the man she chooses. All Honolulu knows the man is Elias. She turns down both suitors for him.
>
> **[APPROVED — CR-027]** The brothers come round for their own reasons. Elias's children would rank through her alone, below the king's line; he claims none of her lands, which make her one of the kingdom's great landholders; and an American who has defied Washington takes her out of the reach of the missionary party that Wyllie believed had plotted in 1854 to put her on the throne. In **November 1858**, two years after the Confederation came into force, Elias and Victoria marry at Kawaiahaʻo Church in Honolulu, the church whose choir she leads. The wedding seals a partnership already legally binding, not a bride given in exchange for it. Elias is about thirty-four and Victoria twenty. Each expects to influence the other; neither yet imagines how dangerous that expectation will become.

**§8** (add as a new paragraph after "not a mechanism for erasing its members' autonomy."):
> **[APPROVED — CR-027]** At the ceremony Victoria leads the Kawaiahaʻo choir. Late that night, among the court, Elias hears her chant a mele of her own composition. He has known her since she was thirteen; from that night her voice stays with him for the rest of his life.

**§8** (replace "They marry in February 1857 with the treaty already binding."):
> They marry in November 1858, with the treaty two years in force.

**§11** (add as a new paragraph after "His principle of broad civic incorporation increasingly coexists with ruthless military punishment."):
> **[APPROVED — CR-027]** In 1863 Victoria founds the Kaʻahumanu Society, named for the queen whose name she bears as Kuhina Nui, to nurse the victims of smallpox and care for the sick and elderly. She signs her acts as Kaʻahumanu IV, leads the Kawaiahaʻo choir and composes chants in the old style, among them laments for her nephew, the Prince of Hawaii, who dies in 1862.

**§12** (replace "Lot succeeds Alexander as Kamehameha V in November 1863."):
> When Alexander dies on 30 November 1863, Victoria, as Kuhina Nui, holds the powers of the crown for a day and proclaims her brother king. Lot succeeds as Kamehameha V.

**§12** (replace "Victoria continues to hold the office; Lot judges its abolition politically costly and unnecessary."):
> Victoria continues to hold the office. The historical Lot abolished it in 1864; here he judges its abolition politically costly and unnecessary, and his 1864 constitution names his sister his heir.

**§12** (add as a new paragraph after "through which Hawaiian interests can be argued."):
> **[APPROVED — CR-027]** Victoria keeps a kahuna as well as her pew at Kawaiahaʻo. In May 1865 he dies, promising to rise on the third day, and does not. In February 1866 she falls gravely ill; physicians brought from Monterey save her where, in our history, she died that May. The kahuna who failed and the doctors who succeeded turn her toward one test for any power, Hawaiian or haole: whether it can show results. She keeps the chants, the language and her faith.

**§17** (replace the passage from "Lot dies in December 1872 without a direct heir," through "even after the crown's restoration in 1914."):
> **[APPROVED — CR-027]** Lot dies in December 1872 without a direct heir. Under Article 22 of his constitution the crown passes to his sister, and Victoria becomes Queen of Hawaii without an election. She appoints her half-sister Ruth Keʻelikōlani Kuhina Nui: a great landholder and governor of Hawaiʻi island who speaks no English and keeps the old ways, a reassurance to the chiefs. Lunalilo, the man her brothers forbade her, becomes the face of everyone who fears a queen married to the Providentor. Queen Emma, Alexander's Anglican widow, leads those who look to London.
>
> **[APPROVED — CR-027]** In September 1873 the Queen's Guard mutinies. Its drillmaster, Captain József Jajczay, is a Hungarian veteran of the hussars who escorted Maximilian to Mexico, hired by Lot to train a guard loyal to the crown alone and owing nothing to Monterey's academy. The adjutant general is Colonel Charles Judd, a missionary's son and Victoria's schoolmate at the Royal School. When Jajczay jails four men for deserting the treasury post, the soldiers beat him and Judd, seize the barracks and load two cannon. The admirals at Honolulu offer marines; Victoria refuses them, because Hawaiians will settle this themselves. On the first day she crosses Palace Walk to the barracks with her women and no guard and speaks to the men in Hawaiian. She dismisses Jajczay and Judd, as the men demand, and the men lay down their arms before her. She does not disband the Guard: she gives its command to Major William Moehonua and takes its oath again herself. Jajczay leaves the islands and dies in Costa Rica the next year. Judd, whom she has sacrificed, attaches himself to Kalākaua. She suspects Kalākaua's hand in the mutiny, says nothing, and makes him answerable for the Guard's loyalty.
>
> **[APPROVED — CR-027]** For the admirals preparing for Manila, a kingdom with a guard loyal only to its Queen is the decisive argument: Pearl Harbor lies beside a force Hawaii can use. They insist that the harbour can no longer depend on Hawaiian consent. Lunalilo dies on 3 February 1874. Days later his followers rise in Honolulu in the Queen's name against the confederal demand. Confederal marines land to restore order; there are deaths in the rioting, and each side blames the other. Victoria keeps the Guard in its barracks. She will not let a rising in her name become a war against her husband.
>
> **[APPROVED — CR-027]** In March 1874 she signs the Puʻuloa Convention: a fifty-year lease of Pearl Harbor and its shores to the Confederation and a treaty of common defence. It is a lease, not a cession; no Hawaiian land is alienated. Ruth countersigns as Kuhina Nui, and the legislature ratifies narrowly, carried by the nobles Kalākaua brings to the Queen's side. The reversal of her 1855 refusal is her own act, made to keep the crown rather than lose it to London through Emma or to the planters. Elias wants the harbour for cold reasons: the Manila operation, the transpacific fleet and a kingdom whose legislature an outside power could sway.
>
> **[APPROVED — CR-027]** The illegality comes after. Between 1874 and 1876 the confederal cabinet stretches the Convention by ordinance under the Enabling Law: harbour police, then the Honolulu port administration, then the defence districts, and in 1876 an appointed Territorial Council of planters and confederal officials that takes over the legislature's business. The ordinances breach the Enabling Law's protected provisions and Article XIV's bar on annexation. Ruth refuses to recognize the Council and resigns as Kuhina Nui; the Queen leaves the office vacant. Hawaii's Supreme Court declares the ordinances void. No one can enforce the judgment against confederal marines, and Victoria will not ask her people to bleed for it. She lets the ruling stand on paper and the Council stand in fact, as she once let the constitution's form go to see her brother proclaimed. No missing signature or later claim of necessity supplies consent. The judgment is never reversed, leaving sovereigntists a legal claim even after the Act of Settlement of 1914.
>
> **[APPROVED — CR-027]** Emma becomes the loyalists' counter-queen and remains so until her death in 1885. In 1883 she builds a country house on the Puʻuloa shore outside the leased ground and plants banyans and two thousand coconuts at the gate of the fleet.

**§17** (replace the passage from "The appointed Territorial Council's English Schools Ordinance of 1876" through "This cultural wrong becomes part of the price of the restored crown."):
> **[APPROVED — CR-027]** The Territorial Council's English Schools Ordinance of 1876 removes Hawaiian from government schools. Many Hawaiian parents have long wanted English for their children; the planters on the Council make it the only language. Elias, who needs the Council for the harbour works and the cable, does not overrule it: he will not spend his capital on what he thinks minor, and the 1887 constitution's entrenchment of Hawaiian comes eleven years too late for a generation of children. Victoria fights the ordinance and loses, then pays for Hawaiian-language schools through the Kaʻahumanu Society for the rest of her life. This cultural wrong becomes part of the price of the order.

**§17** (replace "Honolulu carries the massacre's memory"):
> Honolulu carries the memory of February 1874

**§17** (replace "Victoria insists that Thalassia's land remain the Hawaiian throne's Crown land,"):
> Victoria leases the ground from the Hawaiian Crown lands and insists that it remain the throne's land,

**§17** (replace "The capital's beauty rests on land taken under the disputed regime,"):
> The capital's beauty rests on Crown land leased by a Queen governing under the disputed regime,

**§17 heading** (replace "## 17. The island alliance unravels after Lot's death (1872–1874)"):
> ## 17. The island alliance unravels after Lot's death (1872–1876)

**§18** (replace "Kalanimoku, Elias and Victoria’s legitimate son, grows up"):
> Kalanimoku, Elias and Victoria’s legitimate son, born after the 1858 wedding and heir to his mother's Hawaiian crown, grows up

**§18** (add as a new paragraph after "The accident’s circumstances, exact date and medical consequences remain **[OPEN]**."):
> **[PROPOSED — CR-027]** After the accident Victoria stops singing. Elias keeps a phonograph cylinder of her voice, made shortly before; on his deathbed in 1887 he asks for it.

**§18** (replace "Kiyoshi is born in Kagoshima in 1859 to Uehara Hisa, a glass master's daughter and interpreter."):
> Kiyoshi is born in Kagoshima in 1859 to Uehara Hisa, a glass master's daughter and interpreter. **[APPROVED — CR-027]** He is conceived in the spring of 1858, during the Edo negotiations and months before Elias's wedding. When Victoria learns of him remains **[OPEN]**.

**§19** (add as a new paragraph after "even as infirmity makes activity more difficult."):
> **[APPROVED — CR-027]** Kalākaua, the suitor she refused, becomes the Queen's minister of the image and her envoy. He revives the hula, prints the genealogical chants and retells Hawaii's legends for a foreign audience as the equals of the Iliad and the romances of chivalry. His tale of the Iron Knife, Japanese castaways on Maui whose descendants were plentiful, gives the Japanese partnership a Hawaiian prehistory. In 1881 he travels round the world in her name with Judd as his chamberlain, meets the Meiji Emperor and proposes an Oceanian union sealed by marrying his niece, the young Kaʻiulani, to Prince Komatsu; the Emperor politely declines. His motto, *Hoʻoulu Lāhui*, increase the nation, stands over the Queen's mortality figures. In his book he mourns Kekuaokalani, who died defending the old gods against the first Kaʻahumanu's canoes, and he publishes it under the patronage of the fourth. She never lets him near the purse. He dies in San Francisco in 1891, and his project of the image passes to the press seat of the Five.

**§20** (replace "During Honolulu's 1881 smallpox epidemic she nurses at the Queen's Hospital."):
> During Honolulu's 1881 smallpox epidemic she nurses at the Queen's Hospital. **[APPROVED — CR-027]** The hospital is Queen Emma's foundation, and Noe's first patrons are loyalists.

**§21** (replace "A regency article names Victoria Regent until an Act of Settlement establishes the Crown,"):
> A regency article names Victoria, Queen of Hawaii, Regent of the Realm until an Act of Settlement establishes the Crown,

**§21** (replace "Hawaii's assent comes from the appointed Territorial Council created by the illegal incorporation."):
> Hawaii's assent comes from the appointed Territorial Council created by the illegal ordinances of 1874–1876.

**§21** (replace "Victoria is both the widow of the founder and an independent Hawaiian political actor."):
> Victoria is both the widow of the founder and the reigning Queen of Hawaii.

**§22** (replace "Victoria’s standing combines the founder’s widowhood, Hawaiian aliʻi authority, the Kuhina Nui tradition,"):
> Victoria’s standing combines the founder’s widowhood, her reigning Hawaiian crown, Hawaiian aliʻi authority,

**§23** (replace "Hawaiian loyalists who reject the incorporation begin to court her."):
> Hawaiian loyalists who reject the ordinances begin to court her. **[APPROVED — CR-027]** With Emma dead since 1885 they also look to her cousin and heir Albert Kūnuiākea, by common knowledge a natural son of Kamehameha III, never acknowledged and the squanderer of his inheritance.

**§24** (add as a new paragraph after "rather than as guardian obliged to surrender office on the boy's majority."):
> **[APPROVED — CR-027]** The regency's working government sits in the chartered estates. The Constitution gives the Polytechnic its examinations, audit, General Staff and telegraph and the Office of Public Measures the Realm's numbers; the Crown holds its shares in the champions, and the Development Fund has its claim on every surplus. Five people at the head of these institutions run the technocratic state. In 1887 they are Soberanes for the Polytechnic and General Staff, Logan Turner for naval construction and heavy industry, Tesla for power, **[PROPOSED — CR-027]** Herman Hollerith, whose punched cards tabulate Noe's registers from 1888, and William Randolph Hearst, San Francisco-born, who takes over the *Examiner* that year and makes the six-language weekly the Realm's press; from 1895 W. K. L. Dickson, recruited from Edison, gives it moving pictures. Seats pass to successors such as Steinmetz, Baekeland, Doheny, Giannini and Montgomery, and after 1915 to Marcus Vance III; there are always five. San Francisco calls them the Five, Honolulu nā Kahuna, the priests and masters of their crafts.
>
> **[APPROVED — CR-027]** Their arrangement with the Crown is never written down. The Crown has no army beyond the Queen's Guard and no purse of its own; force, money, communications and the numbers sit in the estates. The Five have power but no legitimacy; Japan, the creditors, the Senate and the Hawaiian people accept them because the Crown sanctions them. The Crown does not touch their charters, appointments or the Development Fund; the estates never take sides against the Crown and never let a faction capture them. Victoria is the one person all five trust, because she shields their charters from the Senate and gives them prestige. Hearst wants spectacle and she wants honest numbers with the weak spots shown; he may dramatize the Union's failures, but he prints the Office's tables unaltered.

> The 1914 Act of Settlement establishes the Crown of Pacifica in the House of Thorne-Kamehameha and joins to it the Hawaiian crown Victoria has worn since 1872. It dissolves the Territorial Council and restores Hawaii's legislature. The ʻAha Aliʻi proclaims Julian heir to the Hawaiian crown, to reign as Kamehameha VI; Senate and Chamber confer the Realm's sovereignty by two-thirds. In 1915 Victoria lays down both the regency and her crown, and Julian accedes to both.

> **Victoria Kamāmalu.** Sister of two kings, Kuhina Nui from 1855, Elias's wife from 1858, Queen of Hawaii from 1872, bereaved mother of Kalanimoku and hānai mother of Julian; Regent of Pacifica from 1887 while still Queen, until Julian succeeds her in 1915. She leased Puʻuloa in 1874 and let the ordinances that followed stand, and she spends the rest of her life measuring whether the bargain was worth it.

> **Kalākaua and the Five.** Kalākaua, the suitor Victoria refused, serves her as mythmaker and envoy and dies in San Francisco in 1891. The Five at the head of the chartered estates run the technocratic state under an unwritten arrangement with the Crown. Donner tests it in 1887, Kiyoshi's bid in 1913 and Julian's Senate quarrel in 1915–1917; the Altai report breaks it in 1921.

source_excerpts: **CR-028 integration:** [The bargain of 1847–1848](CR-028.md). Washington accepts California's independence in three steps: the suspension of April 1847, Mexico's recognition at Querétaro in December 1847, and Polk's acceptance of Trist's treaty and the Buchanan–Vallejo Convention in February 1848. California gives a non-alienation pledge, port and commercial privileges and the Basin; Washington takes independence for the Texas road. Ratified treaties, British and French recognition, the bondholders and the Senate's sectional lock hold the result until secession.

Commodore John D. Sloat reaches Monterey in July. His orders were issued in anticipation of a war against Mexico, and he finds a government asserting that its ports no longer belong to Mexico. The memory of Commodore Jones's mistaken seizure of Monterey in 1842 makes him cautious. Rather than simply repeating the historical occupation of 7 July, he maintains a threatening naval presence, questions the republic's legitimacy and refers the conflict to Washington. A reply may be months away. Admiral Seymour arrives aboard HMS *Collingwood* on 16 July; **[PROPOSED — CR-028]** Pico asks the admiral for protection. Seymour's only instruction on California is to observe the Americans, and London has ruled a protectorate "entirely out of the question"; he declines. Britain does not offer military protection, but British witnesses and merchants increase the risks of an unauthorized attack. The Republic learns that it will have no patron.

When Robert F. Stockton replaces Sloat, Elias helps negotiate a naval standstill. American vessels may provision in Californian ports for operations against Mexico but may not seize them. Domestic critics accuse Elias of furnishing an invading navy; officers on both sides argue over what neutrality requires. The agreement is tested when Stephen W. Kearny approaches overland in December. Andrés Pico's Californio lancers defeat his column at San Pasqual. It is a victory won by Pico and his men, not Elias, and it obliges Stockton to reconsider the practical cost of overturning the standstill. **[PROPOSED — CR-028]** At Cahuenga on 13 January 1847, Frémont, cut off and acting on his own authority, signs terms with Andrés Pico to get his battalion out of the country. Kearny's paroled survivors embark at San Diego, prisoners are exchanged, and Bear Flag men who are American citizens receive an amnesty that Californios who lost men at Olompali do not forgive. The standstill is put in writing until Washington replies, and Stockton adheres for the squadron. Kearny never forgives Frémont for treating with a foreign government over his head. With the consul Thomas Larkin, Elias drafts a memorandum of what the Republic could offer Washington. It travels east with Kearny's report.

In 1847 Elias expands the powder works and boatyard at Carquinez and surveys the foothills with experienced local partners. The arrival of the Mormons in the Salt Lake basin complicates the territorial balance: there is a continental neighbor whose political objectives neither Washington nor California controls. **[PROPOSED — CR-028]** The Mormon Battalion, arriving at San Diego after San Pasqual, is interned under the Cahuenga terms and then released to march to the Salt Lake; some of its men work a season at Carquinez first. Kearny has Frémont arrested, and a court-martial in Washington tries him for his conduct at Sonoma and Cahuenga. Benton defends him and threatens to prove that Frémont acted on instructions carried west by Lieutenant Gillespie, orders written for a Mexican province and carried out against a republic. On 31 January 1848 the court convicts Frémont. Polk remits the sentence, Frémont resigns, and his father-in-law breaks with the President. Frémont's future dealings with Elias are colored by a defeat neither man has forgotten.

**[PROPOSED — CR-028]** Kearny's report reaches Washington in April 1847, as Scott's army lands at Veracruz. The Secretary of War has no regiments to spare, and the Navy cannot hold a hostile coast under British eyes. Polk orders his commodore to observe the Cahuenga arrangements and sends Stevenson's New York regiment, already at sea for San Francisco, on to Mazatlán and La Paz. He calls it a suspension. His envoy Nicholas Trist leaves for Mexico with instructions that still claim Upper California, and Polk expects to win at the peace table what he will not fight for on the coast.

**[PROPOSED — CR-028]** California sends two missions. In Washington, Mariano Vallejo, Frémont's former prisoner and the most pro-American man to sign the declaration, leads the envoys with Pablo de la Guerra. Secretary of State James Buchanan had written in 1845 that an independent California would receive the kind offices due a sister republic; in September 1847 he initials with them a conditional text, insurance in case the peace leaves the Republic standing. In Mexico, Alvarado and Elias reach Querétaro after the fall of the capital and Santa Anna's resignation. They leave Monterey in haste: in October Elias has found gold on the Mokelumne, and he knows the Republic's bargains will hold only if they are made before anyone else does. Peña y Peña's government needs money and a way to call the peace something other than surrender. In the **Convention of Querétaro** of December 1847, Mexico recognizes California. In return California assumes approximately **£3 million of Mexican obligations to London bondholders**, secured against customs and prospective mining revenue. The bonds of Mexico's 1846 conversion carry no land rights, so California buys no territory from them, only a creditor with a reason to want it to survive. William Hartnell carries the convention to London for the bondholders' consent. The convention also guarantees Mexican citizens' property and the Church's, and pledges never to cede itself or its territory to any power. Elias pledges royalties from a find that only five people in the world know of, and he says nothing false: the mines, he tells the Mexican foreign minister, are California's hope. The precise valuation, creditor arrangements and amortization remain matters of financial modeling.

**[PROPOSED — CR-028]** Trist, recalled but staying on, finds the coast no longer Mexico's to give. The treaty he signs at Guadalupe Hidalgo on 2 February 1848 cedes New Mexico, the Great Basin and the Rio Grande line, and binds the United States to respect California's frontier as Mexico has recognized it. Polk is furious. But the House has just voted that the war was unconstitutionally begun, Benton is waiting with the Gillespie papers, the Whigs have a war hero for November, and to reject the treaty he would have to ask a hostile Congress for money to make war on a republic that declared its independence before it knew of the war. He sends the treaty to the Senate together with the **Buchanan–Vallejo Convention**, signed on 28 February. California pledges never to cede, lease or place under protection any part of its territory to a European power. It opens San Francisco, Monterey and San Diego to American warships, with a revocable naval storehouse at Sausalito. It keeps California's ports closed to the enemies of the United States in its wars. It promises to return deserters from American warships. It grants most-favored-nation commerce, whalers' privileges and civil guarantees for American residents, the commercial articles for twelve years. It closes the claims of 1846 by amnesty and a mixed commission, and it renounces the Basin pending a boundary commission. Buchanan asks for an accession clause, and Vallejo refuses, citing Querétaro. Buchanan also offers the United States' guarantee of California's independence, as he had just given New Granada's, and Elias's instructions refuse it: a guarantor has a right to come in.

**[PROPOSED — CR-028]** The Senate ratifies both on 10 March. Calhoun's Southerners vote for a settlement that keeps a free California out of the Union, and the Whigs vote for peace and for the harbors' commerce. Benton calls it the Trist surrender. Polk confides his consolation to his diary: California will come to the United States of itself, as Texas did. Larkin brings the ratified convention to Monterey in June as the first American chargé d'affaires. On Elias's advice the Assembly ratifies at once. The spring's gold finds are already rumoured in the foothills, but the government has said nothing, and no minister tells Larkin anything false. It confirms the gold only in October, when its mining decree is in force. When the news reaches the East, the instruments have been in force for months. Britain, which had refused since 1844 to encourage California's separation, recognizes the Republic once Mexico has. It declares, as it had with France for Hawaii in 1843, that it will take no part of California under any form; France accedes in 1849. Palmerston's circular of 18 January 1848 has already told the world that Britain may take up the claims of its bondholders. California accepts a geographically limited claim whose boundaries will be settled more precisely in 1850. Debt gives British creditors a stake in the republic's survival and a dangerous lever over its finances.

Elias has already studied placer gold discovered in 1842 near Placerita Canyon and follows reports from Sonoran miners, Mexican ranchers and people familiar with the Sierra foothills. **[PROPOSED — CR-028]** In October 1847, at the end of the dry season, he and Caleb travel through the Stanislaus and Mokelumne drainages with an experienced Sonoran placer miner and a Miwok guide, and find coarse gold in the Mokelumne gravels. Elias assays the samples at Carquinez with the metallurgy the colonel taught him. He tells only Pico, Castro and Alvarado, and within weeks he is on the road to Querétaro. The guide keeps the secret for a price: Elias's promise that the Republic will protect a homeland for his people when the miners come. The winter rains close the foothills. In the spring of 1848 the party returns and finds rich gravels and promising quartz-bearing geology. The guide's knowledge of ground, seasons and waterways and the miner's practical methods are essential; the find is not credited to Elias alone. Elias reports the discovery formally, in confidence, to President Pico and the Council of State and registers a small number of private claims. **[PROPOSED — CR-028]** The government keeps an official silence for another six months. Miners and rumours reach the foothills, but no minister confirms anything until the treaties with Washington are exchanged and an emergency mining decree, an assay office and a royalty are in force. Before the exchange it says nothing false; afterwards it calls the reports promising gravels under survey. The silence protects the Republic, and it gives Elias's enemies at home a charge he can answer but never erase: that he registered his claims on state secrets.

The **Treaty of Monterey of 1850**, the work of the boundary commission created in 1848, settles the eastern frontier with the United States. From the 42nd parallel, California's boundary follows the 120th meridian south to latitude 39°, then runs southeast to the Colorado River at 35° north and along the Colorado to the Gila. A related agreement fixes the southern border toward the Pacific south of San Diego. California gains internationally recognized ports and access to Yuma while abandoning claims to the Great Basin it has never governed. The United States retains the inland routes and the Salt Lake country. In consequence, the Compromise of 1850 unfolds without an American state of California entering the Union, altering the arithmetic of sectional politics. **[PROPOSED — CR-028]** The same arithmetic guards the Republic: Southern senators will not admit a free California, Northern Whigs and Free Soilers will not conquer one, and Washington's policy becomes waiting for the ripe fruit to fall. The Americans of the gold rush arrive as foreigners under Californian law, and the Republic's courts, licenses and careers make many of them Californians instead.

At the **Carson Convention** in autumn 1860, Pacifica withdraws its troops and recognizes American sovereignty over Washoe in exchange for property guarantees and transit rights. **[PROPOSED — CR-028]** The convention also renews, for a further term, the commercial articles of 1848, which had run out that year: the ports, the Sausalito storehouse, commerce and the rights of American residents. The crisis becomes a formative wound for Elias: his financial and military power does not suffice when his own constitution allows an organized coalition to block him. It also makes him respect, and increasingly resent, the wife whose judgment has frustrated his plans.

Fort Sumter's bombardment in April 1861 transforms the Confederation's strategic position. California and Hawaii have survived as separate states within Pacifica, but their shared customs, fleet and communications are now exposed to a continental war. Washington remembers the Washoe incident as a violation of American territory; California remembers American threats to its independence. **[PROPOSED — CR-028]** Secession also removes the Southern bloc whose votes had made every proposal against California a sectional impossibility since 1848. For the first time, the men who call 1848 the Trist surrender sit in a Congress the South no longer balances. **[APPROVED — CR-028]** When war comes, the American naval storehouse at Sausalito is sealed and its stores interned. Southern agents solicit bullion, shipbuilding and recognition, while Northern representatives ask the confederal government to supply or finance federal armies. The republic's American-born inhabitants carry divided loyalties into its legislative and military institutions.

1. **The mountain upbringing and French veteran:** Elias's birthplace, family migration and holding, the jurisdiction and creditor claims behind the 1837 dispossession; the French mentor's name, actual Napoleonic service, credibility of his claimed rank, and his eventual relationship to Elias.
2. **Resolved by CR-022:** the pastor's daughter is Abigail Merritt; the source of the marriage story is her own papers; the pastor's denomination is proposed as Methodist and his place remains open.
3. **Texas:** Elias's position during the Council House Fight and his and Caleb's exact experiences on the 1841–42 Santa Fe expedition and subsequent captivity.
4. **The 1846 founding:** the final Santa Barbara convention date, leadership of the Californio coalition, reconciliation of Pico and Castro, and substantive obligations to Indigenous polities.
5. **The naval confrontation, narrowed by CR-028:** Cahuenga, the 1847 suspension, the Querétaro recognition, Trist's California article, the Buchanan–Vallejo Convention and the 1848 recognitions are proposed. Still open: the Olompali casualties (including whether Caleb is wounded), Sloat's exact referral, the commission's survey, and how the debt is serviced before the first royalties.
6. **Gold and public finance:** precise discovery location, named Sonoran and Miwok/Yokuts collaborators, mining claims, private land titles, Indigenous rights, public royalty receipts and the state's credit system.
7. **California's legal consolidation:** transitional courts, common-law reception and retained Mexican rules, Indigenous claims, incorporation and patent statutes, citizenship/franchise, and the scope of Elias's revenue office under President Vallejo.
8. **Resolved by CR-027:** Victoria Kamāmalu holds the Kuhina Nui from 1855, succeeds Lot in 1872 and leases Puʻuloa in 1874; the February rising replaces the massacre. Still open: when Victoria learns of Kiyoshi, the Five's proposed members beyond Soberanes, Turner and Tesla, and scene detail of the 1874–1876 ordinances.
9. **The lost child:** Kalanimoku’s name is settled; individuality, birth year, age at death, accident circumstances and medical consequences for Victoria remain open.
10. **The other sons:** Silas is the eldest (1851, Abigail Merritt; CR-022). Kiyoshi is the second son (1859, Satsuma mother); his 1886 Kuroda adoption and marriage, Fleet-General identity and 1920 death are settled. Proposed maternal biography, early dates and service retain their labels; his branch house and 1907 countship, 1913 bid, the Kāneʻohe anchoring and his renunciation are settled by CR-026.
11. **Resolved by CR-021 F1:** Kaʻanoe (Noe) Ward, c.1860 Lahaina birth, physician, health board, 1886 hānai bargain and contested autumn 1888 death. Guilt remains genuinely unproved, rather than an undecided identity.
12. **Resolved by CR-021:** the 1914 Act of Settlement, Julian’s Hawaiian style Kamehameha VI and 1915 Realm accession, the succession rule, and Kahekili / Ikazuchi as future Kamehameha VII. Exact wedding and heir birth dates, bride and scene detail remain unspecified; the c.1916 birth is still a working date.
13. **Julian’s upbringing:** CR-021 settles his four-language education and 1905–1906 Tokyo year. Individual tutors, friendships and scenes remain to develop within that chronology.
14. **Japanese alternate treaties:** the credible diversion or reshaping of Perry's 1853–54 mission, Satsuma and shogunal negotiations, and the precise clauses of the **1858 Treaty of Edo**; the 1860 *Kanrin Maru* visit is a subsequent exchange.
15. **The American wars:** exact Eastern assignments, audited campaigns, casualties and pre-1865 alliance clauses; the approved 1864 electoral defeat, 1865 peace framework, 1867 ratification, Western line, 1870–1871 war and later continental outcomes now constrain those details. McClellan's connective sequence and several treaty mechanics remain proposed. Northwestern membership dates and Native agreements still require instruments.
16. **Victoria’s conclusion:** she is alive, out of power and in Hawaii in 1932. Her backing of the Thalassia Plan and brokerage of the Lands and Waters Charter are settled by CR-020; final scenes and the private treatment of her relationship with Julian remain to be developed.
17. **The Chronicler:** identity, access to sources, unreliable testimony and how later independent character perspectives challenge his account.
18. **Military and finance:** numerical and engineering evidence for the American wars, Japanese war finance, Siberian coalition (railway capacity: CR-030), champions, migration, common institutions and creditor order remains under audit. CR-020 names the replacement financial model and reports its Story and Stress cases. Those MODEL results do not independently validate fleets, resources, labor capacity or bank balance sheets; see [war_base_assumptions.md](war_base_assumptions.md).
19. **Resolved by CR-021:** Confederation organs and three-language acts; life Providentorship, protected enabling provisions and, as amended by CR-027, the legal Puʻuloa lease of 1874 and the illegal ordinances of 1874–1876; Constitution of the Realm, counties, estates, graded autonomy, plural franchise, ordinances, the joined crowns and Concord consent/cure. The ignored judgment of 1876 remains a legal grievance.
20. **Logan's Kentucky beginnings:** exact birth year and holler, family, early practical work, adolescent migration and Carquinez apprenticeship.
21. **Resolved by CR-021 C:** English–Spanish California, three-language confederal publication, English Realm administration, entrenched historic-land languages, granted county languages and bilingual Concord institutions. Scene-level founding negotiations remain to be written.
