requirements: Prim refuses in 1869–1870; the Manila action of August 1873 precedes the damaged squadron’s arrival at Honolulu and Puʻuloa’s urgency. Detailed battle mechanics remain PROPOSED.

The Republic borrows in 1874; Cánovas’s 1876 sale is financed by a Philippine Redemption Loan, guaranteed by the Confederation and limited by the incremental-revenue covenant. Distinguish purchase, refinancing, guarantee and debt service.
Pacheco, municipal public health, Calamba/Rizal, provincial juntas, the 1896 rising and Calderón develop Filipino agency and the costs of reform. Their authored careers are alternate history.

The Philippines is a confederal dependency until 1887, a Crown dependency until the 1914 settlement, and then its own crown by Cortes offer and plebiscite. Hawaii separately votes on the union; Julian’s Manila oath and proclamation occur in 1915. Detailed pre-1887 Organic Act and combined style retain PROPOSED labels.
Ka Lōkahi gives the three crowns one vote each and ten-year reviews of agreed matters. It is distinct from the two-party Concord, its Hayama Council and five-year executive terms.
The 1867 and 1871 Union quitclaims, Samoan sequence and later island trusts follow the supplied master; Tutuila’s trust transfer and other locally proposed details retain their labels.
source_excerpts: **CR-021 integration:** [The constitution of Pacifica and the Pacific Concord](CR-021.md), revision 9, incorporates the direct author corrections to the approved constitutional framework. The Constitution of the Realm, counties, languages and plural franchise, the 1914 Act of Settlement, 1927 provisional application and 1928 indemnity govern the chronology below. The two crowns of the Concord are co-equal; Julian is styled Sovereign of Pacifica and Mōʻī of Hawaii, and from 1914 also Rey de Filipinas (CR-029). Kaʻanoe Ward is his birth mother; Kahekili is his heir. All seventeen OPEN-021 entries are decided. The remaining uncertainty over Noe's death concerns culpability, not her identity or the recorded circumstances.

**CR-029 integration:** [Manila, Puʻuloa and the Philippine crown](CR-029.md). The Manila Bay action of August 1873 comes first. Neutrality rules send the damaged squadron to Honolulu, and the Manila station makes Puʻuloa urgent. Prim refuses a sale in 1869–70; the Republic borrows in 1874; Cánovas sells in 1876 to settle the Republic's debt and save Cuba. The Philippines is a confederal dependency until 1887, a dependency of the Crown under the Regent until 1914, and then a crown of its own, offered by the Cortes and confirmed by vote, equal with the Hawaiian crown whose people also vote. The Union's guano claims pass by treaty in 1867 and 1871. Micronesia and Tutuila become trusts of Ka Lōkahi, the council of the crowns.

The Western line is agreed in the 1865 peace and ratified by the Union Senate in 1867, alongside Pacifica's Alaska purchase. **[APPROVED — CR-029]** A Pacific article goes with it. The Union renounces its claims under the Guano Islands Act of 1856 to a schedule of named islands: Midway, Baker, Howland, Jarvis, Johnston and Kingman, with a quitclaim to Palmyra, which Hawaii annexed in 1862. The New York guano companies keep their workings until the deposits are exhausted and land their cargoes duty-free at Hawaiian ports, where their labourers were recruited. A nominal sum disappears into the vendor credit. Senators who are selling half the West can give up a few guano rocks under their own statute, which never obliged the United States to keep an island once its guano was gone. Pacifica keeps the Northwest, Great Basin, Arizona, Utah, Nevada and Idaho; western Montana includes the Missouri-headwaters gold camps, while Fort Benton remains Union. Southwest Wyoming includes South Pass, Fort Bridger, the Green River basin and Rock Springs coal. Colorado's Western Slope, North and Middle Park and the San Luis Valley are Pacifican; Denver, the Front Range, Pikes Peak and Leadville stay Union. New Mexico runs east to 103°W. The detailed boundary follows the mountain front, divide crests and Sangre de Cristo exceptions recorded in the territorial plan; surveys remain **[PROPOSED]**. Federal cession does not settle Native title or consent.

The Confederate economy needs credit, markets and protection. A railway treaty in 1866–1867 gives Huntington's line a route across Texas to New Orleans. Johnston succeeds Davis in February 1868 after his 1867 election. Richmond's Mississippi tolls and fugitive raids into Union Tennessee give Grant a popular cause; elected in 1868, he attacks in July 1870 while Europe is occupied by the Franco-Prussian War. Pacifica sends a Gulf squadron, turret ships, mines under Logan, rifles and credit, and closes its Pacific ports to Union shipping. **[APPROVED — CR-029]** Hawaiian schooners raise the Confederation's flag over the remaining American guano bonds in the Phoenix group, at Kiritimati and on Swains, without firing a shot. It sends no field army and undertakes no Asian military commitment during this war.

Union attacks fail at New Orleans in autumn 1870 and stall against entrenched lines in Virginia. Among the Texan volunteers at New Orleans is Silas Pruett, nineteen, who sees Pacifican mines and credit at work. After the association treaties he takes a commission in the Atlantic Auxiliary. In spring 1871 Sherman negotiates with Grant, whose friendship now crosses national allegiances. Richmond restores free Mississippi navigation; Pacifica guarantees Confederate independence. **[APPROVED — CR-029]** The Union quitclaims the Pacific islands Pacifica occupied during the war. The Union Senate keeps its claim to the South. Association treaties in 1871–1872 refinance Confederate debt on customs security, install Pacifican customs co-administration and secure the lower Mobile Bay naval station, Galveston commercial privileges, Atlantic Auxiliary recruitment and Birmingham concessions. Pacifica replaces the surrendered toll revenue. Pensacola remains a nearby Union base; protection and exposure coexist.

Alaska is purchased in 1867 for the Aleutian route to Japan and to exclude a rival northern foothold. **[APPROVED — CR-029]** Midway passes to Pacifica in the 1867 ratification and becomes part of the Hawaiian Crown lands, with its naval ground leased to the Confederation on the terms later used at Puʻuloa. **[PROPOSED]** A subsidized San Francisco–Honolulu–Yokohama–Hong Kong mail line, coaling also at Hakodate, preserves Pacific traffic after Suez opens. Northern gold income belongs to the later Juneau and Klondike developments; the northern administration must initially pay for harbors and transport without a ready gold windfall.

**[APPROVED — CR-029]** Elias first tries to buy. In 1869–70 a confidential offer for the Philippines goes to Prim, who had refused Napoleon's Mexican empire at Veracruz and seen the American war at first hand. Prim declines: no rising in the islands justifies a sale, and his name rests on avenging insults to the flag. He keeps the channel open. Assassins in the Calle del Turco close it at the end of 1870.

Spain's seizure of a Pacifican schooner off Jolo in the spring of 1873 gives Elias his pretext. The Republic refuses compensation and a public offer to buy; a republic cannot be seen to sell territory. **[PROPOSED — CR-029]** In August 1873, with the cantonal revolt dividing Spain's navy, a Pacifican squadron fights a one-day action against the Cavite station in Manila Bay. It does not land. Governor-General Alaminos signs a local convention: an indemnity, the crew's release, and an anchorage for a Pacifican squadron to protect its trade. **[APPROVED — CR-029]** Japan, negotiating treaty revision with every power that holds a treaty, Spain among them, sells the damaged ships coal for the nearest home port and refuses them a dock. The nearest home port is Honolulu.

**[APPROVED — CR-029]** That autumn the *Virginius* brings the Union and Spain close to war over Cuba; Pacifica's good offices in Madrid help settle it, and Madrid remembers. In March 1874 Serrano's Republic gives the Bank of Spain its monopoly of notes to pay for the war at home. For the war overseas it borrows Pacifican gold, secured on the Philippine customs and tobacco revenues. Pacifican agents sit in the customs houses, and the Banco Español-Filipino services the loan in Manila. **[PROPOSED — CR-029]** The price includes the pardon of the Filipino exiles on Guam. **[APPROVED — CR-029]** The Restoration of December 1874 inherits a debt it cannot pay. In 1876, with the Carlists beaten and Martínez Campos's army growing toward a hundred thousand men in Cuba, Cánovas, the historian of Spain's decline, asks the Cortes for a law of sale. He calls it the honourable liquidation of a republican debt that saves Cuba. Pacifica's price is to recognize no Cuban insurgents and to close its ports to their filibusters; Union abolitionists say Pacifican gold pays for the army that keeps Cuba slave. The sale includes the Philippines, Marianas, Carolines and Palau. **[APPROVED — CR-029]** The islands pay for themselves. A Philippine Redemption Loan, guaranteed by the Confederation and serviced from the Philippine customs, raises the price in London and San Francisco, and a covenant limits its service to the gain the islands make over their last Spanish years, published every year. Filipinos still say they paid for their own sale. The government answers that they never paid more than Pacifica added.

**[PROPOSED — CR-029]** Until 1887 the Philippines is a dependency of the Confederation, not a member state, with no members in the confederal chambers. Its Organic Act vests authority in the Providentor's office, not his person. **[APPROVED — CR-029]** Romualdo Pacheco, schooled in Honolulu as a boy and now forty-four, goes from Sacramento to Manila as Governor-General for a long term. He governs with a Philippine Council, and the Audiencia keeps Spanish law. His contempt for the Chinese is the Sacramento faction's; Manila's Chinese merchants and Elias's protection keep him on a short leash. Forced labour, forced crop sales and the tobacco monopoly end, and offices open by examination. The monopoly's factories and leaf are sold to a chartered tobacco company in which the Crown keeps a quarter. The Marianas, Carolines and Palau are separated from Manila under a naval administration at Apra Harbour. **[APPROVED — CR-029]** The sale follows Malcampo's capture of Jolo in February 1876, so Pacifica inherits a Spanish garrison and a war. In 1878 a compact with the Sultan of Sulu, and separate compacts with the datus who hold the real power, settle the south. Their Tausug text is authoritative, and the Sultan alone can consent to undo them. The cholera of 1882 comes in through Jolo and Zamboanga and reaches Manila in August, killing thousands in the city and tens of thousands in the islands. Polytechnic physicians read it as a matter of water. In 1883 a Municipal Ordinance gives every town an elected tribunal, its own funds and no parish priest over its budget, and binds the towns to piped water, quarantine of ships, latrines kept away from wells, and burial away from rivers. Health is taught through the cabezas and the parish priests, with no cordons or burned quarters. The Office of Public Measures publishes deaths by town; Elias deals with the towns over the heads of Manila and the friars, as he dealt with the county boards. In 1878 the Sultan's lease of North Borneo goes to a Pacifican Borneo company rather than to the British. Friar-estate purchases, financed by Philippine land bonds under the same guarantee, resell land to tenants in installments to a land board. Reforms do not erase coercion, and the land board becomes a landlord too.

**[APPROVED — CR-029]** The Manila station, a squadron kept in Asian waters to secure the convention and then the loan, sharpens the admirals' demand for unconditional control of Pearl Harbor and carries the strategic conflict into Hawaii's 1874 crisis. **[PROPOSED]** Pacifica supplies Japan's Formosa expedition that year and mediates Ryukyu in 1879: Japan keeps the islands, China receives trade guarantees. In the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877 Pacifica backs the Meiji government against Saigō and its oldest Japanese friends. Friendship remains a strategy whose beneficiaries can change.

**[PROPOSED]** Hakka families lead early Chinese family migration, jointly licensed brokers can also become traffickers, and an earlier Japanese emigration scheme sustains the Wakamatsu colony and arranged marriages. Filipino reformers and families begin arriving after 1876, especially in Catholic, Spanish-speaking Arizona and New Mexico. **[PROPOSED — CR-029]** From the 1880s Filipino families also come to Hawaii as kindred settlers under Victoria's programme of restoring the Hawaiian people. Victoria's international programme combines passage, reception, training and scholarships with household, employer, philanthropic and public funding. Its workbook schedule remains a scenario, not a new population guarantee.

**[APPROVED — CR-029]** Papal arbitration in 1885 confirms Pacifica's Carolines on condition of freedom for the Catholic missions, while granting Germany trade and coaling rights; Germany keeps the Marshalls, and the settlement records Pacifica's claim to Wake, taken five years earlier for a future cable. Leo XIII's price and Pacifica's are one bargain: the Philippine parishes pass to Filipino secular priests, Filipino bishops are named with the right to succeed, and the friar estates are paid for partly into an endowment that stays in the islands. The cause for which Gómez, Burgos and Zamora were garrotted in 1872 is won by treaty. Port Hamilton in 1885–1887 becomes a near-war Britain loses diplomatically. British withdrawal rests on a proposed China–Russia–Pacifica guarantee of Korean territory. The decision gives Pacifica a duty to protect Korea without owning it. Foreign commitments pause around the 1887 succession; the network must survive its founder before it can expand again. **[APPROVED — CR-029]** The pause has a price in Samoa. Hawaii had signed the 1878 treaty for Pago Pago on the Confederation's behalf, and in 1886–87 Kalākaua carries a Polynesian compact to Malietoa Laupepa. In August 1887 Germany's consul deports Malietoa and installs Tamasese, and Pacifica, burying its founder, does not answer.

**[APPROVED — CR-027; amended CR-029]** For the admirals of the Manila squadron, who brought their damaged ships into Honolulu that September because neutral Japan would sell them coal but not a dock, a kingdom with a guard loyal only to its Queen is the decisive argument: Pearl Harbor lies beside a force Hawaii can use. They insist that the harbour can no longer depend on Hawaiian consent. Lunalilo dies on 3 February 1874. Days later his followers rise in Honolulu in the Queen's name against the confederal demand. Confederal marines land to restore order; there are deaths in the rioting, and each side blames the other. Victoria keeps the Guard in its barracks. She will not let a rising in her name become a war against her husband.

**[APPROVED — CR-029]** In Samoa the hurricane of March 1889 wrecks the German warships at Apia while a Pacifican cruiser steams out to sea; the Berlin Act of June makes Germany, Britain and Pacifica the protecting powers, and the partition of 1899 gives Pacifica Tutuila. In the Philippines the land board's evictions at Calamba in 1890–91 turn José Rizal from a physician into a critic. In 1892, when he founds the Liga Filipina, the Regent answers with elected provincial juntas. The Philippine Office of Public Measures grades each province: Pampanga, Bulacan, Batangas, Ilocos Norte, Cebu, Iloilo and chartered Manila first, the Cordillera and Moroland administered. The evicted tenants are resettled at New Calamba on the Pacifican Borneo company's land at Marudu Bay as a self-governing colony. When cholera returns in 1888, the quarantine at Mariveles and the ordinance towns hold it to a few hundred deaths, where Spain's islands had buried twenty thousand. The Office's tables say so in every province. **[PROPOSED — CR-029]** In 1886 the peso goes onto a gold-exchange basis, ending the silver chaos Spain had left. Its reserve is built from the profit on coining a token peso and held in San Francisco, and the Banco Español-Filipino remains the bank of issue. **[APPROVED — CR-029]** Manila hemp makes the islands indispensable: every navy's rope and every wheat farmer's binder twine is spun from it, and a Pacifican cordage champion spins most of it.

**[APPROVED — CR-029]** In August 1896 the excluded rise: artisans and clerks of Tondo and Cavite, perhaps eight thousand, in a secret society with no ilustrados in it, over rice prices, estate installments and debt. The chartered towns refuse to join, Rizal declines to endorse them, and gunboats seal Manila Bay and the Cavite shore. The rising lasts weeks. A German cruiser division arrives to protect German nationals; it finds Pacifican ships in strength and leaves for China. A young advocate, Felipe Calderón, defends the accused, and the Regent commutes the sentences. The Union's illustrated weeklies still call her Pacifica's Weyler. In the spring of 1897 a steamer bought in Japan by Filipino exiles, a pan-Asian patron and a Chinese revolutionary, with a vice-minister looking the other way, is followed from Nagasaki and stopped in the Balintang Channel. Pacifica protests in private, because Japan's war with Russia is near and Tokyo needs the fleet. The vice-minister goes, the ship goes back, and its rifles find their way to the Chinese revolutionaries. The exiles learn that Japan will not take their side against Pacifica, and the southward school in Tokyo learns what acting without the cabinet costs.

The approved Klondike policy holds the Alaska boundary firmly while offering Canada fair transit; a proposed Skagway–Whitehorse railway, assay and banking capture route income from Canadian gold. **[PROPOSED]** Honolulu and San Francisco shelter Chinese reformers and revolutionaries after 1898; a limited Boxer relief contingent promptly withdraws and turns its indemnity into scholarships. A settlement with Britain during the Boer War fixes canal, Alaska, Samoa and Pacific recognition before the next stage of rivalry. **[APPROVED — CR-029]** Pacifica recognizes British Fanning as the station of the Pacific Cable; Britain recognizes Pacifican sovereignty over the equatorial islands from Palmyra to Baker.

The 1914 Act of Settlement establishes the Crown of Pacifica in the House of Thorne-Kamehameha and joins to it the Hawaiian crown Victoria has worn since 1872. **[APPROVED — CR-029]** Victoria will not join her crown without asking her people, as she did not ask them in 1874. The restored legislature and the ʻAha Aliʻi put the union to a plebiscite of Hawaiian subjects, and the loyalists campaign against it. It dissolves the Territorial Council and restores Hawaii's legislature. The ʻAha Aliʻi proclaims Julian heir to the Hawaiian crown, to reign as Kamehameha VI; Senate and Chamber confer the Realm's sovereignty by two-thirds. In 1915 Victoria lays down both the regency and her crown, and Julian accedes to both. Hawaiian is restored as the Crown's language and in its schools. The ʻAha Aliʻi keeps custody of Hawaiian crown and kuleana lands; Thalassia's ground is confirmed as land of the Hawaiian throne. The Polytechnic retains its charter.

**[APPROVED — CR-029]** In the same months the Philippine Cortes offers the Philippine crown, and a plebiscite confirms the offer. Its terms are signed before the vote, because Filipinos remember what was promised at Biak-na-Bato and never written down. Calderón's organic law gives the kingdom a single-chamber Cortes with a permanent commission, its own budget and army, and provinces under Gobernadores who are never posted to their home province. Neither crown is subordinate. The Realm takes over what remains of the Redemption Loan, about $9.5 million. The Crown of Pacifica becomes a crown made of three sources: Hawaiian rank, a Filipino people's offer and the Senate's law. Each crown keeps its own legislature, language of the Crown and coronation, and the alternat names each first in its own texts. A Kuhina Nui in Honolulu and a Lugarteniente General in Manila govern day to day in the Sovereign's name, on his instructions and without the old veto. Ka Lōkahi, the council of the crowns, gives the Realm, Hawaii and the Philippines one vote each over the succession, the agreed matters renewed every ten years and disputes between them. Hawaii votes for the union narrowly; the Philippines, broadly. **[PROPOSED — CR-029]** Julian's style becomes Sovereign of Pacifica, Mōʻī of Hawaiʻi, Rey de Filipinas, and each land promulgates it with its own crown first. **[APPROVED — CR-029]** In 1915 he swears before the Cortes in Manila, as Spanish kings swore, and is proclaimed under the raised standard. No bishop crowns him. At the Te Deum in the Cathedral, sung by the first Filipino archbishop, Victoria, Kīnaʻu's daughter, sits in a pew and sings the one hymn her church shares with Rome.

The Senate votes the rescue loan but refuses the treaty: Pacifica would pay sixty-five percent of common costs, Japan's mass threatens dilution, and county boards want leverage against the Commissioners. **[APPROVED — CR-022]** Harlan Tate, Sacramento's senator and Silas's old adjutant, leads the refusal, adding that foreign coupon-clippers already draw nearly $300 million a year from Pacifican industry. Julian claims provisional application under the treaty prerogative pending consent, though the Senate has already refused. This is illegal in substance. **[APPROVED — CR-029]** The Hawaiian and Philippine delegations to Ka Lōkahi declare for the Concord. The declaration gives Julian no legal authority, but it shows who holds the order together. The same year Ka Lōkahi takes the Marianas, Carolines and Palau into its trust, **[PROPOSED — CR-029]** with Tutuila, and the navy keeps Guam's harbour on lease. Japan's Emperor ratifies on the Privy Council's conditional advice and the Diet votes its quota; its side follows Japanese law and can lapse if Pacifica never obtains consent.

22. **Resolved by CR-021 G, as amended by CR-029:** the Formosan Revenue Convention, Chinese commissions, revenue order, joint administration and technical schools; the Philippine purchase, its status before 1914 and the Philippine crown of 1914; the Pacific islands. All OPEN-029 entries are decided; the rite of the Manila accession follows B7.
23. **Northern Pacific sequence, resolved by CR-031:** Russia retains the northern coast until 1921. The Okhotsk coast west of Ola Bay, Nikolayevsk, Chukotka and the Arctic islands east of the Kara Sea then pass to the Siberian Republic, with Okhotsk to the Sakha land; Kamchatka and the Koryak coast become a republic under Japanese protection. Japan retains its southern gains and the Transbaikalian protectorate and holds the majority of the Siberian coast's fishing lots by convention; Siberian ships pass the straits. The Commander Islands and the Arctic leases go to Pacifica. Detailed survey mapping is an implementation task; a fortification freeze is **[OPEN-031-11]**.
24. **CR-016 implementation:** OPEN-016-04 is resolved by Noe’s approved biography and contested evidence; the uncertainty is culpability. The regency, adoption, life offices and constitutional designation are fixed by CR-021. Silas's family and date, Donner responsibility and the 1888 restriction are decided by CR-022; the Vance arc retains its qualifications; Soberanes’s unspecified early biography and service remain qualified.

requirements: The successful Ob campaign uses one five-section railway schedule through Chinese-owned Manchuria with Japanese running rights and a Pacifican wartime board.
Russian-gauge engines built on Entente credit, paid and fed railwaymen/miners, civilian paths, summer depots, the Amur route to Sretensk and Kara Sea convoys remain PROPOSED mechanisms.
The 28,000-man contingent and 50,000-man corps/two-week reserve test are MODEL/PROPOSED assumptions; railway capacity and cost do not become established history.
Vance’s logistics rule develops his competence without settling OPEN-018-18’s lineage, command succession, Altai acts or ending.
open: Numerical/engineering feasibility remains under audit. OPEN-018-18 continues to qualify Vance’s detailed personal arc.
source_excerpts: **CR-030 integration:** [The railway behind the Siberian victory](CR-030.md), revision 2. The coalition's victory rests on one operational schedule: five railway sections from Vladivostok to the Ob, a Pacifican railway board that inherits the engines and cars Pacifican works built for Russia on Entente credit and pays and feeds the railwaymen and miners, depots filled behind the Ob the summer before the battle, the Amur summer route to Sretensk and a first Kara Sea convoy. The narrowest stretches lie far behind the front, on the Chinese line and the single-track branch into Transbaikalia. Capacities and costs are MODEL estimates.

<!-- CR-025: wartime credit, Japanese industrial expansion and the later bank crisis; mechanism approved, quantities MODEL. -->
San Francisco syndicates gather the Treasury's money, Pacifican savings and foreign subscriptions into the Entente loans. Investors in the neutral Union buy through Pacifican correspondents even while Washington competes with Thalassia; they keep their own claims and their own risk. Washington discourages loans to belligerents at first, so in 1914 Pacifica's own savers carry the loans alone. When the Union's banks grow wary of unsecured Entente paper at the end of 1916, loans secured on the Allies' requisitioned foreign securities, many of them Pacifican bonds, help carry the last two years of the war, and Pacifican savers take up more than before. Much of the money comes back as orders, and Japanese shipyards, mills and trading houses take a large share of them. **[PROPOSED — CR-030]** Russia's share comes back as locomotives and freight cars. Pacifican works build Russian-gauge engines on Entente credit and ship them through Vladivostok, and most of them go to work on the Siberian and Manchurian lines.

The Siberian war gives Julian the decisive military test he seeks. Pacifica commands a coalition of Japan, China and Siberians, with Britain inside the coalition. Japan provides the mass of the army; China provides manpower and the Manchurian railway; Siberians defend a country of their own. Pacifica contributes command, finance, railway organization, artillery, armored trains, aircraft, river flotillas and an expeditionary contingent. **[PROPOSED — CR-030]** At its height in the winter of 1919–1920 the contingent numbers about 28,000 men: railway troops, gunners, armored-train crews, airmen, river sailors and a reserve brigade.

**[PROPOSED]** In 1918 Pacifica pays and supplies the Czechoslovak Legion. **[PROPOSED — CR-030]** The Legion sails from Vladivostok in 1920, once Siberian and Japanese troops can take over its stretch of the line, and the wagons it has lived in go back to carrying freight. The coalition moves west from Japanese Vladivostok through Chinese-owned Manchuria under a single command. Its local partner is the Siberian Regionalist government, initially under Pyotr Vologodsky, while Zhang Zuolin supplies the Chinese cooperation. A Pacifican railway board runs the line west of Chita. **[PROPOSED — CR-030]** Trained before the war, the board takes over the engines Pacifican works built for Russia and pays the railwaymen and the coal miners on time in sound money. It feeds their families from its own stores so that nobody leaves the line to look for bread. New loops, larger water mains and strengthened bridges on the single-track branch from Manchuria double its trains within a year. Three paths in ten stay with Siberian grain, coal and passengers: the railway half of the land-and-grain guarantee. **[PROPOSED — CR-031]** The board's worst enemy in 1919 is not the Red Army but the ataman at the junction, who holds its trains for payment and shoots whoever he calls a Bolshevik. Tokyo stops his subsidy, and that summer the Transbaikal Cossack circle meets at Chita with a Japanese diplomat in the hall. A frontline officer with his own St George's Cross moves that the Host recognise the Siberian government and put its regiments under the coalition. The ataman's officers walk out, the vote carries, and he leaves for Dairen on a Japanese pension. The Cossacks of the Onon and the Argun ride west to the Ob. Chinese ownership, Japanese running rights and common wartime administration keep the supply route usable without giving its territory to Japan.

The coalition fights for an independent Siberia, leaving Kolchak’s all-Russian ambition to overreach. **[PROPOSED]** As Omsk falls in late 1919 it takes its planned position behind the Ob at Novonikolayevsk. In the winter of 1919–1920 it defeats the Red Army’s attack across the frozen river. **[PROPOSED — CR-030]** The battle is prepared the summer before. While the line is free and the rivers are open, the depots behind the Ob are filled, barges come up the Amur and the Shilka to Sretensk, and the first Kara Sea convoy carries stores up the Ob and the Yenisei. In the battle the trains bring only what the depots cannot hold. The victory is settled; tactics and strengths remain proposed. A peasant land-and-grain guarantee supplies a political basis for holding the railway country. **[PROPOSED — CR-031]** The guarantee travels down the Lena. Yakutia keeps its own committees under Vasily Nikiforov, who founded the Union of Yakuts in 1906 and went to prison for it, and elects an assembly in 1919, and when Kolchak's officials are overthrown on the Okhotsk coast, at Anadyr and in Kamchatka that winter, relief ships and an amnesty answer them instead of a punitive column. Pacifica freezes the debt books of its own San Francisco traders in Chukotka until a commission can write them down. German clients in the west and Chinese cooperation prevent Moscow from concentrating its full strength in the east.

The Ob becomes the intended treaty line; **[PROPOSED]** the Yenisei is the defense plan’s fallback. The Kuzbass lies behind the forward line, with the Vasyugan swamp to the north and the Altai to the south. Long supply distances and the open steppe make holding the front a continuing problem of capacity, legitimacy and local support. **[PROPOSED — CR-030]** The narrowest stretches of the supply line lie far behind the front: the Chinese line over the Khingan and the single-track branch into Transbaikalia. A retreat to the Yenisei would shorten the front but not the supply line, so the alliance depends on Chinese goodwill as much as on its guns.

Fleet-General Kuroda Kiyoshi dies in Siberia in 1920. **[PROPOSED — OPEN-018-18]** His death gives Marcus Vance III a command he never wanted. **[PROPOSED — CR-030]** Vance's timetable decides how fast the coalition can move west: a division goes forward only when the line can feed it. A cautious railway and logistics officer, Vance has designed the line and its fallback; he fears failing the dead whose name he carries. His competence helps win the war while exposing him to a decision that damages the partnership he serves.

**[PROPOSED]** By 1922 the settlement has become a standing alliance of Pacifica, Japan, China and the Siberian Republic. Germany’s eastern order confines Moscow from the other side. The Siberian republic must remain visibly Russian and governed by Siberians if the coalition is to retain local support. Japanese settlement proceeds in a mixed frontier society whose Russian, Buryat, Chinese and Korean inhabitants retain interests of their own. The victory enlarges the empire’s freedom of action while making its frontier obligations permanent. **[PROPOSED — CR-030]** In peacetime the front needs little of the railway. Its real cost is the capacity kept in reserve for war, so that a corps of 50,000 men can reach the Ob within two weeks of a call.

1. **The mountain upbringing and French veteran:** Elias's birthplace, family migration and holding, the jurisdiction and creditor claims behind the 1837 dispossession; the French mentor's name, actual Napoleonic service, credibility of his claimed rank, and his eventual relationship to Elias.
2. **Resolved by CR-022:** the pastor's daughter is Abigail Merritt; the source of the marriage story is her own papers; the pastor's denomination is proposed as Methodist and his place remains open.
3. **Texas:** Elias's position during the Council House Fight and his and Caleb's exact experiences on the 1841–42 Santa Fe expedition and subsequent captivity.
4. **The 1846 founding:** the final Santa Barbara convention date, leadership of the Californio coalition, reconciliation of Pico and Castro, and substantive obligations to Indigenous polities.
5. **The naval confrontation, narrowed by CR-028:** Cahuenga, the 1847 suspension, the Querétaro recognition, Trist's California article, the Buchanan–Vallejo Convention and the 1848 recognitions are proposed. Still open: the Olompali casualties (including whether Caleb is wounded), Sloat's exact referral, the commission's survey, and how the debt is serviced before the first royalties.
6. **Gold and public finance:** precise discovery location, named Sonoran and Miwok/Yokuts collaborators, mining claims, private land titles, Indigenous rights, public royalty receipts and the state's credit system.
7. **California's legal consolidation:** transitional courts, common-law reception and retained Mexican rules, Indigenous claims, incorporation and patent statutes, citizenship/franchise, and the scope of Elias's revenue office under President Vallejo.
8. **Resolved by CR-027:** Victoria Kamāmalu holds the Kuhina Nui from 1855, succeeds Lot in 1872 and leases Puʻuloa in 1874; the February rising replaces the massacre. Still open: when Victoria learns of Kiyoshi, the Five's proposed members beyond Soberanes, Turner and Tesla, and scene detail of the 1874–1876 ordinances.
9. **The lost child:** Kalanimoku’s name is settled; individuality, birth year, age at death, accident circumstances and medical consequences for Victoria remain open.
10. **The other sons:** Silas is the eldest (1851, Abigail Merritt; CR-022). Kiyoshi is the second son (1859, Satsuma mother); his 1886 Kuroda adoption and marriage, Fleet-General identity and 1920 death are settled. Proposed maternal biography, early dates and service retain their labels; his branch house and 1907 countship, 1913 bid, the Kāneʻohe anchoring and his renunciation are settled by CR-026.
11. **Resolved by CR-021 F1:** Kaʻanoe (Noe) Ward, c.1860 Lahaina birth, physician, health board, 1886 hānai bargain and contested autumn 1888 death. Guilt remains genuinely unproved, rather than an undecided identity.
12. **Resolved by CR-021:** the 1914 Act of Settlement, Julian’s Hawaiian style Kamehameha VI and 1915 Realm accession, the succession rule, and Kahekili / Ikazuchi as future Kamehameha VII. Exact wedding and heir birth dates, bride and scene detail remain unspecified; the c.1916 birth is still a working date.

14. **Japanese alternate treaties:** the credible diversion or reshaping of Perry's 1853–54 mission, Satsuma and shogunal negotiations, and the precise clauses of the **1858 Treaty of Edo**; the 1860 *Kanrin Maru* visit is a subsequent exchange.
15. **The American wars:** exact Eastern assignments, audited campaigns, casualties and pre-1865 alliance clauses; the approved 1864 electoral defeat, 1865 peace framework, 1867 ratification, Western line, 1870–1871 war and later continental outcomes now constrain those details. McClellan's connective sequence and several treaty mechanics remain proposed. Northwestern membership dates and Native agreements still require instruments.
16. **Victoria’s conclusion:** she is alive, out of power and in Hawaii in 1932. Her backing of the Thalassia Plan and brokerage of the Lands and Waters Charter are settled by CR-020; final scenes and the private treatment of her relationship with Julian remain to be developed.

18. **Military and finance:** numerical and engineering evidence for the American wars, Japanese war finance, Siberian coalition (railway capacity: CR-030), champions, migration, common institutions and creditor order remains under audit. CR-020 names the replacement financial model and reports its Story and Stress cases. Those MODEL results do not independently validate fleets, resources, labor capacity or bank balance sheets; see [war_base_assumptions.md](war_base_assumptions.md).

source_excerpts: **CR-031 integration:** [The Treaty of Harbin: the North, the victors' terms and China's articles](CR-031.md), revision 4. The Siberian Republic is a federation of graded autonomy: provinces, an autonomous Sakha land with a port at Okhotsk, and a North-East Territory from Ola Bay to Nikolayevsk with Chukotka. Kamchatka and the Koryak coast become a republic under Japanese protection; Transbaikalia is a protectorate under a Transbaikal Council and a civilian Resident after the Cossack Host turns Semenov out in 1919. China recovers Russia's privileges, Amur navigation to the sea and suzerainty over Mongolia. Pacifica takes the Commander Islands, Arctic leases and a charter, insists that Siberian ships pass the straits, and is complicit in the Kamchatka Company's forced labour. The fortification question is **[OPEN-031-11]**.

**[PROPOSED]** In 1918 Pacifica pays and supplies the Czechoslovak Legion. **[PROPOSED — CR-030]** The Legion sails from Vladivostok in 1920, once Siberian and Japanese troops can take over its stretch of the line, and the wagons it has lived in go back to carrying freight. The coalition moves west from Japanese Vladivostok through Chinese-owned Manchuria under a single command. Its local partner is the Siberian Regionalist government, initially under Pyotr Vologodsky, while Zhang Zuolin supplies the Chinese cooperation. A Pacifican railway board runs the line west of Chita. **[PROPOSED — CR-030]** Trained before the war, the board takes over the engines Pacifican works built for Russia and pays the railwaymen and the coal miners on time in sound money. It feeds their families from its own stores so that nobody leaves the line to look for bread. New loops, larger water mains and strengthened bridges on the single-track branch from Manchuria double its trains within a year. Three paths in ten stay with Siberian grain, coal and passengers: the railway half of the land-and-grain guarantee. **[PROPOSED — CR-031]** The board's worst enemy in 1919 is not the Red Army but the ataman at the junction, who holds its trains for payment and shoots whoever he calls a Bolshevik. Tokyo stops his subsidy, and that summer the Transbaikal Cossack circle meets at Chita with a Japanese diplomat in the hall. A frontline officer with his own St George's Cross moves that the Host recognise the Siberian government and put its regiments under the coalition. The ataman's officers walk out, the vote carries, and he leaves for Dairen on a Japanese pension. The Cossacks of the Onon and the Argun ride west to the Ob. Chinese ownership, Japanese running rights and common wartime administration keep the supply route usable without giving its territory to Japan.

The coalition fights for an independent Siberia, leaving Kolchak’s all-Russian ambition to overreach. **[PROPOSED]** As Omsk falls in late 1919 it takes its planned position behind the Ob at Novonikolayevsk. In the winter of 1919–1920 it defeats the Red Army’s attack across the frozen river. **[PROPOSED — CR-030]** The battle is prepared the summer before. While the line is free and the rivers are open, the depots behind the Ob are filled, barges come up the Amur and the Shilka to Sretensk, and the first Kara Sea convoy carries stores up the Ob and the Yenisei. In the battle the trains bring only what the depots cannot hold. The victory is settled; tactics and strengths remain proposed. A peasant land-and-grain guarantee supplies a political basis for holding the railway country. **[PROPOSED — CR-031]** The guarantee travels down the Lena. Yakutia keeps its own committees under Vasily Nikiforov, who founded the Union of Yakuts in 1906 and went to prison for it, and elects an assembly in 1919, and when Kolchak's officials are overthrown on the Okhotsk coast, at Anadyr and in Kamchatka that winter, relief ships and an amnesty answer them instead of a punitive column. Pacifica freezes the debt books of its own San Francisco traders in Chukotka until a commission can write them down. German clients in the west and Chinese cooperation prevent Moscow from concentrating its full strength in the east.

Moscow signs the Treaty of Harbin in 1921. Its name and year are settled; the detailed settlement remains **[PROPOSED]**. The Siberian Republic holds the country from the Ob to Lake Baikal, governed from Irkutsk with its Regional Duma at Tomsk. Japan already holds the Ussuri region, Vladivostok and Sakhalin; it gains a client sphere in Transbaikalia around Chita. **[PROPOSED — CR-031]** The sphere is the whole province from Baikal to the Argun: a council of Buryats, Cossacks and townsmen under a civilian Japanese Resident, with Japanese settlers, the Chernovsky coal and the Nerchinsk mines, and the junction of the line to Manchuria. Japan renounces the pan-Mongol schemes it once backed. The Cossack Host that turned out its ataman in 1919 sits in the council, and he stays in Dairen on his pension. **[APPROVED — CR-031]** The Siberian Republic extends to the Okhotsk coast west of Ola Bay and to Nikolayevsk. **[PROPOSED — CR-031]** It also holds Yakutia, Chukotka and the Arctic coast, with the islands Russia claimed in 1916 east of the Kara Sea. It is a federation more than a state: its constitution of 1922 makes Yakutia an autonomous Sakha land with its own assembly, language, communal land and a port at Okhotsk, at the same moment as Moscow's rival offer, and it governs the empty coast and Chukotka as a territory with a commissioner and a council of the districts and clans. The Ob becomes a shared river, and the straits into the Kara Sea stay open to merchant ships. **[APPROVED — CR-031]** Kamchatka and the Koryak coast as far as Ola Bay become a republic under Japanese protection. **[PROPOSED — CR-031]** Siberia never held them: every ship that reached Petropavlovsk sailed from Vladivostok, and in some summers the Japanese fishermen on the peninsula outnumbered everyone who lived there. When the Petropavlovsk council rose against Kolchak's governor it had no grain, and the relief ships that came were Japanese. Tokyo remembers Nikolayevsk, where partisans killed its garrison and residents in the spring of 1920 and burned the town. The army demanded the Amur coast in reprisal; the treaty gives satisfaction there instead, with a Siberian trial of the partisan leaders and an indemnity. The same massacre sends Kamchatka's frightened Russians to ask for Japanese protection, and Harbin recognises their republic and its Resident. On the Siberian coast a twenty-five-year convention gives Japanese boats the majority of the lots. Out of fairness, Pacifica insists that Siberian ships may pass the straits of a sea that is now Japanese on three sides. China secures the Amur and gains a sphere in Outer Mongolia and Tuva, with Siberian trade and settlement rights. **[PROPOSED — CR-031]** The treaty is signed in a Chinese city and gives China what Moscow had promised and would not have delivered. Russia's extraterritorial rights, its concessions and its share of the Boxer indemnity are renounced, the indemnity going to Chinese schools. Chinese ships may pass down the Amur to the sea, Mongolia returns to Chinese suzerainty under its own Mongol government, and the Manchurian railway returns to Chinese management, improved at the coalition's expense. Pacifica gains command of the standing alliance, its finance, the Lena gold concessions and the railway west of Chita. **[PROPOSED — CR-031]** It gives up the old San Francisco claims to Wrangel Island and the De Long islands, which lie west of its own 1867 Alaska line, and takes instead the Commander Islands, home of Aleuts moved there from the Aleutians a century before, with long leases for Arctic stations and a charter for the northern sea route. Thalassia repudiates a Kamchatka concession that Lenin signed with a Los Angeles engineer, and refuses to back a private colony on Wrangel Island.

Shared infrastructure, technical education and investment also lift the partners. Japan becomes the Pacific's second industrial power; the Gulf, Philippine crown and Siberia develop at different speeds and retain their distinct political statuses. **[PROPOSED — CR-031]** In 1927, the year of the Concord, Japan charters the Kamchatka Company, a national-policy company on the Manchurian model with a third of its shares in Pacifican hands. Its canneries and roads bring Japanese settlers to the peninsula, and it brings Karafuto's ways with them: bonded gangs in the work camps and Korean contract labourers, whose papers need Seoul's consent and Pacifica's. A year later the great gold strike comes not in Kamchatka but behind Ola Bay, on the Siberian side of the line, and the free miners on Pacifican dredges ship their gold out of Nagaevo within sight of the Company's quays. Thalassia signs the Korean papers and asks nothing about the camps. Returning graduates spread techniques as well as filling Pacifican posts. China, Korea and other trading regions gain more slowly through rail, power, schools and markets. Their growing demand feeds the champions, while dependence on Pacifican finance and standards gives the 1920s an anti-colonial undertow. Japanese national officers meanwhile organize Restoration circles against the imperial class.

22. **Resolved by CR-021 G, as amended by CR-029:** the Formosan Revenue Convention, Chinese commissions, revenue order, joint administration and technical schools; the Philippine purchase, its status before 1914 and the Philippine crown of 1914; the Pacific islands. All OPEN-029 entries are decided; the rite of the Manila accession follows B7.
23. **Northern Pacific sequence, resolved by CR-031:** Russia retains the northern coast until 1921. The Okhotsk coast west of Ola Bay, Nikolayevsk, Chukotka and the Arctic islands east of the Kara Sea then pass to the Siberian Republic, with Okhotsk to the Sakha land; Kamchatka and the Koryak coast become a republic under Japanese protection. Japan retains its southern gains and the Transbaikalian protectorate and holds the majority of the Siberian coast's fishing lots by convention; Siberian ships pass the straits. The Commander Islands and the Arctic leases go to Pacifica. Detailed survey mapping is an implementation task; a fortification freeze is **[OPEN-031-11]**.
24. **CR-016 implementation:** OPEN-016-04 is resolved by Noe’s approved biography and contested evidence; the uncertainty is culpability. The regency, adoption, life offices and constitutional designation are fixed by CR-021. Silas's family and date, Donner responsibility and the 1888 restriction are decided by CR-022; the Vance arc retains its qualifications; Soberanes’s unspecified early biography and service remain qualified.

requests.title: Settlement, Native recovery and the shape of Pacifica's population
requests.authorization: Author request of 28 October 2026 to merge CR-033 to CR-036 in order and update the documentation, after decisions recorded in the decision record; drafts reviewed in fresh context before adoption.
requirements: The gold rush settles rather than passes through: light licences, assisted passage of women and families, secure titles, Pacific shipping and Americans moving west. About 1.2 million people at the start of 1861 (MODEL).

No mass killing of Native Californians: disease reduces them to about two-thirds of their 1848 number by the later 1890s, and they grow again under fair treatment, keeping a health gap. Whatever the Republic does for them must also pay for the Republic.

The Republic is the sole lawful buyer of Native land. Treaties of 1851–52 reserve homelands under a three-part compact: reserved homeland leased only through the Republic, ceded land bought by deed against annuities in goods, and the Republic as trustee collecting rents for a fee with published accounts.

A Land Fund kept apart from the revenues pledged to London pays the annuities from settlers' instalments; its margin helps pay for assisted passage (about 47% in the workbook). Militia service is paid in land warrants good only on bought land. The public register is the title; old grants are confirmed by survey against a fee in land; squatters buy on instalments.
Land still leaves Native hands through long leases, assigned annuity claims and court rulings, with a fee to the Realm on every lease.

Japanese immigration predominates over Chinese from the 1900s; Filipino migration is mostly after 1914. Population figures in the prose follow the workbook of 28 October 2026 (MODEL): about 5.6 million Japanese-origin and 4.8 million Chinese-origin Pacificans and about 36 million people in 1932.

Whether the Native turn of the later 1890s hangs on a named event; names of the commissioners, the act and the compact.

requests.title: Science: the scholars Europe would not promote, two elements, and the world that loses them

The colleges' purposes: Yerba Buena College for pure science and finance, the Sutro School for the deep earth and heat, the Colegio de Santa Fe for the interior and the treaties; the interior has prestigious schools and advances of its own, including Deseret's irrigation science.

requests.title: No cliques: keeping the examination state's institutions open
requests.authorization: Author, 28 October 2026: "I approve the county rule and the proposed changes from CR-037. You can go ahead and merge them into main."
requirements: Pacifica stops any ethnic or religious group from capturing an institution by favouring its own; the rules apply to every group alike. The test is the examination, never a quota.

From the late 1870s Soberanes's examinations use numbered, recopied scripts; examiners never judge candidates from their own state or college; first postings are away from home; appointment boards include outsiders.

From 1888 the Office publishes appointments against the examination lists for every chartered body, college and licensed profession; persistent gaps bring audits; officials declare relatives and former students. The first great audit (1890) falls on an established mixed clique on the savings and development bank's board, and Victoria refuses both to stop it and to set quotas.

Counties may be culturally concentrated and are measured against their own pass lists. A passed-over rate below two-thirds of the best-placed group over five years, or one family, marriage network or congregation holding more than a third of senior posts, counts against the order standard; treasurer, auditor, examiner and chief of police are posted from outside by the Office, in rotation.
The Japanese naval party's reserved squadron stays, with its critics, until the 1932 renewal.

requests.title: The machinery's own safeguards
requests.authorization: Author decisions of 28 October 2026, ending: "For CR-038, yes they should get freedom above the central minimum. Please forgive my typo. I approve of the names and the lists of the grants."
requirements: Retirement at 68 for every senator, judge, county Commissioner, estate head and senior officer; the Constitution sets it for appointed senators and the regency extends it. Only the Crown, the Regent and the Truce's named holders are exempt.

Vallejo College at Monterey from 1889: one academic year for rising officers of every estate, the navy, the champions and the counties, with no restriction by sex; free choice produces two informal sides, the Presidio (engineering, technology, management; the Carquinez men) and the Kaʻahumanu House (health, welfare, education).
The Office's unannounced inspectors check county returns against figures hard to fake.

From 1888, Realm scholarships (five years' work anywhere in Pacifica, League teaching included) and posted grants (five years in the named post only); senior pay set by the Senate against the champions' managers' pay and published.
County halls under a Realm enabling law, held by an Office inspector and trustees to a central minimum, free above it, fostering cohesion and results-based pride in Pacifica.
Hawaii abolishes penal labour contracts on joining the Confederation in 1856; works crews hire on fixed terms from the 1860s; the general guest-worker programme stays in 1890.

A trades congress chartered by law in 1895 keeps funds, the tradesmen's register and a reference wage table; it never hires, trains or pays; independent unions stay legal; guest workers reach it only through its Guest Workers' Aid.

The Federal Republic of the Gulf is founded in 1900, the year the canal opens; the Gulf compact is signed at its founding and sets the admission tests from the start. No Gulf compact in 1895.

As Mōʻī he takes the harbour back into the Hawaiian crown; the fleet stays as the crown's tenant at the Mōʻī's pleasure, renewed at each accession. requests.title: The crown of 1907, the failed peace and the Russian war
requests.authorization: Author, 28 October 2026: "I want like a combination of A and D … it starts out with Julian's earlier coronation, his Europe tour, and trying to prevent war in Europe. The European powers, in their stubbornness, still end up dragging everyone in the world into World War I, which leads to the Bolshevik Revolution, the Red Terror, and Julian and his Pacifica coalition having to invade and ultimately arrest Lenin, Trotsky, and Stalin." On the 1905 war: the Kiyoshi confrontation and naval battle "should also be a part of the major CR-040 rework". Second round: "R2 - renounce … R3 - 1916 after daughters is ok … R4 - approved … R6 - approve R7 - approve R8 - arrested, tried and execute for state crimes (of which they were guilty) R11 - Federal Russia … R13 - Ka Lokahi keeps its ten year review cycle, agrees on Japan joining". K1: "I think this is the stronger version and it really provides a satisfying conclusion to Kiyoshi's biography." Third round: "Yes I approve r5 - makes Julian more human, which is good. F1 as well. R13 also. The supercession table is also approved."
requirements: Kiyoshi's May 1905 victory is over Russia's Petropavlovsk cruiser squadron (one cruiser taken, two damaged); Russia's battle fleets survive and Russia turns west.
Silas renounces in December 1906, for himself and his descendants; he still confesses Donner in autumn 1912 and dies in winter 1912.
Kiyoshi claims early in 1907 as count and squadron commander, renounces in March 1907, and becomes Fleet-General in the later 1907 renewal.
The Act of Settlement of 1907 joins the crowns; Julian accedes to the Realm and Hawaii in November 1907, marries Chiyo that month and swears before the Cortes in December 1907.
Kahekili is born about 1916, after daughters.
Ka Lōkahi forms in 1907, reviews in 1917 and 1927; its 1927 review agrees that Japan joins, binding the Hawaiian and Philippine crowns but not the Realm without the Senate.
Julian tours Europe from 1908 and helps settle Bosnia (1909), Agadir (1911) and the Balkan wars (1912–1913).

July 1914 fails: Franz Ferdinand's death, Vienna's anger at the procedures, Berlin's fear of a westward Russia, Julian's shelved Black Hand warning and his withheld oil sanction; Zimmermann receives his envoy on 5 July.

Stages 3–4 (integrated 29 October 2026 with CR-041): Red Terror hostages and the Office's lists (R6); Lenin taken by a coalition armoured train (R7); Lenin and Trotsky tried and executed for state crimes (R8); federal Russia (R11); Kiyoshi takes Kronstadt by stratagem, kills Stalin and dies in May 1920 (K1).
open: The tour and Bosnia/Agadir/Balkan details remain PROPOSED; the indemnity of 1905 needs remodelling.
K1 details: the boatswain's mate, Kiyoshi's sword, a death poem.

CR-041 (29 October 2026) supersedes, for Stages 3–4: the Ob crossing of January 1920 (Vance holds the Volga bridge at Zelenodolsk in June 1919), the form of the 10 September 1918 recognition (ratification of the July treaty), the mechanism of the 1919 bargain (a promised vote, delivered at Tomsk in 1921), and 'Omsk falls to the Red Army'. Apply both together.

requests.title: The Russian war re-planned: one summer, one winter (Plan C), the tri-partite Siberian treaty and the Tomsk vote
requests.authorization: Author, 29 October 2026, in the planning session on CR-040 Stages 3–4: "I like the shape of Napoleon's plan much better than the one currently in the timeline. What it still needs is the Russian partner." On the three timetables: "Ok I approve of C. Can you update the battle timeline accordingly?" On the decisions: "Bring them into the new CR and let's decide on all of them right now." "For N10 I would like a Hawaiian name. For N13 b." On N6 after the Alash documents: "I approve. You can add it into the CR just like that (the more detailed version of shape C). Pacifica keeps the oil from Emba and should get favorable conditions in Baku as well." The Baku share is joint with Britain at the drafter's recommendation, accepted by the author's instruction to write it up. Inherited items S1–S9 and new items N1–N16 are approved as recorded in CR-041.md; the Ukraine, Bessarabia and Turkish-frontier sectors remain OPEN. Integration review (29 October 2026) moved the signing to 4–6 August 1918 so that it follows the commission draft it adopts.
requirements: Pacifica seizes the Siberian line in one week from 26 May 1918 with the Legion's rising as trigger; no declaration of war; the stated objectives are the Entente's. The recognition of a state of war with the Council of People's Commissars comes in September 1918 after the hostage-taking.

Kazan is held in September 1918 (second battle, Pacifican river flotilla and a brigade); the Volga is the coalition's line through the winter of 1918–19; the Perm wing reaches Glazov and cuts the Vologda–Vyatka line at Kotelnich in January 1919.

The Siberian treaty is signed at Omsk on 4 August and Samara on 6 August 1918 by Komuch, the Provisional Siberian Government and Alash Orda under Pacifican guarantee, built on Komuch's Alash declaration and the Sapozhnikov–Bukeikhanov draft of 29 July–3 August 1918, printed by the Office and deposited in Peking and Tokyo; Julian ratifies it publicly on 10 September 1918 after the Romanov discovery and the Terror decree.

Komuch's credit is conditional on enforcing the Constituent Assembly's land law without landlord reclamation. The Omsk coup of 18 November 1918 is attempted and fails in one night; the Directory survives; Kolchak declines the title, refuses the Baltic under Kiyoshi in 1919 and becomes federal Russia's navy minister after Harbin.

The Red spring offensive of 1919 is spent on the Volga: Vance holds the Volga bridge at Zelenodolsk in June 1919 while the trains clear (replacing the Ob crossing of January 1920, which is deleted). Omsk never falls. Wrangel takes the southern command in October 1919 when Denikin stalls at Orel and takes his guns from the Directory's hand.

The 1920 sequence is unchanged: Tula in February; Trotsky taken at the Oka bridge at Serpukhov by Kutepov's troops and the armoured train Ofitser; Moscow in March; Petrograd by land; Lenin taken on the Vologda–Vyatka line at the Kotelnich bridge by the Pacifican armoured train Māui; Kronstadt in May (CR-040 K1).

The 1919 bargain's mechanism: Wrangel's price is the unity of Russia including Siberia; since the treaty is signed, Julian promises to deliver Siberia's own vote and does so in 1921, when the Siberian Regional Duma at Tomsk votes to enter the federal compact under the guarantor's credit, Office and paymaster. Nobody puts the question to Alash: the Alash–Siberia union of 1918 is dissolved and Alash becomes a land of Russia without being asked. Victoria's charge gains the count that he asked one people and not the other.

Oil: Pacifica keeps the Emba (Dossor) concession from 1918; Grozny and Maikop concessions come from Wrangel's government against the reconstruction credit; Baku is a joint Anglo-Pacifican concession with Azerbaijan under Entente guarantee, Pacifica operating, Britain strategic.

Kiyoshi's Baltic squadron: Izumo (flag), Nisshin, Akashi, twelve Japanese destroyers retained in European waters in spring 1919, with two Pacifican turbine cruisers, six destroyers, minesweepers, a seaplane tender, motor torpedo boats and a landing force; winter base Reval and Libau; enters the Kronstadt roads at the end of April 1920.

Southern border shape C: Don, Kuban and Terek as federal lands of Russia; Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan independent under Entente guarantee; Turkestan a federal land of Russia; the eastern Donbas Russian.
Ballin's death on 9 November 1918 is a one-line beat; no Soviet state survives 1920; Nikolayevsk and the Kamchatka concession stand as drafted.
open: Which Ukraine (Hetmanate or Directory) and the Black Sea coast; Bessarabia; Kars, Ardahan and Batum.
What Alash keeps inside Russia after 1921 beyond courts and the kibitka tax; the fate of its regiments.

The hostages of 1918: how many railway advisers shot, and the one the reader has met. Who from Thalassia attends the Romanov burial. Where Kiyoshi's sword rests; a death poem. The day of Lenin's capture and the name of the Pacifican commander at Kotelnich. Whether the Tomsk vote is shown or reported.

VERIFY before integration: Legion day-dates for Omsk, Samara, Krasnoyarsk and Vladivostok; Kolchak's October 1917 departure from San Francisco; the Tomsk Duma dispersal of 26 January 1918; Ironside's Kotlas plan; the Red recapture of Ufa on 9 June 1919; the Romanov Bridge name; Mikhailov's role in the coup; Boldyrev's refusal of Kolchak; Krivoshein in Kyiv in late 1918; the Provisional Siberian Government's declaration of 4 July 1918.

requests.title: Huludao: a door of Pacifica's own at the end of the Chinese line
requests.authorization: Author, 30 October 2026: "The Dairen (Dalian) question ties into Victoria's proposed friendship with Cixi, which is still unexplored. I would suggest that it remain Chinese thanks to Victoria's negotiations. The ataman then goes to Urajio on a Japanese pension. I would say that the Harbin-Mukden line does exist, at least by 1912, in this timeline. Huludao works fine as a port and I think it makes sense to buy it early on. … Let's leave Japan's reaction to this specific event off page for now." Then: "I approve the change as a split (pledge and option in 1898–99, trust in 1908–10). Let's leave the Victoria Cixi scene for a later edit. Please write this up as a short CR" and "Ok please merge this CR". Then (H6): "Seeing as the financing and construction of the Mukden–Jinzhou–Huludao line occurred around 1908-1910, it would make sense that the venture was jointly British and Pacifican in this timeline, perhaps with Britain as the senior partner. The idea could have been discussed during Julian's visit to England."
requirements: H1: Dalian and Port Arthur stay Chinese in the settlement of 1898–99 through Victoria's negotiation with the Empress Dowager; Russia does not get Port Arthur and Japan takes no mainland harbour. Dalian keeps its Chinese name.

H2: China pledges that no part of the Liaodong Gulf coast will be leased or ceded to any power and gives Pacifica first refusal on a harbour at Huludao; Pacifica takes nothing in the year of Kiaochow.

H3: In 1909 Julian exercises the option as the Huludao Harbour Trust, chartered under a Qing commission on the Keelung pattern (Pacifican director and engineers, San Francisco bonds secured on the harbour dues, Chinese sovereignty, customs and police); works begin in 1910 and go on through the revolution; the Republic confirms the commission.
H4: A Chinese line runs from Harbin through Changchun to Mukden by 1912.

H6: The railway from Mukden past Jinzhou to Huludao is built in 1908–1910 by a British and Pacifican syndicate with Britain the senior partner, first discussed in London on Julian's visit of 1908; the bondholders hold the line's receipts.
H5: The Transbaikal ataman retires to Urajio on his Japanese pension, not Dairen.
Japan's reaction to the trust stays off the page; the Victoria–Cixi scenes are a later edit.
open: Who builds and finances the Harbin–Mukden line (the 1896 Pacifican credit is the natural source).
Japan's reaction to the trust (off the page by author decision).
The Victoria–Cixi scenes.
Huludao's winter ice conditions (VERIFY before canon calls it ice-free).
